#5440. CZ Fires Back at Binance Dump Claims as Vitalik Bullish on Ethereum Quantum Upgrade

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Two of the industry’s most influential figures are pushing back against very different concerns. Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao, known as CZ, has rejected accusations that the exchange sold crypto during the latest market crash. Meanwhile, Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin is backing a faster approach to protecting the network against future quantum computing threats.

Their comments arrive as crypto suffers a sharp correction, leveraged traders absorb billions in liquidations, and Ethereum developers reconsider how quickly the network should prepare for a post-quantum future.

Changpeng Zhao has directly rejected speculation that Binance contributed to the latest cryptocurrency sell-off by selling digital assets.

“No, Binance did not sell crypto,” CZ wrote in a post on X.

Instead, the former Binance CEO said he had personally been buying crypto after receiving stablecoins over the past few days.

His response came as Bitcoin plunged toward $62,000, marking its lowest level since July. The wider market experienced approximately $2.02 billion in liquidations over a 24-hour period, with long positions accounting for $1.68 billion.

CZ also offered several possible explanations for the market weakness, including institutional ETF outflows, expectations of another Federal Reserve rate hike, security concerns, and investors potentially moving capital toward Anthropic’s anticipated IPO.

Why are crypto prices down?No one knows for sure. Correlation does not prove causation. Here are some potential reasons.Money shifting to the Anthropic IPO: https://t.co/jYwVi4huAYETF outflows: U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.9 billion in outflows over seven trading… pic.twitter.com/XL2aB1ZL9W

U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $1.91 billion in net outflows across seven consecutive trading sessions through November 13. Spot Ether ETFs also suffered $398.9 million in weekly withdrawals.

The Binance selling allegations carry particular weight following the exchange’s October 29 security breach, but CZ public denial provides a clear counterargument to speculation that exchange selling accelerated the market decline.

His personal buying comments also show that he sees the current weakness differently from traders rushing to exit their positions. Defending the exchange’s reputation during a period of market stress is becoming just as important as explaining the direction of crypto prices.

While CZ is addressing immediate market concerns, Vitalik Buterin is looking much further ahead.

The Ethereum co-founder has dramatically changed his assessment of leanPCS, a proposed cryptographic technique designed to make Ethereum more resistant to quantum computing attacks.

“Over the past few weeks I’ve gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull,” Buterin wrote on X.

Over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail.At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data…

The statement shows growing confidence in an approach that could help Ethereum introduce quantum-resistant cryptography without dramatically increasing transaction costs and blockchain storage requirements.

The proposal, outlined in EIP-8288, focuses on combining individual digital signatures and cryptographic proofs into a shared mathematical proof. This is good for Ethereum because quantum-resistant signatures can be considerably larger than the cryptographic signatures Ethereum currently uses.

A standard Ethereum signature occupies approximately 65 bytes. Some proposed quantum-resistant alternatives could require between 1,000 and 6,000 bytes. Storing those larger signatures individually could consume substantial block space, potentially increasing network costs.

LeanPCS attempts to solve that problem by allowing computers to aggregate multiple signatures and verification checks before submitting a compact proof to Ethereum. Rather than permanently storing every bulky signature individually, the network could verify a shared proof covering multiple transactions.

Buterin favors this approach because it could provide a practical route toward quantum resistance without requiring Ethereum to commit immediately to a much larger architectural redesign.

Ethereum’s quantum preparation is already underway, with the Ethereum Foundation targeting 2029 for core post-quantum infrastructure milestones. The potential threat remains years away, but Ethereum developers increasingly recognize that replacing cryptographic foundations requires considerable preparation.

CZ and Buterin are confronting different problems, but both developments highlight the pressures facing the crypto industry. Binance needs to maintain market confidence while investors question exchange activity, security, and institutional capital flows.

Ethereum needs to strengthen its cryptographic foundations before quantum computing potentially threatens the security assumptions underlying today’s blockchain infrastructure.

CZ’s comments offer reassurance during an immediate market downturn, while Buterin’s endorsement could accelerate an important technical discussion within Ethereum.

#5439. Anne Hathaway Welcomes Her Third Child with Husband Adam Schulman

Congratulations are in order for Anne Hathaway and her husband, Adam Schulman. It appears the couple has welcomed their third child, after "The Devil Wears Prada" actress was spotted with a newborn in New York City on Nov. 17.

The photos, shared first by TMZ, depict Hathaway, 44, strolling around her hometown with a friend, and an infant snuggled up into a baby carrier.

The actress first shared news of her pregnancy in June, revealing a growing baby bump in an Instagram video captioned, "Baby, I'm yours."

Together, Hathaway and Schulman already have two sons: Jonathan Rosebanks Shulman, 10, and Jack Shulman, 7.

Shortly after sharing the news, Hathaway appeared on "Late Night with Seth Meyers," and said that so far, the experience of a third pregnancy had been "amazing."

She noted that she and her jewelry designer husband were surprised to learn they had another bundle of joy on the way.

"I mean, we knew what we were doing, but we were so shocked it worked," she revealed on the talk show. "We were so shocked it went this way, so we're calling this one our buzzer-beater," she joked.

According to a People magazine source, up until the announcement, Hathaway had worked diligently to keep the news of her pregnancy a secret during "The Devil Wears Prada 2" press tour.

"She wanted to reveal the pregnancy on her own terms. The press tour was about celebrating the movie and getting fans excited to see it," shared the source.

Press tours for "Verity" and "The Odyssey" have kept Hathaway busy shortly in the time since, but according to the source, she was able to "focus on family" and soak up "a little downtime" in the time between the films.

"She's grateful for where she is in her career and for the opportunity to be part of a film that means so much to so many people. Complaining just isn't Anne. She approaches things with gratitude and professionalism, and that's exactly how she handled the press tour," the source added.

Although Hathaway is a longtime New Yorker who originally hailed from New Jersey, the family primarily resides in an Ojai, CA home the couple purchased for $3.6 million in 2014.

The couple told Architectural Digest that it was a love at first sight situation with the property, and they knew they had to have it from the moment they first viewed it... even if it needed a handful of updates.

"It was the ideal combination of romance and great design," Hathaway said. "Our initial instinct was that this was going to be a very important place in our lives. I could really see raising a family here."

The 3,400-square foot home has a gorgeous Swiss chalet-inspired aesthetic that's been customized after the couple spent years renovating the home.

According to a previous listing, the home had four bedrooms and four bedrooms before it was purchased. However, records indicate that Hathaway and Schulman also purchased a parcel of land directly next to the property, so there's a good chance they may have expanded.

Based on baby's first public outing, it appears as though they may be splitting their time between the Sunshine State and the East Coast.

The "Princess Diaries" actress has previously shared glimpses of her personal life, explaining that she really lives for simple pleasures.

"I still get the paper delivered every day and I love sitting down with it," she told People magazine in an interview for her "World's Most Beautiful" cover story.

She explained that on a slow day, she loves cuddling with the family's new puppy, and finding time to speak to loved ones.

"I'm always zipping from one thing to another," she admitted. "I'd love to have breakfast with a friend. I'd love to go for a walk, maybe do a little window-shopping, maybe go to a museum. I'm very meandering on my days off."

In the interview, she also shared her appreciation for Schulman, noting that he "supports" her "completely," especially in a year as busy as the one she's having now.

"I'm so lucky that he's my partner that I spend my life with. If I didn't know that before this past year, I think I really know it know because with absolutely everything, he's just, he's on it. He holds it down," she gushed. "I hope that doesn't sound like I'm bragging, but he's a dream partner to me."

#5438. Exclusive: Cogent Security’s DefenseOS adds policies and automations for AI agents

Vulnerability management startup Cogent Security Inc. today launched DefenseOS, an operating system designed for artificial intelligence agents that carry out defensive cybersecurity work inside the enterprise.

Arriving with DefenseOS are two new capabilities, Agent Policies and Agent Automations. The first is designed to give Cogent’s AI agents a deep understanding of the enterprise environment, while the second puts recurring security work on an automated schedule.

Cogent is pitching DefenseOS at security teams that are struggling to keep up as AI speeds up the discovery of vulnerabilities. In October, Microsoft Corp. fixed more than 1,400 security flaws in a single Patch Tuesday release, more than it fixed in all of 2025. The window between disclosure and exploitation has also shrunk, by Cogent’s count, from months in 2024 to only hours this year.

Prioritizing at that pace requires context such as which assets are business-critical, which are exposed to the internet and who owns them. According to the company, that information is spread across documents, teams and tribal knowledge, and most organizations see only a fraction of it.

In its role as the context engine for Cogent, DefenseOS ingests data from scanners, business systems and other security tools. Once the data has been normalized and deduplicated, DefenseOS encodes how the enterprise functions to deliver accurate risk scoring, prioritization and remediation. The platform serves as the AI harness that sets the working environment and limits for Cogent’s agents.

The first of the two new capabilities, Agent Policies, is described by Cogent as creating a context layer that builds and grows via agents, turning how an enterprise works into rules. Those rules then shape how the Cogent platform handles asset context, risk scoring, prioritization and remediation. The company claims the feature strips out much of the operational overhead that enterprises formerly had to put into running a vulnerability management program.

The second, Agent Automations, acts as the execution layer within DefenseOS. Using it, security teams can build agentic workflows that run automatically to generate alerts and reports, investigate vulnerabilities and deliver remediation guidance on a consistent basis.

Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Geng Sng said recurring reports, known investigations and routine alerts take up a large share of a security team’s week. With Agent Automations, he said, teams can “define that work once” and have Cogent’s agents run it on their schedule.

“Every enterprise runs its security program differently, and moving at machine speed means grasping those differences,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Vineet Edupuganti. “DefenseOS unifies the context of an enterprise environment, surfacing rules into Agent Policies that a customer can codify, and creating the runtime environment for continuous cyber defense led by AI agents.”

The launch follows the release earlier this month of VR-1.1, a new version of Cogent’s frontier reasoning model that writes fixes for newly disclosed software vulnerabilities.

DefenseOS and Agent Automations are available now to all Cogent customers. Agent Policies has launched in beta for new Cogent deployments ahead of general availability at a later date.

Founded in 2025 and staffed by former researchers and operators from Google DeepMind, Abnormal AI Inc. and Coinbase Global Inc., Cogent says Fortune 500 security teams using its platform have cut the exposure window for critical vulnerabilities by 97%. The company has raised $53 million to date, including a $42 million Series A led by Bain Capital Ventures in February.

#5437. This Week Brings a Chance for Clarity After Mortgage Rates Rise on Hot Inflation and Hawkish Fed Remarks

Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of big news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

The Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5436. Exceeding Expectations Every Step of the Way

Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Starck Real Estate

Most important thing you learned this past year: The value of recognizing and drawing out the potential in others, sometimes before they even see it in themselves.

Who has most influenced your success? My father, Andy, who led the company for nearly 40 years. I consider it a privilege and a blessing to have been able to work and learn alongside him.

As a third-generation member of your family’s real estate firm, how do you honor the firm’s legacy while bringing your own perspective and ideas to the business?

We consider ourselves a family business made up of family businesses, so inherent in that is a sense of responsibility to the people and the families we serve. And so it’s a stewardship of what has been entrusted, not only to me, but to everyone in our company. The more we grow and find success, the more we’re able to invest in our agents and give in meaningful ways to charitable organizations and the communities we serve.

What is the most valuable lesson you’ve learned from the previous generations of your family who worked in the business?

The firm was founded by my grandparents on the values of service to others over ourselves and doing business with complete truth and integrity, which is part of the reputation we’ve worked hard to build over the last 66-plus years. While we firmly believe that good things happen when you treat others the way you would want to be treated, we take it above and beyond the Golden Rule to the Platinum Rule, which is treating others the way they want to be treated. Taking that one step further, our focus is on providing double platinum experiences—or exceeding expectations in order to treat others in a way they can’t even conceive.

What factor has the largest influence on the real estate industry today?

Distractions, particularly the technology in our pockets, which brings to mind the following Robin Sharma quote: “The enemy of mastery is not mediocrity. It is distractions. The addiction to distractions ruins many potentially awesome lives.” We’re privileged to work in this noble profession, which will always be a relationship-based business. Technology can be a wonderful tool when it’s used properly, but we believe that focusing on relationships and service is the best way to build a sustainable business that’s successful in any market.

How does your company make its agents’ jobs easier?

We operate on the belief that we only succeed as a company when our agents succeed, so we’re passionate about providing value and support so that their businesses and families can thrive. That means saving them time or making their jobs easier by taking things off their plate so that they can focus on doing the things only they can do. Another core thing we talk a lot about is the go-giver mindset, which is rooted in the idea that when you give and give and then give some more, good things happen.

As we approach the end of 2026 and head into a new year, what are you most looking forward to?

Our business is constantly changing, so it’s all about embracing that and looking forward to how we’re going to grow and get better while at the same time serving our agents better. It’s all about controlling what we can control. I’m optimistic about the future.

#5435. Semperis updates Lightning identity security platform to defend against AI agent attacks

Enterprise identity protection and cyber resilience company Semperis Ltd. today released the latest version of its Semperis Lightning identity security platform, which is designed to help organizations defend against identity attacks by artificial intelligence agents and conventional attackers alike.

Delivered through a single console, the new version of Lightning is said to combine exposure management, attack-path analysis and detection-and-response workflows. Along with Microsoft Corp.’s Active Directory and Entra ID, the new release supports Okta Inc.

Semperis says organizations using Lightning can adopt AI tools for productivity while reducing the risk of agents compromising critical resources. According to Chief Executive Mickey Bresman, identity systems have become “the main control plane” in the agentic age.

Though AI agents move at machine speed through the enterprise, Bresman said, they still depend on the identity fabric for access. With Lightning, organizations are said to be able to create, enforce and monitor what he called “agentic execution boundaries.”

Chief Product Officer Alex Weinert, who joined Semperis in April 2025 after serving as vice president of identity security at Microsoft, said security teams “do not need another flat list of identity findings.” Context on what can actually reach the identity control plane is what they need instead, he said. Agentic identities, he added, are opening new routes to privileged systems.

On the exposure side, Lightning, which now comes with a growing catalog of more than 220 security indicators, continuously scans identity infrastructure for exposures in human and nonhuman identities. The results are then scored, according to Semperis, before being triaged in a single workflow.

The platform’s live identity graph, which Semperis describes as a map of relationships and attack paths, covers routes to domain administrators, privileged accounts and other critical assets. According to the company, remediation guidance from the graph is prioritized by risk so that teams can respond faster.

Nonhuman and agentic identities are discovered automatically, Semperis says, and added to a searchable inventory of every identity in an environment. The company claims Lightning can scale to the largest multitenant, multiforest environments.

Built-in rule templates are designed to detect suspicious activity in Active Directory and Entra ID, such as unusual logons over Kerberos and NT LAN Manager. The company is also offering what it calls generative assistance alongside the templates.

Semperis introduced Lightning in April 2024 with Lightning Identity Runtime Protection, a machine learning-powered identity threat detection service. The company extended its resilience offerings to Okta and Ping Identity Corp. environments in February, when it acquired MightyID Inc.

More than 1,200 organizations, including over 25% of the 100 largest U.S. companies, are said to use Semperis. The company last raised $125 million in growth financing from JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Hercules Capital Inc. in June 2024. Earlier investors include Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co. LP, Insight Partners, Ten Eleven Ventures and Paladin Capital Group.

#5434. Daniel Craig Stepped Away From James Bond Role To Spend More Time at Home

Daniel Craig first stepped into the role of James Bond 20 years ago, and now, he has officially passed the duties along to someone new: Robert Pattinson.

Craig made his 007 debut in the 2006 film “Casino Royale” and held the legendary gig for 15 years. He had originally planned to play the British spy for four films, but ended up having a successful five-movie run with “Quantum Solace” (2008), “Skyfall” (2012), “Spectre” (2015), and “No Time To Die” (2021).

In addition to filming one more motion picture than he had planned, Craig, 58, has spoken out about how physically demanding it is to be James Bond. In the time between the last two films, he told The Sunday Times he was “getting old.”

“I’m creaky,” he admitted in the 2019 interview. In 2024, he told The New York Times, “I find it really hard, this job, and it gets harder as I get older.”

Beyond the grueling stunts and action required for each installment, the role demanded a huge time commitment that pulled Craig away from his family.

“The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo” star married actress Rachel Weisz in June 2011 in an intimate New York ceremony. Together, they welcomed a daughter named Grace in September 2018.

Craig also has an older daughter, Ella Loudon, 34, whom he shares with his first wife, Fiona Loudon. He’s also a stepfather to Weisz’s son, Henry Aronfsky, 20, from her former relationship with filmmaker Darren Aronofsky.

Although Craig has said that he’s “not a method actor,” he described himself as a “nightmare to be with” while he’s working.

“I want to go home and forget it all and just be normal and be like, 'Hey, family,' but half my brain’s at work,” he said. But having a young daughter at home has changed his approach to his career.

“I don’t want to be away from home as much as I have in the past,” he explained.

Craig and Weisz, who both hail from England, have called New York home for quite some time.

In April of this year, they sold their Brooklyn brownstone for $11.8 million. They had picked it up for $6.75 million in 2018.

Built in 1901, the 6,600-square-foot abode spans five levels, which are accessible by elevator. It included a roof deck, a patio, and a backyard garden.

The six-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom residence was damaged by a fire in 2016, before the couple snapped it up. According to Architectural Digest, the previous owner, novelist Martin Amis, had transformed the home into a “clean, blank slate” in light of the damage, and Craig and Weisz put their own spin on it in the nearly eight years they lived there.

The off-market transaction came just a year after the couple sold an adjacent townhouse for $4.05 million.

They still hold ties to the Empire State, with an upstate retreat in Marbletown, NY, that Weisz purchased for $2.1 million in 2008. Nestled on an idyllic 124-acre parcel, the 2,500-square-foot stone home dates to 1785 and includes four bedrooms and three bathrooms.

Overseas, Craig and Weisz have a $4.2 million Victorian mansion in a conservation area in North London. It was a home the “Vladimir” actress had purchased before they were married.

According to the Daily Mail, they sought to heavily renovate the 1840 home in 2023, but had to alter their plans when an objection claimed the proposal would clash with the home’s original style. The renovation was ultimately approved in 2024.

#5433. Spara’s Scout AI assistant acts on sales opportunities before reps know to look

Artificial intelligence sales agent startup Spara Inc. today introduced Scout, an AI assistant designed to act on sales opportunities before salespeople know to look for them.

Working around the clock, the new service analyzes context from customer conversations, emails and customer relationship management data to identify opportunities, prepare personalized outreach and complete work before reps realize it needs doing.

Scout is aimed at addressing a limitation of most AI assistants, which still require users to tell them what to do, according to Spara. The service instead works within the daily workflows of salespeople, providing an always-on partner that keeps track of customers and helps move work forward without constant direction.

Signals analyzed continuously by Scout include job changes, company news, buying signals and CRM activity across a salesperson’s accounts. From there, the service determines when to engage customers and prospects, as well as who to contact. Instead of requiring another platform to manage, Scout delivers its findings through Salesforce Inc.’s Slack and text messages.

Over time, Scout retains what it learns about each account, along with the salesperson’s preferences and previous outreach. Doing so is said to allow the service to anticipate next steps and deliver more relevant recommendations.

Outreach messages are drafted in the salesperson’s voice, with reps kept in control of what gets sent. Going beyond recommendations, Scout can join customer calls and contribute to conversations in real time, helping salespeople move opportunities forward.

“Sales has always been a game of speed, timing and relationships, but there’s only so much one person can keep track of in a day,” said David Walker, co-founder and chief executive of Spara. “Even the best sales organizations can’t realistically give every rep the support they need to act on every opportunity at exactly the right moment.”

Spara also released early results from users of the new service. Salespeople using Scout were found to have increased the number of personalized emails sent eightfold in their first two weeks of use. Outreach generated by Scout drew a 10.5% reply rate, against 3.5% for traditional sales sequences, according to the company. Early users also booked 29% more meetings.

Chris Brown, a partner at Spara investor Inspired Capital who has worked with the team since the beginning, said Spara has built agents that go-to-market teams trust with their most important customer conversations. Scout is now “putting that trust to work for individual sellers,” he added.

Scout is available for free starting today at spara.com/scout.

Founded by Walker and Zander Pease, Spara offers a platform for building AI agents that carry out sales work across chat, email, text messaging, voice and interactive product demos. The agents handle tasks ranging from engaging and qualifying leads to following up with prospects, booking meetings and managing renewals. Notable customers include Justworks Inc., Rho Technologies Inc. and Mindbody Inc.

Spara launched in September 2025 with $15 million in seed funding. Including additional funding since then, the company has raised $20 million to date, with Radical Ventures and Inspired Capital leading the seed round.

#5432. Engel & Völkers sets sights on Aruba as brokerages add agents

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

Brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into new markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it plans to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, said in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

Rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the company.

Jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

Howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the company.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter said in a statement.

#5431. Exclusive: Envoy targets defense contractors and semiconductor fabs with Visitors Critical

Workplace management platform company Envoy Inc. today launched Visitors Critical, a new tier of its visitor management service for defense contractors, semiconductor fabs and other high-security sites.

The new tier is aimed at a problem Envoy says is common at those sites, where visitor security is still run across email, spreadsheets and separate systems and letting the wrong person in can be costly. Penalties, debarment or a lost facility clearance are all possible after a wrong entry at a compliance-driven site. The person who signed the authorization can also be held liable, according to the company, which noted that settlements under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations have reached $51 million.

“We’ve spent the last 13 years building Envoy to deliver the highest levels of security, safety and compliance in a way that feels natural to the people using it,” said founder and Chief Executive Larry Gadea, who worked as an engineer at Google LLC and Twitter Inc. before starting the company in 2013.

Visitors Critical scans a visitor’s government-issued ID and matches their face to the photo on it. Names are also screened against denied-party and export-control lists through Visual Compliance and Descartes MK, both from The Descartes Systems Group Inc. Contractor qualifications are checked through ISN Software Corp. From there, visits are sent for approval based on the organization’s own written policies. The approver’s reasoning is then kept on record in case of an audit.

Among Envoy’s existing customers is Attalon Inc., the former aerospace and defense business of Coherent Corp. Every visitor to all 12 of Attalon’s sites has their ID scanned by Envoy before being screened against denied-party lists. Tim Carr, Attalon’s director of security and environment, health and safety, said that an auditor who inspects one site “has effectively inspected them all.”

The launch comes as new Envoy research of 1,000 security leaders found that 62% of enterprise leaders are very confident they would pass a physical security audit without preparation. Some 63% of that group had a security incident in the past year. At sensitive workplaces, 44% of leaders could not say with confidence who was in their building the previous day.

Visitors Critical is available now. Hardware-based ID verification, which uses supported readers to authenticate the document itself and catch forged IDs, is being offered through an early access program.

Envoy claims more than 16,000 workplaces in 170 countries as customers, including 92 of the Fortune 500. The company launched Response, a threat intelligence and incident management product, in August. It raised $111 million in a Series C round in January 2022 at a $1.4 billion valuation.

#5430. Study Finds a Nearly 50% Drop in Renters Becoming Homeowners Since 2009

As economic pressures continue to rise, a shocking new study has found that the share of renters who convert to homeownership has fallen 46% since 2009.

TransUnion, a leader in global information and insights, released its 2027 Personal and Commercial Lines Annual Insurance Outlook on Tuesday, which focuses on what the insurance industry needs to stay profitable in a changing market.

The report states that personal line underwriting has been strong throughout this year, but companies need to assess their strategies going forward as fewer people buy cars and homes, therefore reducing the pool of potential policyholders.

According to the report, the share of renters who convert to homeownership was 3.9% in 2025, a sharp decline from 7.2% in 2009.

This represents a shocking 46% decrease in the share of renters transitioning to homeownership in just 14 years.

Combined with a 2025 report from the National Association of Realtors®, which stated that the median age of first-time buyers climbed from 33 to 40 in just five years, TransUnion concluded that the pool of potential policyholders is shrinking.

The decrease in renters buying homes goes back to affordability and economic pressure, according to Ryan Thomson of The Assumable Guy.

“Renters didn't stop wanting to own. Rates tripled and prices kept climbing, so the monthly number stopped working,” Thomson tells Realtor.com®. “In Colorado Springs, where I sell, 71% of households could afford a median-priced home in 2019. By 2023, it was 25.3%. So renters stay put. Or they move wherever the payment still works.”

TransUnion also found that Florida, Texas, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Tennessee had the greatest influx of new residents between July 2025 and June 2026, with Florida gaining nearly 87,000 net-new residents.

The most significant outbound migration was seen in Massachusetts, New Jersey, Illinois, New York, and California, with the Golden State alone with a net loss of 146,000 residents.

This migration pattern is likely taking place as people chase affordability, looking for places that offer more space for lower costs.

“A household may want a certain lifestyle, but not be able to afford it given the high costs of housing and of living in general in the area. State and local taxes may also play a role,” Cameron Walker, a real estate expert at Clever Real Estate, tells Realtor.com. “Texas, Florida, and the Carolinas may be more affordable and have lower state and local taxes.”

The TransUnion report notes that the growing states all have an elevated exposure to hurricanes, severe convective storms, and other catastrophic weather compared to the states people are leaving.

While the growing states are all located near the Sun Belt and generally considered more affordable than coastal states such as New York and California, the increased risks elevate costs beyond purchase price.

“People may be assuming the Sun Belt states are generally affordable, and that isn't always the case,” Walker adds. “Property values are increasing in Sun Belt states because of in-migration, which increases property taxes and insurance costs, and inflates housing costs.”

For insurance companies, TransUnion recommends strategies like focusing on retaining and creating more value from current customer, winning policies from competition, and combining risk mitigating and marketing efforts when discussing migration.

For the housing market, improving outlooks and rebuilding the renter-to-homeowner path comes down to affordability and opportunity.

“We need to increase the supply of entry-level, affordable housing. This includes promoting the construction of new housing in high-demand, high-growth communities. The industry needs to offer new financing options and improve responsibility to help new homebuyers qualify to enter the housing market,” says Walker.

“People aren’t giving up their dreams of homeownership. They’re postponing them because the housing market has changed and the financial requirements to homeownership are out of the reach of many. The markets that can provide jobs and affordable housing will thrive, and gain the most, from future homeowners.”

#5429. ‘Momentum is the cure of all fear’: Mauricio and Alexia Umansky talk ‘Special Forces’

Jumping out of a helicopter into water below, rappelling down a 22-story building, enduring chemical warfare gas exposure — if you’ve never seen Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test, these are just a few of the tasks that must be completed.

It’s a reality TV show in which celebrities do physical challenges from the actual Special Forces selection process playbook. It’s like a competition show, but there are no eliminations, and no one gets voted off.

To leave, participants must voluntarily withdraw, be medically withdrawn by a DS (directing staff) due to injury or be dismissed for refusing a direct order. During the final test, the DS ejects those who fail the interrogation or selection test.

Season 5 is set in the Malaysian jungle. It features Candace Cameron Bure, Brandi Glanville, Oliver Hudson, Ruby Rose, George Santos, Bre Tiesi, Matt Barnes, and Mauricio and Alexia Umansky, among others.

At the time that this article was published, Alexia was still in the competition. Mauricio voluntarily withdrew after a rib injury sustained during a hand-to-hand fighting challenge with former NBA player Matt Barnes. Mauricio said the injury took two or three months to heal.

The following challenge involved gas, and Mauricio didn’t think his ribs could take it. He said he feared having a bad lung injury in the Malaysian jungle. Alexia agreed with the decision, saying the gas was the “most painful thing” she’d ever experienced in her life.

Inman spoke to Mauricio and Alexia midway through the season about the experience, the latest industry news and what’s next for The Agency.

What follows is the conversation, edited for length and clarity.

I think for me, 100 percent, the heat. I think I anticipated intense heat and intense humidity, but you don’t know what it’s like until you really feel it … It was so unbearably hot, and in our barracks that we slept in, there was no windows, and when you were inside, you actually couldn’t tell like what was even happening out there. But it was almost like … “Good, let me be locked in this metal box because the outside is crazy.”

Mauricio: I think for me, it was just the intensity of what a jungle really is. The first day we got there … when we were all showering and waiting to shower, there was a scorpion crawling on my leg, about to go in my boot, which I felt it and took it off just in the nick of time. Because if it went in my boot, it would have stung me, no question, right?

Alexia: It’s so hard to choose because literally every single thing was hard. Part of me wanted to say the car rides leading up to each challenge, because we didn’t know what was coming, and it was always so intense in the car. My heart would start pounding … the bottom line is the hardest part is just making sure that your mindset is correct [in] doing all these things and waking up each day and moving forward because that’s really what gets going is just moving forward and choosing to keep on going.

Mauricio: Yeah, I think Alexia nailed it. I mean, for me, it was really all about the little victories. The only way to survive is by looking at small victories, small steps … we used to say just make it to the next meal, just make it to the next day, just make it to tonight.

For me, the hardest part was leaving, was having to voluntarily withdraw. I did not want to have a medical withdrawal, so I didn’t want to go see the doctor and have them withdraw me.

Mauricio: Not one thing for me. What about you, Alexia?

Alexia: No. There’s nothing about this that’s easy.

Alexia: We loved everybody so much. I mean, we still talk all the time, and we still love each other so much. The words of affirmation we all told each other to this day are so special … But I think my first answer would have to be Candace [Cameron] Bure … she’s so strong, and we got looped together for a bunch of things because of our height similarities.

Mauricio: Well, I have to say that the person who surprised me the most was Alexia … the strength of her mind, her strength and what she did was extraordinary.

Alexia: Oh my god, yeah. Are you kidding me? All the time.

Alexia: Definitely thought it was pretty cool. It was an honor to be punched in the chest by DJ Tanner … I actually appreciated very much that she didn’t hold back because I just felt like I was treated like an equal, an individual.

Alexia: I’ve never punched anyone or anything … the second she threw the first punch, I knew she was so much stronger than me. But my goal was to just not fall down. I really didn’t want to fall down, so I was just trying to stay up the entire time. It felt like a fight went on for so long.

Alexia: I had zero plans on talking about that while we were there. Before we go into the course, they make you talk to some psychologists … they do ask you before the show, “What’s the worst thing that you’ve ever been through?”

And I remember thinking, like, “Are we gonna go there? … That would be so inappropriate. Everything’s in my power, and I’m not gonna go there” … Once I was finally in there, I understood why they asked … you’re stripped down to the very core of you, and you’re tired, and you’re pushing yourself, and you’re emotional, you’re exhausted … And Bre Tiesi, she got emotional, and [she said to me] ”I haven’t cried in years. I hate crying.”

It was really about discovering and repurposing the strength that I always felt that I had, but there was a time that I had felt that I had lost that.

And each night, as I was going to sleep, I just remember thinking to myself, “This is so rewarding, and this is so empowering, and this is so incredible for someone that has gone through what I have” … some people [feel like they] get their voice back. I always felt like I had my voice, but I feel like I got to discover a strength I always knew I had that someone had pushed me to question, and feeling that was just incredibly healing.

Alexia: No, not my parents. I had told two of my sisters before, and then, obviously, I told my dad on the course, and then, before the show aired, I ended up calling my mom and [sister] Portia to tell them because I obviously did not want that to be the first time they read it. And even though I spoke about it on the course, I’m still very, very afraid to tell them afterward, too.

Mauricio: It was extremely difficult … I was just proud of Alexia every single day, every single moment … hearing that story was just another revelation of her conquering and finally talking about something that I wish she never held back … I just wanted to reach out and just hug her. But by the same token, I also wanted to give her space and let her be her in that moment that she was sharing with everybody. So there was like a lot of stuff going through my mind.

There was anger toward this kid that did this … But [watching her let go of it] was beautiful to watch … from my perspective, it was like, “Do I reach over and become a dad and just give her a big hug, or do I let her go through this moment, psychologically speaking, of letting it all come out?”

And I was just proud of her all the way around.

In hindsight, I love that she was able to share that, get it off her chest with us, with everybody, with the world. I think it’s super powerful.

Yes, I live by a lot of different small philosophies. Certainty versus doubt. Momentum is the cure of all fears. All of these are the different things where you just have to move forward, right? In order to accomplish something, you kind of just have to move forward, right? … the moment that I went from being an agent to opening up a brokerage, you jump off the cliff; you hope the parachute catches.

To today … here we are in a really difficult real estate market. I mean, it is not fun out there right now whatsoever. Yet [The Agency is] still growing. We’re still putting money out there. We’re still doing things right. So yeah, to me that’s just a philosophy that I always live by.

Mauricio: I don’t know. We’ll just keep going. I really like that show Traitors. I would love to be on that show. That could be a fun one for me, so I’m putting that out into the universe.

Alexia: My dream would be to do a reality TV show with my family … We did Buying Beverly Hills, and we’ve done Real Housewives for like [16] years now. But we’ve never done something all of us together, just us, and I think that’ll be really cool.

Mauricio: I’m going to leave that one on the table. If anything, it’s for 2030. There’s still plenty of time to do that and make that decision. But I love LA, and I think I can help LA a lot. I think we live in an amazing city, and if the moment comes, and I’m set up in the right position in the business and I feel like I can actually win, I might do it. But I wouldn’t do it if I didn’t feel like I could actually win.

Mauricio: It’s an absolute mess, what’s going on in our in our in our industry right now, particularly with the listings. My take is, it’s quite simple. I think that there’s a lot of change that’s happening. I believe that it’s somewhere in the middle. Like I do everything.

I believe sellers should have choice, but I believe that we should be sharing those private listings amongst everybody — every agent, every brokerage firm, not just keeping it for themselves. I feel like there’s a lot happening right now in the industry where everybody’s really looking out for themselves: the MLSs, NAR, Compass.

Actually, Compass, I think, wants to collaborate, wants to share, but they’re in a big, big fight. But in the meantime, this Clear Cooperation Policy is what is allowing them to keep all the listings to themselves and not share them … The PLS is exactly what that was, and I still think that if Clear Cooperation Policy didn’t pass, it would have been an amazing business to have right now.

Mauricio: We are really positioned as the premier luxury brokerage firm outside of Compass right now. They’ve got Sotheby’s, they’ve got Christie’s, they’ve got all of those different brands, and we’re the only independent luxury brokerage firm out there right now.

So I’m excited to be in that position. Competitors make you better every single day … I’m excited in terms of where we sit, where we stand in a very difficult time; I’m not excited about the market. We really need to do some things to improve it. We’ve had three years of very, very difficult conditions, and it’s going to be very difficult for people to survive. And those that do survive will come out better.

I think we’re in a good position to survive, but we’ve got our work cut out for us over the next year, year and a half. But we’ll continue to grow. We’ll continue to expand, and I’m excited to just be a part of this industry. But man, it’s hard out there right now.

#5428. LanceDB raises $57.5M to accelerate AI model training with multimodal data platform

LanceDB Inc., the developer of database technology designed to speed up artificial intelligence models, today announced it has raised $57.5 million in early-stage funding to bring a multimodal lakehouse to researchers, model builders and platform teams.

Bessemer Venture Partners and Innovation Endeavors led the Series B round. Other investors in the round included Theory Ventures, Dimension, Swift Ventures, CRV and Y Combinator, bringing the company’s total funding to $98.5 million.

AI is making it easier to create and interpret increasingly complex forms of data, but creating it also brings an infrastructure problem. LanceDB is tackling this problem by providing a unified multimodal data lakehouse, giving researchers, enterprise outfits and AI agents a unified way to access, find, prepare and train on that data without spending weeks managing the underlying infrastructure.

“Typically, research teams have to put different parts of their dataset in different places, and they lose weeks or months getting a whole training dataset ready for that single training run at the end of the day,” co-founder and Chief Executive Chang She told SiliconANGLE in an interview. “There’s a missing data layer for AI today, and that’s what we’re trying to build.”

LanceDB’s technology is built on Lance, an open-source data format designed for AI workloads that combines structured information with images, video and other large files. Unlike traditional analytics formats optimized for processing entire tables, Lance supports the rapid retrieval and modification of individual records, making it particularly useful for searching and preparing massive training datasets.

The company built this format into a large-scale data lakehouse for retrieval, which is needed for the sheer scale of information needed to train modern AI models. A lakehouse combines the flexibility of a data lake, which can store enormous amounts of raw information, with database-style capabilities for organizing, querying and managing that data.

“Part of what makes multimodal data different and more difficult is the size of the data,” She explained.

By bringing multimodality to the lakehouse format, LanceDB brings different forms of AI training data into a single platform, allowing developers to search, organize and prepare their datasets without maintaining separate systems for each data type. It can connect directly to customers’ existing cloud storage, where the data remains, while distributing computational workloads across the infrastructure required to process it.

Multimodal AI involves more than combining text, audio, images and video. Autonomous vehicles, robotics and world models also involve three-dimensional sensor information, geospatial coordinates, time-series data and annotations that explain what the sensors are detecting.

For example, a self-driving car doesn’t merely capture an image. Its sensors might produce a three-dimensional representation of the surrounding environment, which then needs to be associated with information that identifies roads, pedestrians, vegetation and other objects.

The sheer amount of data included in lidar 3D clouds, images, video, audio and more can take up, on average, 10 to 20 petabytes of data in a single table for many large training workflows, with some becoming even larger – potentially approaching 80 to 100 petabytes. Researchers and model builders may maintain huge pools of data across different systems because conventional platforms weren’t designed around the requirements of multimodal AI.

Researchers must then assemble, reconcile and store different components of a training dataset to enrich it for training. The curation itself can take weeks or months just to move, prepare and process. LanceDB’s answer is to manage the infrastructure itself without ever copying or moving data from enterprise or research storage, giving it a single unified access point.

“The data stays in place,” She explained. “It remains yours. We don’t need to copy it.”

In short, LanceDB isn’t simply introducing a new way to store data; the objective is to provide a way to access the data less often, without needing to copy, convert or move it through network infrastructure. This greatly speeds up what She refers to as the “AI flywheel,” which is currently driven by feeding AI models good data as quickly as possible to mint and roll them out.

“The faster we can make that spin, the faster research teams can get to higher quality models and allow us to make even more interesting AI applications,” She said.

Notable customers include Runway AI Inc., which adopted LanceDB’s enterprise platform as its AI training needs expanded. Netflix Inc. built a media data lake on the technology for content creation. And Microsoft Corp. uses the platform as a data layer for training models on tens of billions of rows of image and code data. The platform lets these organizations consolidate data management, search, curation and feature engineering into a unified workflow, helping researchers prepare training datasets at petabyte scale without juggling separate infrastructure systems.

“A training example at Runway doesn’t stay still,” said Runway Chief Technology Officer Kamil Sindi. “It starts as a video and a prompt, then we add embeddings, resolution and duration metadata, whatever the next experiment needs. We first started using the Lance format in 2024 because it was the only option that handled unstructured data, column appends, distributed reads and ad-hoc SQL all at once. We’ve since become a LanceDB Enterprise customer.”

She said LanceDB intends to use the new funding to expand its multimodal data platform and accelerate the AI model development cycle, particularly by improving large-scale data curation, feature engineering and data loading to keep thousands of graphics processing units supplied efficiently during training. The company will also deepen its support for emerging AI workloads, including video generation, world models and robotics, where researchers must manage growing volumes of first-person sensor data, synthetic data and other multimodal information.

#5427. Stronger Together: HomeServices of America Celebrates Top Agents, Fuels Future Growth

Above: HomeServices of America President and CEO Chris Kelly addresses the crowd at the company’s “Stronger Together” Conference

While real estate success is often measured individually—with an emphasis on closed transactions, milestones achieved and accolades earned—some of the greatest opportunities for growth present themselves when real estate professionals come together.

That philosophy was at the heart of HomeServices of America’s 4th Annual “Stronger Together” Conference, held Oct. 26 – 29 at the Fontainebleau Miami Beach. The oceanside event brought together more than 400 agents from the HomeServices’ owned brokerage companies to celebrate the professionals whose achievements earned them a place among the company’s best—each invited on the strength of their success.

Collectively, these agents rank in the top 1.5% of approximately 1.4 million Realtors® nationwide—averaging seven times the sales volume of the national average and three times more transactions. Generating $10.2 billion in annual sales volume, Stronger Together agent attendees are responsible for helping 16,483 families move each year.

“Our agents earned their place at Stronger Together, and we wanted every moment to reflect how much we value them,” HomeServices of America President and CEO Chris Kelly said in a release.

The mastermind behind the reinvigoration of the organization, Kelly has led HomeServices of America’s transformation from a quiet holding company into a bold parent company focused on providing strategic direction, cohesion and resources across its family of brokerage, mortgage, insurance and title services.

Central to that vision is a commitment to investing in people, performance and long-term growth that extends throughout the organization—a commitment reflected in reflections and anecdotes shared with RISMedia after the event from both HomeServices of America executives and attendees alike.

Playing a key role in educating and elevating the performance of brokerage owners, operators, team leaders, office managers and the sales associates in the field each and every day, HomeServices of America Chief Coaching Officer Jimmy Burgess takes pride in seeing that work come together.

“I’ve been part of this event for a long time, and what still gets me is the room. Every person in it earned their seat, and they’re all generous with what they know,” says Burgess, who spent the week watching agents trade ideas between sessions as much as in them.

“It’s a privilege to say thank you to people who work this hard, and to send them home with a few new ideas and a few new friends,” he adds.

Reflecting the company’s commitment to delivering the complete real estate experience—a theme central to HomeServices of America’s strategy—this year’s event mirrored that philosophy by offering agents inspiration, practical insight and community in one setting. Newly introduced Super Sessions, which go beyond a traditional breakout or panel, and inspiring voices provided top-performing agents everything they need to keep winning in today’s market.

For clients, that complete experience is delivered through OnePoint, the integrated platform HomeServices of America launched earlier this year to provide a more streamlined, end-to-end experience to buyers and sellers alike.

“We changed a few things this year, including the Super Sessions and a main stage with three voices instead of one, because folks at this level already know their craft. What they want is room to keep growing,” explains Kelly.

“It’s the same thinking behind OnePoint: Give people what they need in one place, so they aren’t piecing it together alone,” he adds. “When our agents grow, their clients feel it.”

Providing agents the tools and motivation to keep succeeding, entrepreneur, investor and bestselling author Jesse Itzler kicked off the conference with a keynote presentation challenging attendees to redefine wealth through experiences, relationships, mindset, health and purpose.

In addition to Super Sessions designed to give agents the time and depth to explore a multitude of topics impacting the industry, attendees also heard shared perspectives on kindness, connection and determination. Another Stronger Together highlight was a live recording of the “Stay Paid” podcast with Kelly, Burgess and Prosperity Home Mortgage President and CEO Justin Messer.

“A gathering like this sets a standard for the industry,” says HomeServices of America Senior Vice President Lacey Conway. “With more than 400 agents in the top 1.5% nationally, the program had to match the people in the room, and it did.

“From the keynote to the ‘Super Sessions’ to the speakers on (the topic of) belonging, you could see the same things we see in these agents: Curiosity, discipline and a willingness to keep learning when they’re already at the top,” she says.

HomeServices of America is putting that same forward-thinking mindset into action across the board.

“What stands out about HomeServices is that it keeps building while it’s winning, and OnePoint is a good example. Bringing brokerage, mortgage, title and insurance together as one coordinated team is a real answer to what clients want,” says HomeServices of America Chief Marketing and Strategy Officer Brian Boero, who led one of the conference’s Super Sessions.

“The energy in the room at Stronger Together had that same appetite for what’s next…and that’s a sign of a company that plans to keep leading,” he adds.

The value of coming together: Ideas, connections and new perspectives

Attending HomeServices of America’s Stronger Together event along with 15 top-producing agents, Long Companies CEO Kevin Kaplan says that being able to bring together hundreds of the most successful real estate professionals from across the HomeServices network to learn, share ideas and build relationships is what ultimately makes the conference so valuable.

“What sets Stronger Together apart is that the focus goes beyond traditional sales skills and tactics. It’s about mindset, leadership, motivation and challenging yourself to think differently about your business and what’s possible,” says Kaplan, who believes that surrounding yourself with successful people who challenge and inspire you is one of the greatest opportunities for growth.

“Our agents came away energized, with new ideas, valuable connections and fresh perspectives on how to take their businesses to the next level,” he adds. “In my view, this was the best ‘Stronger Together’ event yet, and we’re already looking forward to 2027.”

For Elizabeth Nunan, president and CEO of Houlihan Lawrence, the conference was equally as powerful.

“Stronger Together was an outstanding conference from start to finish. The speakers were exceptional, the content was timely and relevant, and the opportunities to connect, network and share ideas made it even more valuable,” she says.

“Our agents left feeling inspired, energized and excited about what’s ahead. In fact, they’re already making plans for next year in Nashville. That’s always a pretty good indication of a great event,” adds Nunan.

For RISMedia Founder and CEO John Featherston, what stood out most was the energy and the positive, can-do attitude throughout the event.

“I had the privilege of attending the 4th Annual Stronger Together conference, and watching the attendees connect with so many other passionate real estate professionals reminded me just how valuable it is to meet face-to-face and collaborate with industry leaders to share knowledge and techniques—and why it’s so important to success in our industry,” says Featherston, who applauded Kelly and his team for delivering an informative, meaningful and well-received experience for attendees.

“When you couple the industry talents educating attendees—from Jimmy Burgess’ coaching insights and Brian Boero’s informative, practical information—with incredible guests such as serial entrepreneur and best-selling author Jesse Itzler and award-winning singer, songwriter and author Nicolle Galyon along with several other incredible speakers—Stronger Together was a smashing success,” he adds.

“Congratulations to Chris and his team for a job well done!”

Paige Tepping is RISMedia’s senior managing editor.

#5426. We keep coaching real estate agents to be salespeople. That was never the job

OPINION: Lance Pendleton argues that real estate agents are consultants, not salespeople. Learn what to ask before you pay for a coaching program.

I was the national head of agent development at Compass, and I’ve been in front of more than 30,000 agents since. I’ve also sold the thing I’m about to take apart, so keep that in mind while you read.

Here’s the usual scenario: You sign up for a coaching program. You’re excited, and you should be. Everybody wants to feel a little less alone in a job you mostly do by yourself, in your car.

You didn’t fail the program. The program failed you. How come?

The reason is simpler than anybody wants it to be. Nearly every coaching program in this business teaches professional sales skills to people who are not in sales. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators.

Nobody has ever talked a family into a house they didn’t want to live in. What we do is help people through the largest and most emotional decision of their lives with the least amount of damage. We read a room. We tell someone the truth about their kitchen, and we hold a deal together at 9 p.m. on a Sunday when the buyer’s father has opinions.

That is not selling. We’re consultants, advocates, advisors and educators. If you can fog a mirror, you can get a license. Very few people can do those four things well, and I’ve yet to see a program that teaches them as a skill set.

This isn’t the coach’s fault. Coaches were trained the same way the rest of us were. Build the database. Reach as many people as you possibly can. Add value, and then add more of it tomorrow.

There’s a word buried in there that I think is the dumbest one in our industry, and I say that with love. Value.

We all have the same value. Every one of us can pull a comp, open a door, write an offer and get to a closing table. What almost none of us have is a point of differentiation, the thing that tells a consumer specifically what you do for them and why it ought to be you. You can follow “add value” for a decade and stay interchangeable with the other four agents the seller interviewed.

There’s a second reason the homework never gets done: Agents live in two periods of time: now and not now.

Now is the pipe that burst three hours before a closing. Now is the appraisal, the inspection, the client calling at 10:30 p.m. about something that could have been a text. Now is loud, it’s permanent, and it pays this month. Not now is quiet and pays in three years, if at all.

The trouble is that everything producing long-term income security in this business sits in the not-now column. The National Association of Realtors’ 2026 member profile puts median gross income at $88,500 for agents with 16 years or more in the industry, and $8,000 for agents with two years or less.

The veterans report a median 49 percent of their business from repeat clients and another 32 percent from referrals. For the newest agents, both of those medians are zero.

Somebody will say that’s just arithmetic, that you need a past client before you can have a repeat one. That’s the point. The whole gap is 15 years of relationships, and not one hour of that work feels urgent on a Tuesday. This is a patient business being coached like an impatient one.

We do something else I think is worse. We coach in a permanent state of enthusiasm. Everything is fabulous; every market is an opportunity; you’re crushing it; this is your year. I call that toxic positivity, and it does real damage. You sit in a hard month with two deals coming apart, you hear all of it, and you quietly conclude the problem must be you.

What would help is unglamorous. This job burns through five things: prioritization, organization, time management, impulse control and emotional regulation. By Thursday of an ordinary week, most good agents are running low on at least two.

There’s nothing wrong with any of those people. Real support builds bumpers around those five, the same reason a bowling lane for kids has them. You don’t make the gutter disappear by concentrating harder.

That work means dealing with people as they are, for who they are. Not more, more, more. Not the next great thing. One thing, chosen for that person, small enough to start on a Thursday when everything else has gone sideways.

We haven’t served this business well on that, and I include myself. I’ve sold the four-week cycle. It’s a comfortable thing to sell, because Week 1 always works.

If you’re picking a program this fall, ask what gets cut. Anybody can hand you 15 things. The one worth paying is the person who tells you which one matters and which 14 you can skip.

We’re not in sales. We never were. Until the coaching in this business is built for that job, we’ll keep running very good people through programs that leave them feeling like the problem.

You aren’t the problem. This is still the best time there’s ever been to be a great agent. We just have to stop training you for somebody else’s job.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of Reframe Lab, a coaching and consulting practice for real estate agents, and the former national head of agent development at Compass in Connecticut. Get connected on Instagram.

#5425. Tech Roundup: Zillow Preview listings go live in RealScout

Can AI time savings be measured? Lofty is trying. Plus: $1.65 billion in October proptech funding, Airbnb’s AI travel agent and Zillow Preview in RealScout.

This week’s Inman Tech Roundup covers Lofty’s new monthly index, which tallies how much time its AI saves agents, a $1.65 billion October for proptech funding, Airbnb’s early-2027 launch window for its AI travel agent and Zillow Preview’s new home inside RealScout.

Lofty is launching the Lofty AI Index for Real Estate, a monthly report tracking how much time its AI tools save real estate agents. The inaugural edition found Lofty AI products, including Lofty Cowork, completed 1.13 million tasks in October, saving real estate agents 131,248 hours.

The index counts tasks Lofty’s AI completed, such as follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins and CRM updates, then estimates how long each would take an agent to do manually.

Among the findings: 387,824 leads got an AI follow-up text or email; solo agents saved 30 percent of their hours on daily planning; and agents in Michigan saved more time than any other region.

“Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true. We decided to cut through the smoke and mirrors around AI results and create measurable clarity with the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations and stand behind it,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty.

The time-saved figures rest on the company’s own estimates of manual task times, and the release doesn’t say how many agents are behind the totals, which makes per-agent impact hard to gauge. Since this is the first edition, there’s no prior month to compare against yet.

For real estate agents weighing AI tools, Lofty’s index is a step toward the kind of hard numbers the industry has been missing. It gives them a benchmark to press other vendors on when they make time-saving claims.

However, the most useful measure is their own: tracking whether hours freed up by AI actually turn into more conversations, listings and closings.

Note: Lofty is the official AI partner of Inman.

Proptech companies raised about $1.65 billion across 34 funding rounds in October, according to the Center for Real Estate Technology & Innovation (CRETI), which called it one of the strongest months of 2026.

The money was heavily concentrated. Construction and development took roughly $872.4 million, or 52.8 percent of the total, while residential pulled in $604.4 million, or 36.6 percent. Three deals alone accounted for nearly 75 percent of October capital: Bedrock Robotics’ $600 million Series C, Unlock’s $433.1 million debt financing and ICON’s $200 million Series D.

Debt was a big part of the story. About $588.6 million, more than a third of the month’s total, came through debt rounds. That includes Unlock’s financing for its home-equity agreement platform and CrowdProperty’s roughly $133.5 million round for residential development lending.

That means much of October’s residential funding didn’t go into software at all but into financial products tied to home equity and property lending.

CRETI noted that funding signals investor conviction, not proof of ROI, and said the bar for founders is rising to show a credible link between their technology and a material financial outcome.

The numbers suggest investors are betting less on new real estate agent-facing software and more on the expensive, physical end of housing, such as building homes faster and cheaper and financing the transactions around them.

If that capital pays off, the bigger impact on agents and brokers may come indirectly, through more housing supply and new ways for homeowners to tap equity, rather than through the tools on their desks.

Airbnb plans to roll out its AI travel agent to consumers in the first half of 2027, the company said in its third-quarter shareholder letter, firming up a timeline it had previously pegged only as sometime in the next year.

Instead of a text-heavy chatbot, the AI agent will assemble a custom interface around each guest’s request, pulling from hundreds of travel-specific components such as maps, photos, comparisons, calendars and itineraries. It will also handle post-booking tasks like reservation changes, refunds, rebooking and payment issues, which Airbnb argues outside AI agents can’t easily do.

CEO Brian Chesky told analysts that general-purpose AI agents are fine for routine tasks but not for trip planning.

“Travel is aspirational,” Chesky said. “Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience.”

The announcement came alongside a strong third quarter for Airbnb. Revenue grew 19 percent year over year to $4.87 billion, beating Wall Street estimates. Airbnb raised its 2026 growth forecast to the high teens, up from the mid-teens. Chesky called it the company’s fastest revenue growth in more than three years.

Airbnb’s bet is one real estate portals and brokerages are weighing, too: that owning the search experience and the transaction behind it beats handing consumers off to general-purpose AI agents.

If a custom, visual AI agent wins over travelers, it’ll strengthen the case for real estate platforms to build their own AI home-search tools rather than relying on outside chatbots to send them buyers.

RealScout is now showing Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of participating brokerages in its collaborative home search platform, putting pre-MLS inventory in front of buyers searching with their own agents.

The integration, first announced in September, extends Zillow Preview’s reach beyond Zillow, Trulia and Realtor.com to RealScout’s network of more than 100,000 agents.

Preview listings appear in client searches and listing alerts that include Coming Soon properties. Buyers can message their agent directly about a home, and each Preview listing is replaced by its MLS listing once the home goes active. Agents and brokerages don’t need to opt in to see eligible listings.

RealScout CEO Andrew Flachner framed the move as a transparency play, with a not-so-subtle shot at private listing networks.

“Listing transparency comes down to whether a buyer can choose the agent they trust without worrying that the right home is hiding behind another brokerage’s velvet rope,” Flachner said in a statement. “With Zillow Preview listings from hundreds of brokerages now available in RealScout, agents can give their clients more of the market through the home search experience they already share.”

For agents, the integration means clients can see pre-MLS listings from participating brokerages in the search tool they already use, without signing up for Zillow or leaving the agent relationship. It also gives buyer’s agents an earlier look at upcoming inventory, which matters most in tight markets, where a few days’ head start can decide who gets a showing first.
