#5424. Red Hat and Microsoft bring OpenShift virtual machines to Azure

IBM Corp. subsidiary Red Hat and Microsoft Corp. are expanding their longtime engineering partnership to enable enterprises to run virtual machines on Microsoft Azure using Red Hat’s OpenShift Virtualization platform, providing an alternative to traditional hypervisors and what Red Hat called a path to modernizing legacy applications.

The collaboration, announced today, involves changes to Azure’s underlying computing architecture to connect it natively with Linux through Microsoft direct virtualization. That’s an Azure feature that gives performance-sensitive workloads near-bare-metal access to underlying hardware components.

Red Hat said this provides a direct pipeline between key hardware such as graphics processing units and isolated workloads. The companies are also working to give Linux-based workloads more direct access to Azure’s hardware resources, including graphics processing units.

Separately, Red Hat said it’s making its Lightwell Network vulnerability remediation service available through Microsoft’s Azure Marketplace.

The virtualization initiative addresses growing enterprise concerns about hypervisor licensing costs, hardware availability and the complexity of managing virtual machines alongside newer containerized applications. Red Hat said those pressures have intensified as organizations seek to accommodate AI workloads without abandoning existing applications.

Virtualization market leader Broadcom Inc. recently took aim at the same issue by open-sourcing its software for provisioning and managing virtual machines using the same protocols that the Kubernetes container orchestrator uses. At the center of the effort is Microsoft’s direct virtualization, which lets Linux-based and cloud-native platforms running on Azure virtual machines access the same virtualization and hardware capabilities available to Azure-native services.

Red Hat said it will be the first commercial Microsoft partner to support the technology through OpenShift Virtualization on Azure Red Hat OpenShift, the jointly engineered and managed Kubernetes service offered by the two companies.

The agreement includes collaboration on several upstream open-source projects, including KubeVirt, LibVirt, QEMU and the Linux kernel. KubeVirt enables organizations to manage virtual machines and containers using Kubernetes tools.

Microsoft has extended KubeVirt beyond the Linux Kernel-based Virtual Machine hypervisor by adding support for its own hypervisor. That allows OpenShift Virtualization to run on Azure virtual machines using Microsoft’s direct virtualization technology.

The approach is designed to let organizations consolidate traditional virtual machines, containerized applications and AI workloads on a common platform. Red Hat said its migration toolkit for virtualization will help customers move workloads from existing hypervisors.

The companies said the architecture will also improve resource utilization by supporting CPU and memory overcommitment, enabling more workloads to share available infrastructure. Kernel-level isolation is intended to protect sensitive workloads without compromising performance.

“Enterprises shouldn’t have to choose between managing rising hypervisor costs and accelerating their IT roadmaps,” Chris Wright, Red Hat’s chief technology officer, said in a statement. He said the collaboration would provide a common foundation for modernizing existing virtual machines and running AI workloads.

The companies did not announce a general availability date for the new virtualization capabilities.

Red Hat also said Lightwell Network is immediately available through private offers on Azure Marketplace, allowing customers to obtain remediated versions of vulnerable open-source software dependencies.

Lightwell addresses a persistent application security problem: correcting vulnerabilities in third-party software without forcing upgrades that could disrupt production applications.

The service provides version-specific fixes through secured repositories, accompanied by signed software artifacts and supporting provenance, software bills of materials and vulnerability information where applicable.

Customers can incorporate those fixes into existing development and deployment pipelines without replacing their vulnerability scanners, artifact repositories or build systems. Findings can surface in Microsoft Defender for Cloud, while Azure Policy provides governance controls.

Customers can purchase Lightwell subscriptions through Azure Marketplace and apply eligible spending toward their Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitments.

#5422. Bitcoin Bottom? Is the Market Preparing for a Reversal or One Final Crash?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin found its bottom? Bitcoin is fighting to hold $65,000 after a brutal weekend selloff pushed BTC USD below $62,000. The rebound offers bulls some relief, but the market is showing signs of a much deeper liquidity problem.

The world’s largest crypto has lost 13% since the 8th of November, with Ethereum and XRP also hitting multi-month lows. Billions in leveraged positions have disappeared as traders rush to reduce exposure.

Yet the selloff has created an interesting setup. Extreme fear, forced liquidations, and heavily discounted prices could signal that much of the speculative excess has finally been removed.

The problem is that capital continues leaving the crypto market. Stablecoin supply has contracted for five consecutive weeks, while US spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded seven consecutive sessions of outflows.

Bitcoin now faces a defining question: has the market finally found its bottom, or is another crash waiting around the corner?

The latest liquidation wave has given the Bitcoin bottom argument some credibility. When leveraged traders are forced out, selling pressure can eventually exhaust itself, leaving the market with fewer speculative positions vulnerable to another cascade. What comes down must go up, and vice versa.

The weekend recovery also shows that buyers are willing to defend the $62,000 region. BTC rebounded to $64,000 – $65,000 after briefly touching $62,006 this morning.

Market sentiment has also deteriorated sharply. Extreme fear is returning as investors abandon riskier positions and traders become increasingly defensive. This is often where market reversals begin. Sellers who wanted to exit have already sold, while longer-term investors start looking for attractive entry points.

Galaxy Research has also presented a bullish argument. In an October 26 report, the firm said it believed Bitcoin’s bottom was already in, pointing to diminished selling pressure, reduced speculative positioning, and stronger long-term fundamentals.

However, a convincing recovery needs more than a short-lived bounce. Bitcoin must attract fresh spot demand and reclaim important resistance levels before bulls can claim victory.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The biggest obstacle to a Bitcoin bottom is the lack of fresh money entering the market. Stablecoin supply has contracted for five consecutive weeks. Glassnode puts the 30-day decline at $17.1 billion, marking the fastest contraction since June 2022.

Stablecoins provide much of the dollar liquidity used to purchase cryptocurrencies, so when investors redeem stablecoins for traditional dollars, the market loses potential buying power.

Bitcoin ETFs are sending another warning. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost $2.35 billion over two weeks, extending a difficult period for institutional demand. Corporate buying has weakened too. Public companies collectively sold 11,647 BTC worth approximately $869 million. Strategy remained a buyer, adding 1,037 BTC, but the wider corporate treasury trend has turned negative.

Macroeconomic conditions are making the situation worse. Hotter-than-expected US inflation and employment figures have pushed interest-rate expectations higher. Futures markets now fully price a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

BREAKING: October PPI Inflation rises to 6.5%, its highest level since November 2022.Core PPI Inflation was 5.0%, in-line with expectations of 5.0%.CPI, PPI, and PCE inflation continue to push higher in the US.All signs point toward a December rate hike.

Higher rates strengthen the dollar and make non-yielding assets like Bitcoin less attractive. Meanwhile, the dollar index has climbed to 102.9, adding another headwind for crypto markets.

Coinbase Institutional also warned that Bitcoin could struggle to recover without renewed crypto-native demand. Its analysis places $62,000 among the important support levels, with $58,000–$59,000 emerging as another potential downside target.

The technical picture remains fragile. Bitcoin needs to reclaim the $66,000–$68,000 region before bulls can establish a convincing recovery. A sustained move above $73,000–$75,000 would provide a much stronger reversal signal.

Bitcoin has already experienced a substantial correction, but the rebound hasn’t settled the argument. The bullish case rests on exhausted sellers, reduced speculative exposure, extreme fear, and buyers defending the $62,000 region. The bearish case rests on shrinking stablecoin supply, ETF withdrawals, weaker corporate accumulation, and rising borrowing costs.

For now, liquidity remains the deciding factor. A genuine Bitcoin bottom needs more than liquidation-driven relief rallies. It needs fresh capital entering the market, institutional demand returning, and spot buyers absorbing available supply.

If stablecoin supply stabilizes and ETF flows turn positive, Bitcoin could build a foundation for its next recovery. But if capital continues leaving the ecosystem, the $62,000 floor could give way to another painful correction.

Bitcoin may be approaching its bottom, but the market hasn’t yet shown that buyers are ready to take control.

#5421. Existing-home sales sink to a 16-year low as mortgage rates bite

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

“Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant said she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant said in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”

Yun and Sturtevant said mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant said. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”

Added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

As a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun said, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

“Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he said. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

“If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

“Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she said. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”

Hale said jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

“[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she said. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”

Yun said rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

“One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he said. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the big change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”

However, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

“There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on new pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”

#5419. Chainguard goes self-serve with free Starter plan and $500-a-month Team plan

Software supply chain security company Chainguard Inc. is now offering its products on a self-serve basis, with the launch today of a free plan called Chainguard Starter and a paid Team plan priced at $500 a month.

The free plan covers nearly all of Chainguard’s products, with usage limits set at a level that fits a personal project or a small team. According to Chainguard, users can sign up, pull an image, connect their package manager to its screened libraries and place coding agents in a sandbox in one sitting, with no credit card or sales call required.

The launch comes after Black October, the name given to a run of supply chain attacks and critical vulnerability disclosures in the third week of October. With incidents like those, a team may have only until the end of the day to deal with a bad dependency, according to the blog post in which Chainguard announced the plans. In such cases, the company wrote, “nobody is going to wait on a purchase order.”

Until now, access to Chainguard’s products has typically required a conversation with its sales team first. One exception was Catalog Starter, a free beta plan offered earlier this year that was limited to five container images. Chainguard says the sales-led model, designed around large companies with procurement processes, works far less well for a team that needs a hardened base image ahead of its next deployment.

In most cases, moving a service onto Chainguard requires changing only a single line in the file that defines its container image. Security engineers can also put Chainguard’s images and libraries through their own scanners before signing anything, according to the company.

Starter includes five container images from Chainguard’s catalog of more than 3,000 minimal images, which are claimed to have near-zero known vulnerabilities, with downloads of up to 100 gigabytes a month. A software bill of materials and signed build provenance are provided for every image.

Also part of the plan is Chainguard Libraries, which provides malware- and greyware-scanned dependencies for JavaScript, Python, Java, Go and .NET with a limit of 50,000 pulls a month. Under a fixed seven-day cooldown, newly published versions are held back for a week, which the company says allows a compromised release to be caught before it reaches a build.

Starter also comes with 500 hours a month of virtual CPU time on each of Chainguard Checks and Chainguard Workspaces, which launched in beta at the company’s Assemble London event in October. Checks is designed to provide hardened runners for continuous integration, with Workspaces providing hardened sandboxes for coding agents.

Other features on the free plan include hardened replacements for GitHub Actions, more than 1,000 hardened agent skills, community support and 100 gigabytes of private artifact storage. Starter users also get 1 million tokens a month for Guardener, Chainguard’s artificial intelligence agent, which inventories the GitHub Actions and container images in a customer’s repositories and opens pull requests to swap in the company’s hardened versions. Each Starter account is limited to five users.

The paid Team plan, which is billed to a credit card, includes everything in Starter with higher limits, such as unlimited users, 1 terabyte of image downloads and 1 million dependency pulls a month. Team customers also get base, application and AI images at their latest versions on top of their five chosen images, along with 1,000 hours a month each of Checks and Workspaces, 5 million Guardener tokens and 500 gigabytes of private storage.

Features reserved for Team include backported fixes for known vulnerabilities across five remediated versions, zero-day patches on the day of disclosure, ticketed support and managed policies that set rules for what is pulled and what is blocked. Chainguard says the usual reasons for upgrading include a sixth person needing access, a project outgrowing the usage limits and a team needing a patch for a version it cannot yet move off.

According to Chainguard, the upgrade takes a few seconds from the console that flags which limit a user has hit. Nothing has to be migrated, since the account, images and session all carry over. Customers can cancel at any time from the same console. Storage beyond Team’s included 500 gigabytes will be metered starting Jan. 1, 2027, according to Chainguard’s documentation.

The Enterprise offering is unchanged and still starts with a conversation with the company’s sales team. Enterprise provides companywide use of Chainguard with no usage limits, along with service-level agreements, enterprise compliance features and integrations. Starter is available now.

Chainguard says it has raised $892 million since its founding in 2021. Its most recent round, $280 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund, came in October 2025.

#5418. He sold Bibles door to door. Now he runs a 35,000-home luxury exchange club in 103 countries

What do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

On this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

He explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel important.

They also get into handling rejection, taking big risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy says many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

For agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

"The company has been committed to our success from the start, providing the support we needed to hit the ground running and helping us to successfully implement the playbook. Having the ability to work alongside my family is a wonderful privilege and I wouldn't trade it for the world."

#5416. Arista takes aim at the next AI network battleground: distributed inference

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Awareness of the network’s role in artificial intelligence has steadily increased, with much of the focus on the back end – larger clusters, faster ports and scale-across fabrics that stitch graphics processing units together across data centers. Arista Networks Inc. has seen continued, accelerated growth and has been one of the biggest winners of that buildout.

This week at SC26, Arista announced a shift in focus to the other side of the network. The company also announced a new set of Etherlink R4 routing platforms designed for what it calls distributed inferencing, along with a pluggable optical line system for data center interconnect. The lineup includes:

All are based on Broadcom’s Jericho and Qumran silicon, designed to deliver up to 60% lower power consumption than competing 7-nanometer and 16-nanometer platforms. Everything is available now, except the 7020HR4, which ships in early 2027. The speeds and feeds always make headlines, but the implications of the launch point to where AI infrastructure is heading.

During a pre-briefing, Brendan Gibbs, Arista’s assistant vice president of product line management, argued that the forces driving training across multiple sites will have the same effect on inference. Gibbs also said that roughly 30% of Arista’s AI business is now scale-across, indicating that distributed AI is rapidly becoming commonplace.

Inference will be distributed for three reinforcing reasons:

The implication is that the front-end network, long treated as plumbing, now needs back-end attributes: deep buffers, traffic engineering, multi-tenancy, and encryption, because traffic now leaves the building.

This launch is the opposite of the descriptors we typically associate with Arista. Recent announcements focused on dense 800G, 1.6T, and liquid cooling. The products launched at SC26 are smaller and less expensive. Arista dominates big iron and is now rounding out its portfolio. Arista’s customers range from hyperscalers to neoclouds to enterprises building local AI. The front end needs rich features, not massive bandwidth, and Arista hasn’t had a viable option for that tier until now.

These routers are designed as entry-level but ship with 400G uplinks, which may seem like overkill today but offer investment protection. Gibbs said the goal is a 10-year life cycle, with customers swapping optics rather than chassis. No one knows what agents will do to traffic volumes, and I suspect companies that consider this overkill today will think differently in three or four years. Headroom is cheaper than a forklift upgrade at a remote site. Also notable: Arista co-designed the 7280R4 with a hyperscaler seeking a gray-to-coherent bridge, a sign that it’s building with its biggest customers.

The most intriguing product is the hardened 7020HR4, built for 5G and AI-RAN cell sites. Telcos have largely sat out the AI buildout, yet they own the last mile and real estate near users, exactly what low-latency inference requires. This gives a carrier the backbone to offer a managed AI factory.

My view is that this performs better outside the U.S., where enterprises don’t trust carriers beyond connectivity. In Europe and Asia-Pacific, managed services are far more common, and providers such as BT, NTT and Telstra have the footprint to make it work. With sovereignty requirements, the opportunity for telcos to move up the stack has never been better. Telcos have never been a core market for Arista, so any growth from that audience is additive to its already massive market.

Since 2019, Arista has reported a far lower CVE count than competitors, even after the surge in AI-assisted discovery following Anthropic’s Mythos. I’m skeptical of CVE comparisons because counts depend on testing rigor, installed base and reporting practices, and some vendors now bundle multiple issues into a single CVE.

The more relevant benefit is operational. Customers often don’t apply patches because upgrades cause downtime and break things. If they trust the software, they patch faster, and the risk window shrinks. With Mythos accelerating the retirement of end-of-support gear, quality and longevity become buying criteria, not nice-to-haves.

On the call, Gibbs agreed it’s hard to draw conclusions from CVE counts but explained that CVE counts were a measure of Arista’s software quality. This has been Arista’s calling card since it was a startup. While CVEs provide one metric, the bigger proof point is its historical track record of quality software.

Also, wire-speed MACsec and IPsec on every port is a differentiator because AI brings different security requirements. However, integrated security does not replace firewalls. I asked Gibbs about this, and he said that Arista has no intention of replacing firewalls and expects Palo Alto Networks Inc. to continue to sit behind it in the line. I’d like to see that formalized into validated designs for distributed inference, like what Nvidia Corp.-validated designs did for the back end.

The optical line system is a similar simplification play. Arista isn’t an optical company and is reselling these products, but offering dark fiber customers a turnkey, EOS-integrated way to move 25.6 Tbps across a metro network removes a real headache.

Customers have responded positively to Arista’s entry into this market. Douglas Fast Net Chief Technology Officer Jon Vradenburg said the company needs “a compact platform that supports the services our business and carrier customers rely on.” Takayuki Sakou of Japan’s STNet cited “higher throughput and improved power efficiency while maintaining the quality of the EOS software we trust.”

The back end of AI networking is largely a solved architecture at this point. The front end is not, and that’s where the next round of competition will play out. With R4, Arista is betting that its routing credibility, built quietly within hyperscaler backbones, can make it the default there as well. Given how much traffic agentic AI is likely to generate, that’s a bet that, like most Arista bets, will likely pay off.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5415. The rise of the multi-market agent: Why local expertise is going global

Wealth is mobile, and so are luxury clients. Here’s how the multi-market real estate agent combines local expertise with a connected brokerage network.

Ask a luxury client where they live, and the answer is increasingly more than one place. A primary home in Los Angeles, a ski house in Aspen, a pied-à-terre in New York, a winter retreat in Miami or the Caribbean.

Wealth has become more mobile, and so have the people who hold it. The agents who serve these clients best are evolving alongside them, building expertise across markets and cultivating relationships that extend well beyond their own backyards.

That shift is changing what it means to be a local expert. For brokerage leaders, it also raises an important question: Are we building networks that reflect how our clients actually live?

Remote work, flexible schedules and a generation of buyers who think of themselves as global citizens have loosened the link between where someone earns, where they live and where they invest.

Today’s luxury buyers are driven by lifestyle, whether that means access to mountains, water, a particular school system or a city’s cultural calendar, and they are comfortable buying in places where they spend only part of the year. What has not changed is their expectation of personalized service.

For these clients, a traditional handoff creates friction. Each time they are passed from one agent to another, they repeat their goals, rebuild trust and wonder whether anyone sees the full picture. A client’s real estate portfolio is one story. Their advisor should be able to tell it across markets.

Going global does not mean going generic. A Manhattan co-op board, a Florida insurance requirement, a Colorado water right and a California disclosure obligation each carry real consequences, and clients need professionals who understand the market in which they are buying or selling.

The mistake is confusing geographic reach with geographic expertise. The strongest multi-market agents know where their knowledge is deepest and where collaboration adds value. The future of the multi-market real estate agent isn’t about being an expert everywhere. It’s about knowing where your expertise ends, who to bring into the conversation and how to make that collaboration seamless for the client.

When a client has a positive experience with an agent in one city, that relationship shouldn’t end at the city limits. But there is a meaningful difference between providing a referral and extending a trusted relationship. If an agent simply passes along a name, the client starts over. If that introduction comes with shared context and a clear understanding of the client’s priorities, the experience feels seamless.

Trust is portable, but only when it is supported by consistent service and relationships built before a client needs them.

A global footprint alone does not create a global client experience. Offices in multiple markets mean little if they operate independently. Brokerages need to provide the infrastructure that makes cross-market relationships work, including introductions between offices, shared market intelligence, consistent training and clear expectations around communication and referrals.

At The Agency, we encourage agents to bring colleagues from other offices into client relationships early, so clients experience a connected team rather than a series of separate introductions. Technology helps agents share insights, access inventory and present properties remotely, but the real advantage comes from the relationships behind it.

Start by looking at the markets that consistently appear in your referral activity and client conversations. Those patterns show where to build stronger partnerships between offices.

Invest in cross-market education so agents recognize regional nuances and regulatory considerations and know when to bring in specialized expertise. Set clear collaboration standards for how clients are introduced, who takes the lead and how agents stay involved. Then measure success beyond the transaction: Did the client feel supported, and was communication consistent?

As brokerage leaders, we should be asking whether our networks are simply growing in size or becoming more connected. Those are very different measures of success.

Local expertise has never been more valuable. What is changing is its reach. The brokerages that treat their agents’ knowledge as a connected network, rather than a set of separate territories, will be better positioned to serve today’s clients and the next generation of buyers who increasingly see the world, not one city, as their real estate market.

Rainy Hake Austin is president of The Agency in Los Angeles. Get connected on Instagram.

#5414. ZTO Reports Third Quarter 2026 Unaudited Financial Results

10.2 Billion Parcels Expanded Market Share to 20.1%Adjusted Net Income Increased to RMB2.6 Billion

SHANGHAI, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ZTO Express (Cayman) Inc. (NYSE: ZTO and SEHK: 2057), a leading and fast-growing express delivery company in China ("ZTO" or the "Company"), today announced its unaudited financial results for the third quarter ended September 30, 2026[1]. The Company grew parcel volume by 7.0% year over year while maintaining high quality of service and customer satisfaction. Adjusted net income increased 2.6%[2] to RMB2.6 billion. Net cash generated from operating activities was RMB3.7 billion.

Operational Highlights for Third Quarter 2026

[1] An investor relations presentation accompanies this earnings release and can be found at http://zto.investorroom.com.

[2] Adjusted net income is a non-GAAP financial measure, which is defined as net income before share-based compensation expense and non-recurring items such as impairment of investments in equity investees, impairment of goodwill, gain/(loss) on disposal of equity investment and subsidiary and corresponding tax impact which management aims to better represent the underlying business operations.

[3] Adjusted EBITDA is a non-GAAP financial measure, which is defined as net income before depreciation, amortization, interest expenses and income tax expenses, and further adjusted to exclude the shared-based compensation expense and non-recurring items such as impairment of investments in equity investees, impairment of goodwill, gain/(loss) on disposal of equity investment and subsidiary which management aims to better represent the underlying business operations.

[4] One ADS represents one Class A ordinary share.

[5] Adjusted basic and diluted earnings per American depositary share attributable to ordinary shareholders is a non-GAAP financial measure. It is defined as adjusted net income attributable to ordinary shareholders divided by weighted average number of basic and diluted American depositary shares, respectively.

Mr. Meisong Lai, Founder, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of ZTO, commented, "In the third quarter of 2026, ZTO held to its strategic principle of high-quality service, high-quality market share and low end-to-end costs. Parcel volume reached 10.2 billion, up 7.0% year over year and 4.1 percentage points ahead of the industry average. Operating profit rose 23.8% to RMB2.98 billion, and adjusted net income was RMB2.6 billion. Daily average retail parcel volume grew 57% year over year and accelerated from the second quarter as higher-value services scaled up generating a favorable mix shift that lifted margin."

Mr. Lai added, "China's express-delivery industry continued to benefit from constructive regulation, and anti-involution has become an industry consensus rather than a policy slogan. Competition is more rational, pricing gradually recovered into the peak season, and competition shifted from a price focus to quality and value. ZTO's Quality-First approach, built on industry-leading efficiency and equitable network policies, is driving that shift into results. We are not trading long-term quality for short-term market share, and we are not buying volume at any price. Rooted in Shared Success culture, we help our partners and couriers earn more while keeping reasonable profit for the company. This is how we are able to sail through any industry and economic cycles."

Ms. Huiping Yan, Chief Financial Officer of ZTO, commented, "For the third quarter this year, our core express ASP rose 13.7% year over year, which was supported by an improved revenue mix from higher-value key-accounts, including rapidly expanding reverse-logistics business. Despite cost pressure from high oil prices, combined unit sorting and transportation costs decreased by 2 cents, thanks to end-to-end digitization and lean operations. SG&A, excluding SBC, was approximately 4.2% of revenue, down from 5.3% in the same period last year. Adjusted net income grew 20.7% year over year taking into consideration of RMB376 million tax refund received in the same quarter last year. Operating cash flow was RMB3.7 billion, and capital expenditure totaled RMB1.3 billion."

Ms. Yan added, "Our results reflected our simple but consistent financial discipline: we seek profitable growth through scale leverage without sacrificing fair price, optimize asset utilization and rely on technological innovations to stay cost competitive. With volume growth decelerated, we are directing focus and effort on building last mile cost advantage and strengthening earnings by our franchise partners and couriers. With that, we are maintaining our parcel-volume growth guidance for the year, and are well positioned to further expand our industry volume leadership."

Third Quarter 2026 Unaudited Financial Results

Total Revenues were RMB14,361.6 million (US$2,142.1 million), increased 21.0% from RMB11,864.7 million in the same period of 2025. Revenue from the core express delivery business increased by 21.6% compared to the same period of 2025 as a result of a 7.0% growth in parcel volume and a 13.7% increase in parcel unit price. Within core express delivery revenue, key account revenue, generated by direct sales organizations, increased by 68.3% mainly driven by increase in e-commerce return parcels. Revenue from freight forwarding services decreased by 8.1% compared to the same period of 2025. Revenue from sales of accessories, largely consisted of sales of thermal paper for digital waybills, increased by 2.8%. Other revenues were mainly derived from financing services.

Total cost of revenues was RMB10,829.3 million (US$1,615.2 million), an increase of 21.6% from RMB8,908.7 million in the same period last year.

Line-haul transportation cost was RMB3,327.7 million (US$496.3 million), increased 0.8% from RMB3,302.0 million in the same period last year. The unit transportation cost decreased 5.9% or 2 cents mainly attributable to better economies of scale and improved load rate through more effective route planning offsetting higher diesel prices.

Sorting hub operating cost was RMB2,595.9 million (US$387.2 million), increased 8.4% from RMB2,394.1 million in the same period last year. The increase primarily consisted of (i) RMB110.8 million (US$16.5 million) increase in labor-associated costs partially offset by automation-driven efficiency improvements, and (ii) RMB66.0 million (US$9.8 million) increase in depreciation and amortization costs associated with automation facilities and equipment upgrades. As of September 30, 2026, there were 805 sets of automated sorting equipment in service, compared to 761 sets as of September 30, 2025.

Cost of accessories sold was RMB139.9 million (US$20.9 million), increased by 3.2% compared with RMB135.6 million in the same period last year.

Other costs were RMB4,570.4 million (US$681.7 million), increased 59.1% from RMB2,872.2 million in the same period last year, which was mainly due to an increase of RMB1,665.7 million (US$248.4 million) for pickup and dispatching costs paid to network partners associated with serving key account customers, primarily for handling e-commerce return parcels.

Gross Profit was RMB3,532.4 million (US$ 526.9 million), increased by 19.5% from RMB2,956.0 million in the same period last year. Gross margin rate was 24.6% compared to 24.9% in the same period last year.

Total Operating Expenses were RMB555.9 million (US$82.9 million), compared to RMB550.9 million in the same period last year.

Selling, general and administrative expenses were RMB599.3 million (US$89.4 million), decreased by 5.3% from RMB632.6 million in the same period last year, mainly due to (i) RMB13.3 million (US$2.0 million) increase in compensation and benefit expenses, offset by (ii) RMB44.6 million (US$6.7 million) decrease in depreciation and amortization costs associated with administrative facilities and equipment.

Other operating income, net was RMB43.4 million (US$6.5 million), compared to RMB81.7 million in the same period last year. Other operating income mainly consisted of (i) RMB106.6 million (US$15.9 million) in losses on disposal and impairment of fixed assets, (ii) RMB94.7 million (US$14.1 million) of government subsidies and tax rebates, and (iii) RMB55.3 million (US$8.2 million) of rental and other income.

Income from operations was RMB2,976.5 million (US$444.0 million), increased 23.8% from RMB2,405.0 million for the same period last year. The operating margin rate increased to 20.7% from 20.3% in the same period last year.

Interest income was RMB103.1 million (US$15.4 million), compared with RMB185.2 million in the same period last year.

Interest expenses was RMB48.0 million (US$7.2 million), compared with RMB54.4 million in the same period last year.

Gain from fair value changes of financial instruments was RMB103.5 million (US$15.4 million), compared with a gain of RMB102.3 million in the same period last year. Such gain or loss from fair value changes of the financial instruments is quoted by commercial banks according to market-based estimation of future redemption prices.

Income tax expenses were RMB570.2 million (US$85.0 million) compared to RMB160.0 million in the same period last year. Net income was RMB2,573.4 million (US$383.8 million), which increased by 1.4% from RMB2,538.7 million in the same period last year.

Adjusted net income was RMB2,571.1 million (US$383.5 million), compared with RMB2,506.1 million during the same period last year.

Basic and diluted earnings per ADS attributable to ordinary shareholders were RMB3.37 (US$0.50) and RMB3.20 (US$0.48), compared to basic and diluted earnings per ADS of RMB3.16 and RMB3.10 in the same period last year, respectively.

Net cash provided by operating activities was RMB3,720.7 million (US$555.0 million), compared with RMB3,211.0 million in the same period last year.

Mr. Xing Liu has tendered his resignation as a non-executive director of the Company, as well as a member of the audit committee and compensation committee of the Board, due to his other business engagements which require more of his time and dedication, effective November 18, 2026. Mr. Liu has confirmed that he has no disagreement with the Board and that there are no matters relating to his resignation that need to be brought to require the attention of the Company's shareholders or The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong Limited. The Company extends its sincere gratitude to Mr. Liu's service and wishes him the best in his future endeavors.

The Board has appointed Mr. Wei Zhu, an independent non-executive director of the Company, as a member of the audit committee and compensation committee, effective on the same date.

The Board has approved a new share repurchase program (the "New Program") in March 2026, authorizing the repurchase of up to US$1.5 billion of its shares over the next 24 months, effective from March 20, 2026, through March 20, 2028. As of the end of third quarter of 2026, the Company had repurchased an aggregated of 17,631,812 ADSs for US$376.9 million (including repurchase commissions) under the New Program, leaving US$1.1 billion of capacity under the authorization.

Based on current market and operating conditions, the Company reiterates that its parcel volume for 2026 is expected to increase by 6.0% to 10.0% year over year, representing a parcel volume range of 40.8 billion to 42.4 billion. Such estimates represent management's current and preliminary view, which are subject to change.

#5413. New-Home Buyers See Lower Rates as Builders Offer More Incentives

A young couple surveys the construction of their new home.

Despite continuous woes in housing construction, homebuyers may see some deals on the table if they buy a new home vs. an existing home.

With affordability having become a large problem for the new-home industry, builders have been offering incentives, price cuts and more to buyers in order to complete sales on their homes.

In October’s existing-home sales report, NewHomeSource and Zonda Chief Economist Ali Wolf even said that, in her opinion, new homes continue to offer better options for consumers with more sales at lower prices, a trend that will likely continue in the new-home market through the end of the year, as builders work to meet their year-end goals.

“As we watch existing home sales next month, buyers will still see more options and incentives for new homes in the fall and winter, making it the prime season for new-home shopping,” she continued.

Now, a new report from Realtor.com® has found that buyers of new homes are also seeing reduced mortgage rates.

The report found that new-home buyers saw an average starting mortgage rate of 5.01% in Q3, compared with 6.15% for existing-home buyers. This translates to about $258 less per month in interest during the first year of homeownership (on a $400,000 home purchase with 10% down).

While some of these rate reductions are only temporary (via rate buydowns), the report also noted that the fixed-rate mortgage also saw a lower rate for new-home buyers. Specifically, new-home buyers saw an average rate of 6.19%, compared with 6.68% for existing-home buyers. This translates to about $117 less per month in interest for the 30-year loan term (on a $400,000 home purchase with 10% down).

“Builders have adjusted to a market where affordability is still a major hurdle, but that adjustment isn’t always visible in the listing price,” said Realtor.com Senior Economist Joel Berner. “Reduced mortgage rates can help make a new home more affordable for buyers while allowing builders to hold asking prices relatively steady.”

#5412. Dell puts a single gateway between enterprise AI agents and the data they crave

Data intelligence is becoming the deciding layer of the enterprise AI factory as companies learn that racks of graphics processing units deliver little value when agents lack trusted, governed context.

Neocloud providers built the first wave of large-scale AI systems, and core enterprise customers now want the same capabilities inside their own organizations. Dell Technologies Inc. recently extended its AI Data Platform with semantic and knowledge graph features aimed at that market shift. But both the challenge and the opportunity lie in pairing structured and unstructured data so agents get full context while maintaining guardrails and human oversight, according to Srinath Alapati (pictured, right), senior director of product marketing for AI Data Platform at Dell.

“The bottom line is if you feed the wrong data, you get the wrong outcomes,” Alapati said. “What we’ve found is in our own testing — by giving the right context — you can improve the accuracy from roughly 60% to like 94%.”

Alapati, Alison Biers (center), senior director of product marketing for compute, networking and global industries at Dell, and Adam Glick (left), senior director of AI solutions product marketing for compute at Dell, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Dell is tying data, infrastructure management and validated designs together to move enterprise AI factories into production. (* Disclosure below.)

Enterprises can’t give agents unfettered access to their systems, which is where Dell’s newly announced Agentic Data Gateway fits. The gateway sits in the orchestration layer as a single point of control, backed by a Model Context Protocol server, Alapati explained. Storage intelligence tells customers what data they hold, who owns it and how large it is, while Dell’s new data intelligence capabilities track lineage and provenance. Hybrid workflows extend that model across the edge, the cloud and the data center, where companies can struggle to meet the data consolidation requirements of other data platform providers.

“They want you to bring all the data to wherever the platform is. That’s not always possible,” Alapati said. “Number one, it’s super expensive. Two is data is always being generated. It’s a never-ending game. You can’t always keep bringing in data, consolidating data. What we do is we only send metadata … That way your data stays where you want to be.”

On the infrastructure side, Dell OpenManage Rack Scale extends management beyond compute endpoints to the network fabric, power and cooling. That gives operators a single operational plane from day zero through day two, according to Biers. A rebuilt, intent-based Dell Fabric Manager replaces the company’s SmartFabric Manager, and Dell’s PowerRack systems treat the full rack as the unit of deployment.

“It is literally six hours from the time it hits your loading dock to full production,” Biers said. “Something that used to take maybe months and months [is] now cut in half, maybe even less.”

More than 6,500 customers now use the Dell AI Factory, and a growing share are core enterprises asking for help putting AI to work, Glick noted. Validated designs built with Nvidia Corp. and other partners cover both the hardware and the full software stack, and Dell is expanding its labs to keep pace with independent software companies joining the ecosystem. Compute still draws most of the attention, but that is only one part of a larger system.

“If you’ve got a factory, compute is your assembly line. It’s the important part,” Glick said. “It’s what you think of when you think of ‘factory’, but that assembly line doesn’t run if you don’t have a warehouse that’s feeding it the raw materials — that’s the data that goes into it.”

#5411. Paychecks are growing, but buyers are still falling behind

Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, while the monthly payment on a median-priced home rose about 9 percent over the past year. Average hourly pay rose 3.1 percent.

The October jobs report showed employers added 165,000 jobs, and consumer prices rose at a slower monthly pace. Over the past year, the monthly payment on a median-priced home has climbed about three times as fast as average pay.

The gain topped the average monthly increase of 48,000 over the prior 12 months, and the unemployment rate held at 4.1 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Nov. 6. The rate has remained within a narrow band of 4.1% to 4.3% since March, according to the BLS. The bureau also revised August and September up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Average hourly earnings for private-sector workers rose 14 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38, a 3.1 percent gain over the year.

At October’s national median existing-home price of $416,700, a buyer putting 20 percent down would pay about $2,243 a month in principal and interest at this week’s average 30-year fixed rate of 7.11 percent, according to an Inman calculation. The same loan at the year-earlier rate of 6.24 percent would cost about $2,050. The difference is about $192 a month, or about 9 percent, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1 percent.

The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4 percent in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6 percent in September, BLS reported Nov. 10. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, rose 0.3 percent, as did shelter.

The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate at 3.75 percent to 4 percent on Oct. 28 in a 10-2 vote, with Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack favoring a quarter-point hike, according to the Fed’s statement. “But inflation is too high,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said in his press conference opening statement. The Fed meets again in December.

Adjusted for inflation, average hourly earnings were unchanged from September to October, according to the BLS Real Earnings report. BLS said a 12-month comparison for October is not available because BLS did not collect October 2025 prices during the federal government shutdown. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent from September 2025 to September 2026, according to the agency’s September report.

The number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million in October, according to BLS. These workers wanted full-time jobs but had their hours cut or could not find full-time work.

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.11 percent for the week ending Nov. 12, up from 6.24 percent a year earlier, according to Freddie Mac.

Existing-home sales fell 5.5 percent from September to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million in October, down 8.8 percent from a year earlier and the lowest pace since August 2010, Inman reported. Annual sales fell in all four regions, and the Northeast was the only region with a monthly decline.

The median price rose 0.4 percent to $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. NAR’s affordability index fell to 100.7 from 107.3 a year earlier, and inventory reached 5.1 months of supply, up from 4.4 months in October 2025.

Forty-three percent of builders cut prices in October, the highest share NAHB has reported since 2020, and 65 percent used sales incentives, according to the National Association of Home Builders. NAHB’s builder confidence index fell three points to 29, its lowest reading since June 2012.

The October data overall shows an economy adding jobs at more than three times its 12-month average pace, while rates and prices keep pressure on buyer budgets. Agents can work from monthly payment figures and available concessions as tools to help keep transactions moving while the Fed weighs its December decision.

#5409. Economic Headwinds Drag Homebuilder Confidence to New Low

Homebuilder confidence in November’s National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) report slumped four points to 25, a new 14- year low amid low consumer sentiment and significant pressure on the housing sector.

Last month’s homebuilder confidence score, a measly 29 points, was already a 14-year low. This month’s new slump sends homebuilder confidence even further back in time to April 2012.

NAHB blamed a variety of causes, the most important of which were “high mortgage rates, ongoing inflation pressure, elevated energy and material costs, (and) rising labor shortages and hesitant buyers.”

“Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today’s economy,” said NAHB Chairman Bill Owens in a statement. “Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction.”

Robert Dietz, NAHB chief economist, focused on the housing market’s supply-side challenges, homing in on “building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability.”

Dietz also added that “(m)ortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back.”

The NAHB/Wells Fargo HMI, an ongoing monthly survey of more than 40 years, asks builders to rate their perceptions of current single-family home sales, potential single-family home sales in the next six months and prospective buyer traffic. Builders’ perceptions on each of these three component indices is scaled onto a range of zero to 100, which is then used to calculate a general homebuilder confidence level.

The three component indices this month were, unsurprisingly, also down. Current sales conditions dropped six points to 28, while future sales conditions dropped two points to 30.

Prospective buyer traffic ticked down two points to 16, another new low for this report. The last time prospective buyer traffic reached these troughs was 15 years ago (excluding a brief period at the start of the pandemic in 2020).

The NAHB/Wells Fargo HMI this month also reported that 46% of builders reduced prices, up 3% from last month. This is the highest share of builders cutting prices in the post-Covid period.

Almost seven-in-10 (68%) builders offered incentives, also up 3%, representing a post-Covid high. November 2026 is now the 20th consecutive month in which at least 60% of builders utilized sales incentives.

Regional HMI scores were similarly gloomy. All four regions experienced declines, but the Northeast and the Midwest experienced the largest declines point-wise at four and five points, respectively. The Northeast now sits at 34 points, the Midwest at 35, and the South and West both tumbled three points to 27 and 23 points, respectively.

Audrey Jiang is an editorial intern for RISMedia.

#5408. 5 questions to ask before you tap ‘invest’ on real estate apps

Real estate investing apps show the average return first. Amanda Neely, CFP, shares five questions on fees, payouts, liquidity and more.

Investing in real estate used to mean buying a building. Now it can mean tapping a button. Crowdfunding platforms, fractional-ownership apps and private lending marketplaces let you put $500 or $50,000 into real estate without ever signing a deed. Plenty of agents use them for their own money, and clients ask agents about them too.

Access is a good thing. But the app puts the friendliest number front and center … an average rate of return. It rarely shows you your actual annualized return after fees and defaults or how far your balance could drop in a bad year.

This fall, I sat down with several people who had all invested through the same program. Each of them had a different understanding of where their money was going.

One had stopped going to the program’s update calls years ago, because nobody on them would tell her whether she was making money or losing it. Every one of them could tell me, to the dollar, what landed in their account each month.

I haven’t put my own money into these platforms, and most of the reasons why are on this list.

Here are five questions to ask before you, or a client, put money into any real estate investing platform.

Some platforms are marketplaces. They connect you to deals that someone else runs. Others steer your money into funds they manage themselves. The second setup isn’t automatically bad, but it means the company can get paid more than once: a platform or membership fee up front, then a management fee inside the fund.

How to check: Find the fund’s name on your statement and look up who manages it. If it’s the same company that recommended it (or a close affiliate), ask for every layer of fees in writing.

Real estate funds on these platforms usually pay monthly or quarterly distributions, and part of each payment is often classified as return of capital. In plain English, part of what you’re paid is your own money coming back.

In real estate, some return of capital is normal. Depreciation lets a property fund pay out cash that isn’t taxed as income yet, and that gets labeled return of capital, too. The warning sign is return of capital paired with a sliding share value.

If the distributions hold steady while the fund’s value per share (often called NAV) keeps dropping, the income is coming out of your principal. You still feel paid every month, and the account is getting smaller.

How to check: In the app, compare the fund’s value per share on the day you bought with today’s. Then look at your year-end tax forms, which show return of capital separately from dividends.

Say you put $20,000 into a private loan that pays you $400 a month for five years. That’s $24,000 back. Spread over five years, it looks like about 4 percent a year. But because part of every payment is your own principal coming home, the annualized return is actually closer to 7.4 percent. The payout made it look worse than it was.

Now flip it. That 7.4 percent only holds if the borrower pays every month. Lending platforms spread your money across many borrowers, and some of them won’t pay. A platform advertising 10 percent that loses 4 percent of its loans to default each year is paying you closer to 6 percent.

How to check: Ask the platform for the annualized return after fees and defaults, not the payout rate. Then ask what that number was in its worst year.

Many of these platforms are newer than the last real estate downturn. A platform that developed when money was cheap hasn’t shown you how it behaves when money is expensive. The company running the app is also a business, and businesses fail. WeWork, the shared-office company, was valued at $47 billion in 2019 and filed for bankruptcy in November 2023.

How to check: Find the platform’s launch date and look for at least one stretch of rising rates or falling prices in its history. Then ask where your investment actually sits. Many platforms hold each property or fund in its own legal entity, separate from the company itself, so your share can survive if the platform doesn’t. If neither answer is clear, size your investment like the experiment it is.

Many platforms expect you to stay in for five years or more. Some charge a penalty to leave early, others limit how much can come out each quarter, and many reserve the right to pause withdrawals entirely. In spring 2020, Fundrise, one of the best-known real estate investing apps, suspended redemptions from its mature funds “until further notice.”

The lockup is part of why these investments can pay more than a savings account, so it isn’t automatically a problem. It becomes one when money you might need in a slow month ends up somewhere that can tell you “not yet.”

How to check: Read the redemption section of the offering documents. Then ask one blunt question: “If I wanted all of it back next month, what would happen?”

When a client asks whether an app is a good idea, try:

“I can’t tell you whether it’s right for you, but here are the five questions to get answered first.”

You come across as the agent who thinks clearly about money without crossing into advice you’re not licensed to give.

Commission income doesn’t arrive on a schedule, so the money you can reach in a slow month matters more than the money that pays the most. Before your own dollars go into a platform, make sure your cushion lives somewhere you can actually reach. Liquidity first, then growth. Treat the app as the growth layer of your plan, not the floor under it.

The average return will always be the number they show you first. Make it the last one you trust.

Amanda Neely is a Certified Financial Planner and the CEO of Counterflow. Connect with her on LinkedIn and Substack.

#5407. Microsoft rolls out new first-party models and updates to agentic AI continuous improvement

Microsoft Corp. today rolled out new generative artificial intelligence models and updates to Foundry, the company’s unified enterprise platform that helps developers and organizations ground, test and deploy AI applications and autonomous agents.

Updates to Foundry IQ, part of Microsoft IQ, now provide an enterprise knowledge graph out of the box, delivering a full estate of unstructured and application data to provide rich context for building applications and delivering on essential use cases.

Microsoft also said Foundry now uses existing transparency and observability capabilities to help customers create learning loops. Internal evaluations allow autonomous agents to establish baselines for quality, safety, latency and cost, enabling continuous behavioral improvements.

This includes human annotations, now in preview, that allow experts to rate and comment on agent traces based on business judgment. It feeds back into an improvement loop. It’s combined with optimization tests against evaluations and comparisons against real-world results. Foundry now also has new capabilities to adapt to supported models with organizational data to apply reinforcement learning while Foundry runs compute.

Each improvement becomes the next baseline and teams can continue measuring results and test changes, allowing them to improve quality.

Microsoft today announced Decision-1.1 is generally available. It’s a fast, cost-effective model designed to make reliable decisions in software at scale.

The generative AI model can make decisions dynamically at low cost, rather than relying on hard-coded rules, while offering superior decision-making capabilities compared with large language models. LLMs spend a lot of time making decisions in routing, classification, prioritization, verification and workflow control by “thinking it through,” which is unnecessary. Decision models are designed to reach answers quickly within constrained definitions and provide calibrated confidence scores, allowing applications to defer when uncertainty is high.

The new model builds on the previous generation, Microsoft-Decision-1, released in October. The new model delivers a significant improvement in intelligence and speed at a competitive price.

The company said it’s built on a new base, Google LLC’s Gemma 4 26B A4, adding multimodal support so it can analyze images in instructions.

Microsoft also extended its MAI, a Microsoft AI first-party family of models added to Foundry for enterprise trust.

These models include the new MAI-Code-2, which can handle demanding agentic coding work; MAI-Code-2-Flash supports high-volume, everyday coding, so developers can choose between performance and cost. Both are now generally available on GitHub, with Code-2-Flash in private preview in Foundry.

MAI-Image-2.7 and MAI-Image-2.7-Flash are now in preview and offer sharper editing and more consistent image generation. These will help brands maintain a consistent look across campaigns at a lower cost.

In cybersecurity, MAI-Cyber-2-Flash is a purpose-built model for cyber efforts and available in preview in Codename MDASH – the company’s agentic code security system in preview for eligible organizations.

Microsoft Foundry itself now has an expanded model pool featuring the top 50 models, supporting a model router and AI Gateway for intelligence model selection. The Foundry also offers more than 11,000 models from OpenAI Group PBC, Anthropic PBC, Meta Platforms Inc., Mistral AI SAS, the open-source community and others.

The company said supported models can be evaluated and deployed in Foundry as part of the same continuous improvement workflow used for agents.

#5405. Compass follows through on Reffkin’s threat, sues 15 MLSs

The brokerage giant announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states.

Several weeks ago at an industry conference, Compass International Holdings CEO Robert Reffkin threatened to sue MLSs that wouldn’t change their rules. Now, the brokerage giant is taking another 15 of them to federal court.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

The announcement marks a major escalation in a fight that has been building since September, fueled by demand letters, legal threats and increasingly pointed public messaging from Compass execs. Eight of the 15 MLSs targeted Thursday are already suing Compass in two separate federal cases, adding another layer to an increasingly complicated legal battle.

A Compass spokesperson described the latest lawsuits to Inman as a follow-through on Reffkin’s warnings at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale in late September, noting that some MLS organizations had filed their own lawsuits before Compass took legal action.

The lawsuits target six MLSs in California, three in North Carolina and six others across the country.

At the center of the lawsuits are MLS rules that require agents to submit listings to the MLS once they begin publicly marketing a property.

Sellers can generally keep their homes off the MLS through an office-exclusive arrangement. But advertising a property on a brokerage website, social media or other public channels typically triggers a requirement to share the listing with the MLS.

Compass argues that those rules unfairly limit competition and prevent agents from offering alternative marketing strategies, even when homeowners want to advertise their properties outside the MLS first.

“Only the law and the homeowner should tell agents how to market a home, and the MLS is neither the law nor the homeowner,” a Compass spokesperson said in a statement shared with Inman. “Agents should be free to compete on the marketing strategies they offer.”

The brokerage also rejected warnings from MLS leaders that allowing public marketing without requiring listings to be shared through the MLS would harm buyers, sellers or competing agents.

Compass pointed to seven of the nation’s 25 largest MLSs that it said already allow agents to publicly market office-exclusive listings without fines. Those MLSs cover approximately 340,000 agents across 12 states, according to the company.

“If what we are asking for is so bad, why has it worked for years in nearly 30 percent of the country?” the spokesperson said.

MLS leaders counter that their rules are intended to ensure that publicly marketed homes are available to other brokers and their buyers. They argue that agents who benefit from access to shared MLS listings should also contribute their own publicly marketed properties.

California Regional MLS CEO Art Carter, who spent months negotiating with Reffkin before the dispute reached federal court, emphasized that point in a recent interview with Inman.

“At some point, you’ve got to say, this is a cooperative,” Carter said.

Carter also warned that withholding listings from MLS databases could leave appraisers and lenders with incomplete information about home sales, making it harder to determine accurate property values.

The new complaints largely echo arguments Compass made in its Oct. 16 antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, accusing MLS organizations of restricting competition through their listing rules. In the complaints filed Thursday against MLSs, Compass seeks triple damages and court orders blocking enforcement of the challenged rules.

On Sept. 8, Compass attorneys sent California Regional MLS a demand letter calling on the organization to stop fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings. The brokerage gave CRMLS until Oct. 6 to comply, warning that it was prepared to spend millions of dollars on litigation if its demands weren’t met.

Similar letters went to other MLS organizations across the country.

On Sept. 23, Compass International Holdings sent a separate letter demanding that MLS organizations stop sharing its agents’ production and listing data with third-party companies that help competing brokerages recruit agents. The letter specifically identified vendors Courted, BrokerMetrics and Brokerkit as examples of companies using MLS data for recruiting.

Compass argued that information provided to MLS organizations for real estate transactions shouldn’t be used to help competitors recruit its agents. It sought greater control over how that data was distributed, including the ability to exclude information associated with its brokerage brands from feeds used by recruiting companies.

Industry experts who recently spoke to Inman questioned parts of Compass’ argument, noting that MLS data serves purposes beyond recruiting and that access is often governed by agreements with brokerages and technology vendors.

Compass later raised the issue in its October antitrust lawsuit against CRMLS, alleging it lost millions of dollars in commissions after agents were recruited away using data the MLS allegedly sold to competing brokerages.

On Sept. 30, Reffkin took his fight over private listings directly to MLS executives at the Council of Multiple Listing Services’ annual conference in Fort Lauderdale. During a contentious session that drew pushback from attendees, Reffkin warned that Compass would begin filing antitrust lawsuits in mid-October against MLSs that continued fining agents for publicly marketing office-exclusive listings.

Photo by Michael Roberts of AJ Canaria Creative Services

He said Compass wanted to display listings on its own website without agents facing penalties, while some MLS executives questioned whether the company’s demands went further and could undermine cooperation.

The dispute reached federal court Oct. 5, when CRMLS sued Compass. Compass filed its own antitrust complaint against CRMLS on Oct. 16.

Amid the escalations, tensions and litigation in recent weeks, MLS organizations have also begun raising money to defend their rules in court. CRMLS announced plans for an MLS Cooperation Legal Defense Fund on Sept. 30, while CMLS subsequently announced a separate legal action fund to be run by an independent nonprofit.

In an Oct. 27 interview with Inman, CMLS CEO Jessica Edgerton said the organization had received preliminary financial commitments and was developing a process for reviewing requests for assistance.

The growing dispute has also coincided with changes to how Compass employees participate in industry leadership. On Nov. 9, Inman broke the news that Compass International Holdings had adopted a policy restricting salaried employees from serving in Realtor association leadership positions. The directive came after brokerage managers and other employees were instructed to step down from association leadership roles, including positions some had spent years working toward.

Compass confirmed the policy change, saying it was extending a similar approach previously adopted by Anywhere Real Estate, which merged with Compass earlier this year. The company did not clarify whether exceptions were permitted or whether the restrictions also applied to MLS boards and committees.

Below is one of the 15 federal antitrust complaints filed by Compass against MLS organizations on Thursday. The lawsuits make similar legal arguments challenging restrictions on publicly marketing listings outside the MLS.
