#5403. Nvidia at SC26: Agents are the new scientists, and they need a lab

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

For most of its history, the high-performance computing market measured progress the same way: how fast a machine could solve a fixed problem. Rankings rose, a new system took the top spot, and the cycle started over. Raw performance remains the foundation of scientific computing, and Nvidia Corp. brought plenty of it to SC26.

But this week, Nvidia argued that speed at solving a single problem is no longer the right way to measure leadership. An equally important question now is how many times a researcher can go from hypothesis to result in a day, and what happens when the “researcher” is an artificial intelligence agent that never sleeps.

That idea ties together Nvidia’s bevy of announcements at the show. The company introduced open science models, a CPU-only supercomputing rack, a new HPC-specific GPU, a batch of CUDA-X libraries, quantum integration for the Slurm workload manager, a quantum co-design platform with IBM and Fermilab, and a co-packaged optics deployment at Lambda. It also marked CUDA’s 20th birthday.

Taken individually, these announcements look like a typical supercomputing show news payload. Taken together, they describe a stack built for a different user, namely the AI agent that reasons through a scientific problem, calls a simulation, reads the result and decides what to try next.

Here’s a summary of what Nvidia announced:

While each announcement is interesting, the more compelling story is what they reveal about where scientific computing is headed. I see five themes.

Ian Buck (pictured), Nvidia’s vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, summed up this thesis when introducing Rubin HPC: “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery.” This marks an important industry shift. Simulation used to be the end product. In an agentic workflow, it’s a tool call within a much larger loop of hypothesis, simulation, and refinement.

When an agent can generate thousands of candidate molecules or material designs, the bottleneck shifts from ideas to the time required to test them. That’s why so much of the SC26 news focuses on loop speed alongside peak flops. Nvidia says cuPhoton cut the time to correlate Event Horizon Telescope black-hole data from more than a month to eight minutes.

At Pacific Fusion, a Nemotron-powered agent running on the same system can analyze plasma simulations as they run, allowing researchers to steer the simulation in real time rather than waiting for it to finish. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory is using Nvidia’s DAQIRI networking library to move electron-microscopy analysis into the experiment itself, so researchers can decide what to measure next while measurements are being taken.

All of these share the same idea: Shrink the gap between asking a question and getting enough of an answer to ask a better one. For researchers, this should change how they evaluate infrastructure. Single-job time-to-solution is an important metric, but time-to-insight per iteration is equally important and should be tracked.

The most important data point at SC26 may have come from a startup, not a supercomputer. Lila Sciences post-trained Nemotron with lab feedback, nearly doubling its accuracy on quantum-dot synthesis protocols to 61%, beating GPT-6 Astra’s 54% at what Nvidia states is 10 to 20 times lower inference cost. Therna nearly doubled accuracy over frontier models in predicting mRNA protein-expression ranges. Terray Therapeutics trained the model to extract reactants, products, and conditions from chemistry diagrams.

That’s consistent with what I’ve been hearing across my enterprise clients: frontier models are a great starting point, but domain-tuned open models often win on accuracy and economics in specialized fields. Science pushes this further than most industries for three reasons. Research data is often proprietary or regulated. Experimental feedback serves as a training signal that general-purpose models lack. Labs want models running on infrastructure they control.

That last point is why Nvidia optimized Nemotron 3.5 Super VL to run on a 128GB DGX Spark. KTH Royal Institute of Technology reports that an agent built on it fixed 81% of broken GROMACS molecular-dynamics setups in a single overnight run on a single Spark.

Nvidia releasing the dataset and the recipes, not just the weights, is important here because the model is a commodity, but the know-how to adapt it is what research teams have lacked.

Nvidia is well-known as the industry’s top GPU provider, but it also offers a CPU rack with Vera. Nvidia is now targeting the part of HPC that has never been accelerated, a market x86 has owned for decades. In Nvidia’s own testing, Vera delivered 1.9 times the performance and 2.4 times the performance per watt of x86 on an OpenFOAM airflow simulation.

DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, has selected Vera for its HLRE-5 system. The new Fortran compiler beta isn’t all that sexy, but it’s an important piece. Huge amounts of scientific code are written in Fortran, and nobody wants to rewrite it. Removing that friction is how a CPU challenger takes share.

Across the portfolio, Vera handles CPU-bound simulation. Rubin HPC is built for sparse, memory-bound science rather than AI training. DGX systems sit alongside IBM quantum computers. Nvidia is extending Slurm, the open-source scheduler most supercomputing centers already use, to schedule QPUs alongside CPUs and GPUs using familiar commands. Nearly 30 data centers are now deploying more than 50 quantum processors, and Alice & Bob, IBM, IQM, Pasqal and Quantinuum have adopted the expanded Slurm.

Nvidia wants to be the company that coordinates whichever processor the agent needs next. An agent doing drug discovery might call a CPU-bound molecular dynamics job, a GPU-accelerated docking run, and eventually a quantum chemistry routine. The vendor that owns the orchestration owns the workflow. Owning the hardware still matters, but less so than before.

The quantum news deserves its own mention because the tone has shifted. Two or three years ago, vendors mostly talked about qubit counts. At SC26, the focus was on error correction, decoding, and integration, which are classical computing problems. Nvidia’s new TCBP-JOBS decoder, available in CUDA-Q QEC 0.9.0, delivers up to 13,000 times faster decoding for error-correction research and reduces some design studies from 12 weeks to 45 minutes. IBM and RIKEN’s hybrid quantum-classical chemistry work, which modeled protein-ligand complexes with up to 12,635 atoms, is a Gordon Bell Prize finalist.

IBM’s Jerry Chow discussed the opportunity: “Scaling quantum and classical together will open new frontiers in high-energy and nuclear physics and beyond.” Nvidia has long embraced a systems approach spanning a broad ecosystem of partners, and IBM adds to that. IBM doesn’t need Nvidia to build qubits; it needs accelerated classical computing to make those qubits useful. That’s a typical position for Nvidia, which becomes essential to quantum, regardless of which qubit approach wins.

Energy used to be a facilities issue in HPC. Now it’s a research constraint because every watt spent on overhead is a watt not available for simulation. Nvidia’s Vera delivers twice the energy efficiency of x86 on the Weather Research and Forecasting model.

Lambda’s deployment demonstrates the same idea at the network layer. Across more than 10,000 GPUs, Lambda used co-packaged optics switches and observed network latency drop by about 4% at rack scale and up to about 10% at pod scale, with a median optics temperature of 36 degrees Celsius versus 51 degrees for pluggable optics. This approach is up to five times more power-efficient and up to 15 times more reliable than pluggables, and engineers can swap the light sources in the field.

As Nvidia’s blog notes, with agentic inference, a single network disruption can cause cascading latency across many agents. When the workload is a continuous loop rather than a batch job, uptime becomes a research metric. Lambda is also the first large-scale neocloud proof point for co-packaged optics, which I expect other GPU clouds will need to address.

It’s fitting that Nvidia marked its CUDA software’s 20th anniversary at the same show. CUDA was introduced at SC06, and Nvidia reports that more than 11 million developers now build on it, with more than 1,000 CUDA-X libraries. From AlexNet to AlphaFold, the pattern has been the same: hardware draws attention, while libraries create lock-in.

The agentic era raises the stakes for that library catalog. A human scientist might know a handful of tools well. An agent can call any of them, so the size and quality of the toolbox matter even more. Every new CUDA-X library is effectively a new skill for every science agent built on the Nvidia stack. That’s the competitive moat that AMD, Intel, and the custom-silicon players have to cross, and it deepened this week.

Most of the performance numbers at SC26 are Nvidia’s own or those of its partners. Historically, I have found Nvidia’s numbers to be accurate, but buyers should validate them against their own workloads. Several key products, including Rubin HPC and HLRE-5, won’t arrive until 2028.

Every additional layer Nvidia owns, from CPU to scheduler integration to quantum decoding, raises the familiar question of how open an end-to-end stack can be. Nvidia’s response this week was a strong emphasis on open source: open models, open datasets, open libraries, and contributions to Slurm.

The bigger takeaway is the shift in what Nvidia is selling. For 20 years, it accelerated the computations scientists ran. Now it’s building the stack for an agent to run the scientific method itself: reason, simulate, measure, refine and repeat. If that model takes hold, the winners in scientific computing won’t be the companies with the fastest single chip. They’ll be the ones that make the whole discovery loop spin fastest. Right now, no one is better positioned than Nvidia for that.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5401. Your ‘just sold’ posts are missing the best part of the story

Turn closings into case studies. Use ChatGPT Voice and footage you already have, plus this free Canva template, to tell the story behind the sale.

I’ve always found it interesting how much time and energy we put into selling a home, only to reduce the entire experience to a “just sold” graphic once the transaction closes.

We spend weeks, sometimes months, developing a marketing strategy, communicating with sellers, negotiating with buyers and navigating challenges along the way, but so little of that work makes it into the content we share afterward.

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with celebrating a closing. But I’ve always felt that the story behind the sale is often more interesting than the sale itself, especially when you consider what a prospective client is trying to figure out when deciding who to hire.

Most sellers probably assume any experienced agent can put their home on the market. What they don’t necessarily know is how that agent approaches marketing, how much effort they’ll put into a listing or how they’ll respond when something doesn’t go according to plan. Those are difficult things to communicate in a listing presentation when every agent is promising some version of the same thing.

For years, I’ve tried to give people a better understanding of our work by creating case studies of the homes we’ve sold. Initially, that meant compiling listing footage into a Reel with a longer caption explaining the transaction. More recently, I’ve been experimenting with carousels that tell those stories across multiple slides using footage we already created to market the property.

What I like about this approach is that people can see what working with us might actually look like, rather than simply taking our word for it.

We recently sold a property in San Pedro where we hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. We found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and we had to start again.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

We eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when we shared the case study, we didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing we’d done. We opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

I liked that opening because it put the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, we explained how we responded, got the property back in front of buyers, and ultimately closed.

We’ve used the same approach to tell different stories, including a transaction in Hesperia, California, where we coordinated a sale for sellers who had moved out of state, and a humorous carousel about a San Diego transaction that generated 15,741 views.

A post shared by KRYS BENYAMEIN | LA & OC Real Estate Agent (@krysbenyamein)

Not every transaction needs an extraordinary twist. Sometimes the interesting part is a problem you solved, a decision you made, or the work that went into making the experience easier for your client. The challenge is recognizing those moments and figuring out how to communicate them.

The storytelling portion generally takes me about 15 minutes, although gathering information and designing the finished post take additional time.

Before writing, I go through the transaction and take inventory of everything we’ve done. I want to know how many open houses we hosted, how many people attended, how many postcards we mailed, how much content we published and how many views our videos generated. I’ll also look at offers received and anything else that helps explain how the sale unfolded.

This has made me more conscious of documenting our work as we’re doing it. It’s difficult to communicate the effort behind a sale if you can’t remember the specifics, and having those numbers also makes it easier to evaluate what worked.

I then gather content we’ve already created, whether that’s property videos, walkthroughs, open house footage, or photographs. Repurposing footage gives that content another life, but agents could create something similar using listing photos.

Once I have everything together, I open ChatGPT Voice and talk through the transaction. I’ll explain the sellers’ circumstances, our approach, the decisions we made and anything unexpected. I don’t organize my thoughts beforehand because I find it more helpful to get everything out and work through the story conversationally.

What I’ve found particularly useful is having ChatGPT ask follow-up questions to identify the most compelling angle. Sometimes what I initially find interesting isn’t what another homeowner would care about, and that back-and-forth helps me consider their perspective.

Once we’ve found the angle, we work on the writing, particularly the opening two slides because Instagram can serve both to your audience. Lately, I’ve preferred carousels with moving video backgrounds, but we’ve also created Reels and experimented with humor. I’ve shared an editable version of our Canva template for anyone who wants to try the format.

If you want to try this with one of your transactions, open ChatGPT Voice and use this prompt:

“Interview me about [Address] I recently closed. Ask me one question at a time about the seller’s goals, our marketing strategy, the decisions we made, challenges we encountered and the outcome. Help me identify the most compelling part of the story and why another homeowner would care. Once we’ve found the angle, help me write a seven-slide Instagram carousel with a strong opening and a natural narrative. Use specific details and results, avoid generic sales language, and don’t invent anything.”

We’ve also been sharing these case studies in emails to our database, giving us another opportunity to demonstrate our experience to homeowners and agents who may eventually refer us business.

If you’ve been in the business for any length of time, you probably have dozens of transactions worth revisiting, with interesting stories buried in them. You don’t need a new closing every week to share those experiences, and you don’t need to make every transaction sound more dramatic than it was.

There’s tremendous value in helping people understand the work we do, particularly when so much happens behind the scenes. If we’re already investing all this time and effort into helping our clients, it seems like a missed opportunity not to share more of it.

Use this FREE Canva template to replicate these results.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5400. Mamdani’s NYC public housing rebuild plan skirts DSA rebuke

Delegates debated and ultimately rejected a resolution opposing redevelopment at two Manhattan public housing properties. Critics cite privatization concerns tied to a shift to project-based Section 8, while the city argues rebuild costs less than renovation.  AI Summary

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s quest to replace aging public housing with new buildings faced a potential political reckoning this past weekend. But Mamdani survived a challenge from like-minded Democratic Socialists.

Delegates to the city’s Democratic Socialists of America convention on Saturday voted down a resolution to oppose the city’s plan to demolish and rebuild two Manhattan public housing developments. It was the only one of nine resolutions to fail at a convention attended by more than 430 delegates.

Mamdani, who didn’t attend the convention, won a year ago on his vow to make New York more affordable. Delivering on that promise has meant sometimes walking a fine line. By proceeding with a plan developed under Eric Adams, a mayor critics accused of being in developers’ pockets, he risks being lumped in with his predecessor.

Democratic socialists now face similar choices elsewhere. In Los Angeles, DSA member Nithya Raman ousted outgoing Mayor Karen Bass on a pledge to build more homes faster. She will likely draw fire from neighborhood advocates opposed to higher density and zoning changes required by new state laws.

The plan is to demolish 2,056 public housing apartments in Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea Houses and rebuild them, with the New York City Housing Authority still owning them. Private developers would then add about 3,500 mixed-income apartments. Current tenants would get new apartments under private management, with rent held at 30% of income.

Had the DSA resolution passed, Mamdani could have faced stiffer backlash against a multi-billion project than he was already facing from tenant rights groups. Instead, Mamdani hopes the project stands as a model for rebuilding other decaying public housing properties elsewhere in the city.

Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea’s 18 buildings were built in phases from 1945 to 1965. Construction largely occurred under Robert Moses’ tenure as the city’s powerful unelected master builder.

Moses supported tall buildings, parks, highways and slum clearance to ease the path, including the site now being redeveloped. He dubbed the area’s tenements and factories blight.

But like public housing across the country, flawed maintenance policies left years of issues unresolved. Pruitt-Igoe in St. Louis began deteriorating within years of the 1954 completion of its 33 towers. The city demolished them by 1976.

Mamdani and DSA members in his administration say the Fulton and Elliott-Chelsea buildings are in such bad shape that tearing them down costs less than renovating them. This approach also adapts to shrinking federal money for public housing.

The administration says NYCHA faces about $78 billion in repair needs. Conversion cash flow is one of the few ways to pay for them.

“Too many leaders have walked away from public housing,” Matt Rauschenbach, a Mamdani spokesman, said in a statement last month. “We are not going to.”

Cea Weaver, who leads the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants and is a DSA member, told Gothamist that leaving the housing in its current disrepair is unacceptable given her socialist values.

The fix has been circulating for years, first under former Mayor Bill de Blasio. Under Adams, NYCHA announced in December 2021 that resident leaders had selected Related Companies and Essence Development as its development partners. Related is best known for Hudson Yards, the 28-acre Manhattan megaproject it built with Oxford Properties.

NYCHA began issuing relocation notices in July 2025, and two buildings are designated for demolition in the first phase.

Critics, including the tenants’ DSA resolution, point to Hudson Yards as evidence that a for-profit firm has no place managing public housing.

“Related Companies is scheduled to make hundreds of millions of dollars from federal funding as well as rents through this project, while we, as socialists, know that a billion-dollar company like Related has no business anywhere near our city’s public housing,” the DSA resolution states.

The resolution says residents have called the project a “land grab.”

Three tenants joined DSA and were elected delegates with the backing of the chapter’s Tenant Organizing Working Group. They argue the plan privatizes public housing. The buildings would move from the federal Section 9 program to project-based Section 8, in which the government subsidizes rent through vouchers.

“We have no interest in being privatized,” Celines Miranda, one of the new delegates, told Gothamist last week. “We have no interest in being demolished.”

The resolution called the buildings structurally sound and criticized developer Related Companies for withholding structural analyses. More than two dozen families, including many seniors, are refusing to move.

Tenants and neighbors also tried to stop the project in court. In July, a state appeals court upheld rulings that denied their requests for preliminary injunctions. The court determined that their challenge was filed after the four-month deadline that began when NYCHA issued its July 2025 decision to proceed.

The court also ruled that relocation, while “inconvenient and difficult,” especially for seniors, did not amount to irreparable harm.

Weaver said the activists do not speak for all residents and that many tenants want the project to proceed.

Only 37% of delegates backed the resolution in a pre-convention survey. It won 44% on the floor, suggesting tenants flipped some votes but not enough to win.

Partnership champions an agile pilot-to-product framework that transforms proprietary machine learning into cross-functional revenue and operational efficiency

SAN JOSE, Calif., Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Los Angeles Football Club (LAFC) today announced a major paradigm shift in how professional sports franchises leverage artificial intelligence, highlighting an innovative co-development framework designed to solve complex business problems. LAFC and AccelerAI launch a co-developed agentic AI system, delivering double-digit growth in enterprise business value.

"Our strategy is built on shifting AI from a speculative tech expense into a core operational multiplier," said Vanessa Montes-Gubin, Chief Marketing Officer of LAFC. When predictive intelligence operates smoothly across marketing, operations, and commercial teams, it allows us to build a more responsive business and deliver highly synchronized, meaningful connection points for our entire global community."

The strength of this co-development model was recently validated through an inaugural matchday attendance pilot. To execute the framework's initial attendance preservation workflows, LAFC and AccelerAI connected advanced predictive engines featuring over 100 contextual data points and partnered with Ticketmaster to validate each seat. By accurately forecasting attendance gaps before kickoff, the system prompted attendance confirmation and organic peer-to-peer ticket transfers through native mobile channels. This single application successfully unlocked double-digit show-rate growth, particularly during volatile weekday windows, while maintaining total ticket price integrity.

"We've always approached technology at LAFC with the expectation that it deliver meaningful business outcomes, and AI is no different," said Christian Lau, Chief Technology Officer of LAFC. "Our work with AccelerAI is focused on bringing together our data, operational expertise and predictive intelligence to address real business challenges. We're moving beyond experimentation by validating these capabilities in a live operating environment and establishing a foundation to scale successful applications across the enterprise. The opportunity isn't simply to deploy more AI; it's to make our entire organization smarter, more efficient and better connected."

"Sports teams have already invested in specialized systems that support every part of the business, but gaps in data visibility and coordination between teams limit their potential," said Albert Shih, Chief Product Officer of AccelerAI. "We see the next opportunity in AI agents that work across those systems to surface insights, coordinate workflows and take action, helping teams move from information to execution. We're bringing our enterprise AI experience to our first partnership in professional sports, and we're grateful to build alongside LAFC. Their deep operational knowledge and commitment to co-development are essential to turning that vision into measurable results."

With its first attendance preservation pilot locked, the collaboration is moving to automate the architecture into a standalone platform, available to other professional sports organizations. LAFC and AccelerAI are already mapping out the next phase of their co-development roadmap, targeting a diverse portfolio of future specialized AI agents designed to drive back-office efficiency, maximize asset utilization, create touchpoints for the LAFC to engage seamlessly with fans and to elevate enterprise revenue opportunities across all lines of club operations.

#5398. A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he said.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

Sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively new sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he said, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move quickly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

What you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he said.

But you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

Often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

But that can be a long road. Sangaré said it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

And when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré said; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

#5397. Idle, then spiking: Why AI agents are breaking Kubernetes resource planning

AI agents are changing the economics of cloud infrastructure, and autonomous orchestration is becoming the way platform teams keep up. Agentic workloads sit idle and then spike without warning. That pattern leaves static resource settings either wasteful or likely to fail.

Container orchestration for AI is fast becoming the backbone of production AI, and agents are adding a new layer of strain. Compute costs are climbing and reliability problems are harder to contain because everything an agent does ultimately runs on CPU and memory, according to Yodar Shafrir (pictured), founder and chief executive officer of ScaleOps Inc.

“Agents and all the agent workloads pretty much made everything way more complex when managing infrastructure,” Shafrir said. “Eventually, all the complexity that existed before just got much worse. Today, the compute cost has grown dramatically. Everything that agents execute eventually runs on compute.”

Shafrir spoke with theCUBE Research’s Paul Nashawaty and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how autonomous orchestration lets ScaleOps adjust resources in real time as AI agents spike, cutting both costs and crashes. (* Disclosure below.)

Agents behave differently from traditional microservices. An agent waits for a human or another agent, checks with a large language model and then runs its task in a burst. Teams must provision for the highest spike while the agent holds its memory the whole time, Shafrir explained. When resources fall short, a crashed step has to rerun and burns tokens all over again.

“We actually see that agents crash due to not having enough resources 80% more often compared with traditional microservices,” Shafrir said. “The reliability is much harder to manage.”

For ScaleOps, the answer is to make resource decisions in real time. It adjusts allocations, replicas and node placement for every application, agent and Model Context Protocol server, which the company says cuts cloud costs by 70% to 80%. Customers such as Adobe Inc. and Salesforce Inc. build trust by first running the platform in read-only mode on their hardest environments, according to Shafrir.

“We understand for every application: What is it connected to? What does it communicate with? What is the business state of every application?” Shafrir said. “We learn from historical patterns.”

ScaleOps has also added a capability that lets other workloads use an agent’s resources while it sits idle. It also uses memory swap so an agent gets memory only when it needs it. The company says this makes running agents 90% more cost-efficient without moving off Kubernetes. Given the cost of always-on agents, Shafrir sees autonomous orchestration as the only workable model.

“We are now in a phase where humans and all the traditional scaling capabilities that existed in the past are pretty much irrelevant for today’s world because they’re too static and they require a human to go and configure them,” Shafrir said. “When things are so dynamic, it no longer works the same way.”

#5396. Lighter Halts Crypto Withdrawals After $15.5M Security Breach as LIT Falls

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Lighter has suspended crypto withdrawals after a suspected security breach drained $15.5 million from two market-maker accounts. Its LIT token fell more than 15% as traders assessed the damage.

The decentralized perpetual futures exchange halted withdrawals and new liquidity pool creation on November 16. The incident reportedly involved compromised API keys belonging to two market makers, rather than a vulnerability in Lighter’s core smart contracts.

Update: Our investigation indicates that today’s incident was caused by a leaked API key for a specific trader's account. The Lighter protocol and smart contracts are unaffected.As a precaution, we have enabled Guardian mode on our smart contract. Our main priority is to… https://t.co/LUuFiY5cK0

On-chain investigators identified a $10.39 million USDC withdrawal from Lighter’s Ethereum settlement contract. Another $5.09 million loss was reported from a second account, although investigators had not independently verified that amount leaving the platform.

The incident has raised fresh questions about security across decentralized derivatives platforms, particularly how exchanges protect large trading accounts and their liquidity infrastructure.

The suspected attacker reportedly gained access to API keys associated with two market-maker accounts. These credentials allegedly provided enough permissions to manipulate their trading positions and liquidity pool activity.

The reported losses were split between two accounts, with $10.39 million and $5.09 million in USDC taken from their respective balances. The alleged attack involved closing existing positions before creating a zero-fee liquidity pool under a compromised account. Attacker purchased nearly all its shares, transferred the victim’s funds into the pool, and redeemed those shares.

Bitquery independently tracked the first major withdrawal through Ethereum. The attacker converted $10.36 million in USDC into ETH within four minutes.

LIVE: tracking the Lighter hack walletAs of 11:36 UTC, 16 Nov:• 10.39M USDC out of @Lighter_xyz → 5,764 ETH• 10 payments of 160 ETH → Hyperliquid → 5,583 XMR1• 4,165 ETH still in the walletWe update as it moves:https://t.co/NZvBlmMEeP https://t.co/JcD3AOQ8Bs

The wallet received 5,764 ETH, subsequently distributing 960 ETH across six fresh wallets. Those wallets moved funds through Hyperliquid and purchased XMR1, while approximately 4,805 ETH remained in the original wallet during Bitquery’s investigation.

Lighter initially described this crypto incident as involving a compromised external party. It suspended withdrawals and new liquidity pool creation while investigating the breach.

The team subsequently clarified that its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. Instead, the incident reportedly originated from a leaked API key belonging to a specific trader.

As of now, Lighter activated Guardian mode on its smart contracts and announced plans to upgrade its contracts through its Security Committee. The exchange also identified recovering funds associated with additional withdrawal attempts as a priority. Its stated target was completing the upgrade and restoring withdrawals by the end of November 16.

LIT traders now face another question: whether the exchange can restore withdrawals quickly enough to prevent a prolonged confidence crisis.

Lighter builds its derivatives ecosystem around Ethereum, while ASTER taps into BNB Chain and Hyperliquid operates its own blockchain. Bitcoin, meanwhile, still has considerable room to develop its decentralized derivatives infrastructure.

Bitcoin Hyper ($HYPER) is positioning its Layer 2 network around that opportunity, combining Bitcoin’s settlement infrastructure with Solana Virtual Machine (SVM) execution for faster transactions and lower fees.

The idea is to bring more sophisticated DeFi applications to Bitcoin, potentially including decentralized perpetual futures trading. Rather than relying exclusively on Ethereum-based liquidity or another standalone derivatives chain, the project aims to connect Bitcoin’s liquidity with high-speed execution.

Its presale has raised more than $33.2 million. The current advertised token price stands at $0.0136, with buyers offered a 35% annual percentage yield (APY) through its staking program.

The project also has a live testnet featuring a bridge, faucet, explorer, and wallet infrastructure. Its roadmap targets further development of its Bitcoin bridge and DeFi ecosystem.

November 26 is the presale closing date, putting the token’s next major launch milestone just days away. So, for those watching the next generation of decentralized derivatives, Bitcoin’s potential role in that market remains an interesting opportunity.

Bitcoin Hyper is betting that combining Bitcoin’s liquidity with Solana-style execution can help establish that missing infrastructure.

Lighter’s immediate challenge is restoring withdrawals and demonstrating that its security upgrades address the vulnerabilities exposed by the incident. The $15.5 million loss is big, but the bigger issue is whether users and market makers remain comfortable keeping capital on the platform.

The coming sessions could prove decisive as traders monitor withdrawal availability, recovery efforts, and further disclosures from the exchange.

#5395. Promise Robotics raises $25M to scale automated homebuilding

Promise Robotics closed a $25M Series B after landing a multiyear D.R. Horton agreement. Its strategy focuses on platform investment and portable production to reduce fixed cost exposure that hurt prior industrialized builders.  AI Summary

Any way you look at it, homebuilding comes down to three things: how many homes a company can produce and sell, how much it costs to produce them, and how consistently the business can turn those homes into positive net margins. There’s no getting around throughput.

Homebuilding leaders who do those three things well rarely have qualms about finding ways to do them even better. Innovation, however, is another matter. Homebuilders like innovation. Many believe it’s necessary, even inevitable. But do they have to embrace it? Do they have to change how they operate to adopt and integrate it? Do they dare risk what works, warts and all, for what hasn’t yet proven to solve the throughput riddle economically?

Evidence suggests that if innovation were a necessity rather than a choice, or a known rather than a leap into a chasm of unknowns, more of the dozens of companies launched over the past decade with promises to transform homebuilding, lower costs and make homes more attainable would still be in business today.

Which brings us to Promise Robotics, a company whose name might as well be its business plan: Say what you’re going to do, and then do what you say.

Fresh off a multiyear commercial agreement with D.R. Horton, the nation’s largest homebuilder, Promise Robotics today announced a $25 million Series B financing round led by White Star Capital, with participation from Horizons Ventures, Radical Ventures and the Public Sector Pension Investment Board.

The financing follows Promise’s agreement to support the production of more than 1,250 homes for D.R. Horton as the company prepares to bring its first U.S. manufacturing facility online in Phoenix in 2027. Promise already operates production facilities in Calgary and Nisku, Alberta, and reports more than 2,000 housing units under contract across three markets.

For Promise co-founder and CEO Ramtin Attar, the latest investment adrenaline shot is an opportunity to show that the company has figured out how to turn advanced robotics, artificial intelligence and factory-built construction into a sustainable business capable of weathering homebuilding’s inevitable ups and downs, which, by the way, are now mostly downs.

That’s where this homebuilding innovation’s never-ending story takes a turn.

Because the history of industrialized homebuilding is littered with companies that developed impressive technologies, attracted enthusiastic investors, and secured commitments from builders, only to discover that the economics of operating their businesses – and the critical factor of the time value of money in a stubbornly high cost of money backdrop – were far less forgiving than the promise of their innovations.

Attar is all too familiar with that history. So are his investors.

“Every investor’s question often starts by asking what went wrong with Katerra, what went wrong with X and Y and Z,” Attar told HousingWire TBD in an exclusive interview.

His determination is to transform Promise Robotics into a fundamentally different kind of construction technology business, one that uses venture capital to develop its technology platform while seeking lower-cost financing to scale its physical production capacity.

“We have been very clear about what we want to use this funding for,” Attar said. “It’s not for funding factories; it’s for funding the platform.”

Attar’s laser clarity on how the strategy will be operationalized may prove more important to Promise’s long-term prospects than the robots themselves. The distinction goes directly to the problem that has defeated so many would-be homebuilding innovators: scaling manufacturing capacity without accumulating fixed costs that become unsustainable when housing demand weakens.

One of the more revealing details from Attar’s latest interview concerns what Promise calls a factory. The company’s Phoenix operation is being set up in a 16,000-square-foot warehouse with existing electrical infrastructure and a loading bay. Attar said the facility requires almost no tenant improvements and is under a relatively short-term lease.

Importantly, the robotic equipment itself can be ported from market to market.

“It was the same two robots that were producing homes in Calgary,” Attar said. “We just moved them to Phoenix two weeks ago. They’re already set up. We’re just hiring, and we’re going to start producing.”

Portability is central to Promise’s effort to avoid the fixed-cost exposure associated with large, purpose-built manufacturing facilities. The company can theoretically deploy equipment in markets where customer demand supports production, rather than making a substantial permanent investment in each market before securing sufficient orders.

The model still depends on reliable demand, efficient material handling, trained workers, and economical installation. But it offers more flexibility to respond to changing market conditions. Attar also described an operational improvement that provides a clearer view of the company’s economic progress.

When Promise initially relied on outside contractors to install its prefabricated components, installation costs averaged about C$9 per square foot. After developing its own installation workforce, the company reduced that figure to about C$4.50.

That 50% reduction is significant, though it applies to installation costs rather than to total home construction costs. For Attar, it shows that the opportunity to improve construction economics extends beyond robotic manufacturing.

“There are still tremendous gains to be made on the human side of things,” he said.

The company’s recursive learning process increasingly involves understanding labor requirements, installation sequencing, material logistics and how production crews work alongside existing trades. Those improvements and the ongoing learning may prove as important as advances in robotic speed or capability.

Promise’s agreement with D.R. Horton establishes a prominent commercial relationship, serves as a lever for inroads among other operators and provides an opportunity to demonstrate its capabilities within one of homebuilding’s most sophisticated production organizations.

The multiyear agreement calls for Promise to support the production of more than 1,250 homes. For D.R. Horton, the attraction is access to automated manufacturing capacity without the expense and operational complexity of owning the infrastructure.

For Promise, the relationship offers the prospect of production volume, operating experience and elevated credibility with other builders. Attar said interest from additional homebuilders has increased following the announcement.

What’s more, the vibe around Promise has extended beyond potential new customers. Committed production volume could also help Promise secure financing for equipment and facilities at lower costs than venture equity.

“If you’ve got commitment, you can start to get creative about accessing [capital],” Attar said. “Using equity to build factories is the most expensive way to go about it.”

He believes that once individual manufacturing operations achieve sustainable economics, they can attract conventional financing. That remains an objective rather than an established financing model across Promise’s network. The company has not publicly disclosed factory-level profitability, capital requirements per deployment, or the utilization rates needed to support debt repayment.

Those measures will be important tests of its ability to expand without continually returning to venture investors for more capital.

According to Attar, Promise’s current production capabilities cover roughly 15% to 20% of construction activity, depending on the market and the components included. The company is working to increase that share to about 40% by incorporating more building systems into its manufacturing process.

In Canada, Promise already produces structural components that can include windows, doors and openings for mechanical systems. It has begun projects involving HVAC and plumbing, with electrical work, insulation, and drywall next.

Builders can begin with familiar framing components, build confidence in the manufacturing process, and gradually move additional work into the factory. That approach accounts for the effort required to change an industry whose production process depends on established relationships among independent trades.

“We’ve got to work alongside trades. We’ve got to work alongside the existing supply chain,” Attar said.

It also creates another challenge. Manufacturing more complete building assemblies can improve efficiency, but those benefits depend on local building codes, inspection requirements, and the ability to coordinate factory production with construction-site schedules.

Promise will need to show that greater factory completion lowers total costs and speeds home deliveries, rather than simply shifting work and complexity from one location to another.

The timing of Promise’s financing introduces another important test. Homebuilders face weak affordability, elevated financing costs, and persistent uncertainty about consumer demand. At the same time, labor availability remains a structural constraint, and immigration enforcement is further disrupting construction workforces in some markets.

That combination creates both opportunity and risk for automated construction.

Builders have stronger reasons to secure reliable production capacity and reduce their exposure to labor shortages. But they also have limited tolerance for new expenses, operational disruption, or technology that takes a long time to deliver measurable returns.

Promise’s model attempts to address that contradiction by allowing builders to purchase output without making upfront investments in robotic equipment.

Attar said the company is also developing installation partnerships to establish clear labor costs, quality expectations and operating standards.

Rather than necessarily employing every installation worker directly, Promise intends to use its platform to coordinate qualified installation teams across markets.

The company is preparing for two additional factory deployments in 2028, with the ambition to reach a pace of one new deployment per quarter by early 2029.

Those targets represent a substantial increase in operational complexity. Technology that works reliably in a small number of facilities must eventually support geographically dispersed teams, different builders, varying local regulations, and multiple supply chains.

Attar identifies workforce development and organizational culture as major challenges in that transition.

“At some point, technology scales really fast. It’s very controllable. It’s very measurable,” he said. “But how do you continue to grasp and build a culture, an environment that people thrive, they’re committed?”

For a business whose ultimate performance depends on the interaction among software, machinery, materials and people, that question looms large.

White Star Capital general partner Sanjay Zimmermann describes Promise as an opportunity to build a new production infrastructure platform for homebuilding.

“Just as impressive is how well this team executes across builders, projects, and markets, with their recent multi-year agreement with D.R. Horton a powerful proof point,” Zimmermann said in the financing announcement.

White Star’s investment thesis rests in part on the expectation that Promise’s production network will become more valuable as it expands.

More factories could generate additional operating data, purchasing opportunities, and production experience. These advantages could improve costs and performance across the network. But the economics must ultimately be demonstrated at the level of individual projects and facilities.

The company’s reported 2,000-plus housing units under contract demonstrate commercial traction, though that figure should not be confused with completed production or recognized revenue.

Likewise, the ability to reduce installation costs or shorten framing schedules does not automatically translate into lower total construction costs for customers. The evidence investors and builders will need includes sustained factory utilization, positive operating cash flow, reliable delivery performance, and measurable improvements in homebuilding economics. These practical measures will test Promise’s claims.

The $25 million Series B gives Promise Robotics more capital to develop its technology and pursue the expansion opportunities created by its growing commercial relationships. The D.R. Horton agreement gives it an important customer relationship and a proving ground for its operating model.

The difficult history of industrialized construction demonstrates that technological sophistication, investor enthusiasm and even strong initial customer interest won’t substitute for sustainable unit economics.

Attar’s approach reflects an appreciation for and hard-earned lessons from that history. Promise is concentrating on established construction activity, minimizing permanent factory investments, developing repeatable operating processes, and seeking financing structures that better match the economics of manufacturing.

Its most important advances may ultimately come from reducing installation costs, improving logistics, increasing utilization, and learning to integrate with builders’ existing operations.

That is a less glamorous story than robots transforming homebuilding overnight. It is also a more credible path to making industrialized construction an enduring part of the industry’s production system.

For an industry that needs more affordable homes but cannot rely on stronger demand, abundant labor or easier financing to solve its problems, Promise represents a potentially valuable experiment in doing more with the resources available.

The next two years will begin to show whether that experiment can become a durable business. And that is the real promise behind Promise Robotics’ latest round of financing: not simply developing a better way to build, but proving that the business of building better can survive long enough to change the industry.

#5394. ELEGOO Showcases New Solutions Across Resin Printing, FDM Printing and 3D Scanning at Formnext 2026

FRANKFURT, Germany, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ELEGOO, a rapidly developing brand in the global smart manufacturing industry, kicked off its participation at Formnext 2026 today, showcasing its latest product developments and offering visitors an exclusive first look at upcoming innovations. At booth 12.0-C02, ELEGOO brought together live product demonstrations, new innovation previews, and creator-led sessions, highlighting its continued exploration of resin printing, multi-material FDM printing, and connected creative workflows.

Kevin Wang, Co-founder and Vice President of ELEGOO, said, "We're continuously exploring new possibilities across different technologies to bring more versatile tools and solutions to creators. At Formnext this year, we're excited to share a preview of our upcoming developments in resin and FDM printing, alongside our latest 3D scanning solutions. The show also gives us a great opportunity to connect with creators and industry partners, exchange ideas, and be part of the conversations shaping the industry."

A First Look at What's Next in Resin and FDM Printing

Among the highlights, ELEGOO presented the Saturn 5 Ultra, its upcoming resin 3D printer. Designed as an all-round desktop resin printer, it combines high-precision performance and improved durability with enhanced productivity and ease of use. Its intelligent resin management system automates resin monitoring and replenishment, while design improvements simplify setup, maintenance, and operation. The Saturn 5 Ultra is currently planned for an early Q1 2027 launch.

ELEGOO also gave visitors an exclusive first look at the Centauri X Ultra, marking a significant milestone in the evolution of the Centauri series with its move into multi-printhead technology. Featuring four independent printheads, this upcoming FDM 3D printer explores new possibilities in multi-color and multi-material printing. Quick printhead switching helps minimize material waste during color changes, while compatibility with rigid and flexible materials enables a wider range of functional and creative applications. Its unexpected debut at Formnext drew visitors to the ELEGOO booth, sparking curiosity about the new addition to the Centauri series.

Experiencing the 3D Scanning Workflow with M1 Ultra

Another key highlight at the booth is the M1 Ultra, ELEGOO's first all-in-one smart 3D scanner. Through live demonstrations, visitors can experience its scanning capabilities and explore a complete workflow, from capturing physical objects to processing digital models with ELEGOOSCAN software. With metrology-grade accuracy of up to 0.02 mm and multiple scanning modes for different object sizes, surfaces, and levels of detail, the M1 Ultra supports applications ranging from reverse engineering and product development to digital archiving and 3D printing.

Connecting with Creators and the Global 3D Printing Community

Beyond product demonstrations, ELEGOO is hosting daily creator workshops at around 4:00 p.m., featuring experienced 3D printing creators who share practical insights, creative applications, and firsthand experiences with ELEGOO products. The sessions have attracted groups of visitors gathering around the booth to watch live demonstrations and interact with the creators, adding an engaging, community-driven dimension to the exhibition. ELEGOO is also holding daily prize draws, offering visitors the chance to win 3D printers and ELEGOO-branded gifts and accessories.

ELEGOO will continue showcasing its products and innovations at Formnext 2026 through November 20 at booth 12.0-C02, Messe Frankfurt, Germany. Visitors are welcome to stop by to experience live demonstrations and explore ELEGOO's latest developments firsthand.

Founded in 2015, ELEGOO is a rapidly developing brand in the global smart manufacturing industry, specializing in R&D, manufacturing, and sales of consumer-grade 3D printers, laser engravers, STEM kits, and other smart technology products. Located in Shenzhen, the Silicon Valley of China, the company has sold millions of products across more than 150 countries and regions. In 2025, the company's total sales revenue surpassed 300 million USD, with more than 1000 employees and over 430,000 square meters of office and manufacturing area. With a focus on programming and 3D printing technology, ELEGOO provides unique and smart creation spaces for diverse consumers to enhance personalized experiences.

#5393. Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

When agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer said yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

Imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

Suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

One of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

That’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”

When I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

Maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

This is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

So, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”

Twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5392. Mortgage rates jump to 7.58% as inflation lifts bond yields

Mortgage rates rose sharply last week, with 30-year conforming loans at 7.58% and jumbo loans at 7.87%. Hot inflation data and higher yields pushed Fed hike expectations above 93%, while builders continued offering rate incentives for new homes.  AI Summary

Mortgage rates skyrocketed last week on the back of rising inflation and bond yields, erasing some of the recent affordability gains for potential homebuyers.

At HousingWire‘s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year conforming loans averaged 7.58%, up 23 basis points from one week ago. Rates for 30-year jumbo loans jumped 31 bps to average 7.87%, while rates for 30-year loans through the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) rose 15 bps to 7.37%.

HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami wrote over the weekend that “last week wasn’t good for mortgage rates or the bond market” due to hawkish statements from Federal Reserve officials and hot inflation data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Additionally, the U.S. conflict with Iran and potential tariff increases against Mexico propelled long-term Treasury rates and mortgage rates upward.

Interest rate traders took notice. According to the CME Group‘s FedWatch tool, more than 93% expect benchmark rates to increase by 25 bps at next month’s Fed meeting. That’s up from 76% one month ago. It would be the second hike of the year by the Fed and put the federal funds rate at a range of 4% to 4.25%.

Kyle Bass, business production manager at Refi.com, pointed to Mortgage Bankers Association application data showing that recent downward moves in rates had positive impacts on loan demand. But with visible volatility in rates on a day-to-day basis, he said, preparation between loan officers and borrowers is needed to lock in the lowest possible rate and get lower monthly payments.

“Borrowers who benefit are the ones who prepared before the number moved. A shadow application, with income documents, statements and credit in order, lets a homeowner ask what their current mortgage could do for them the day rates cooperate. Waiting for a better number only works if you are ready when it arrives,” Bass said.

A report released Tuesday by Realtor.com shows that the new-home segment is giving the typical buyer lower rates and better affordability than existing homes. Homebuilders, who are also under financial pressure, continue to offer rate buydowns and other incentives as they seek to offload their inventory.

Realtor.com reported that the average mortgage rate for a new-home buyer in the third quarter was 5.01%, more than a full percentage point lower than the 6.15% rate for an existing-home buyer. That translates to a difference of $258 in monthly payments for someone buying a $400,000 home with a 10% down payment.

“Builders have adjusted to a market where affordability is still a major hurdle, but that adjustment isn’t always visible in the listing price,” Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com, said in a statement. “Reduced mortgage rates can help make a new home more affordable for buyers while allowing builders to hold asking prices relatively steady.”

The report noted that reduced rates are often temporary and only last for the first few years after origination. But even when comparing 30-year fixed rates, those who bought a new home in the third quarter saved, with average rates of 6.19% compared to 6.68% for existing home-buyers. On the same $400,000 purchase with 10% down, the new-home buyer saves about $117 per month in interest.

“Mortgage-rate incentives can make a meaningful difference in what a buyer pays each month, but it’s important to understand how long the lower rate lasts,” Berner said. “A temporary buydown can provide relief early on, while a lower rate fixed for the life of the loan offers a different kind of savings.”

Selma Hepp, chief economist at Cotality, said in a statement that tariff-driven increases to building materials are putting pressure on the new-home segment. In turn, this winds up being felt by consumers through higher home purchase prices. Regardless of the type of home being purchased, rising insurance premiums and property taxes are also straining budgets.

“For housing, the key question is not simply whether mortgage rates decline, but whether they fall enough to meaningfully improve purchasing power and bring more buyers and sellers back to the market,” Hepp said.” Until then, I expect activity to remain relatively subdued, making the spring homebuying season an increasingly important test of whether the market can finally turn a corner.”

While housing market professionals continue to grapple with fewer home sales and lower mortgage origination volumes, the U.S. economy as a whole continues to show resilience to inflation, tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty.

Melissa Cohn, regional vice president at William Raveis Mortgage, pointed to last week’s Producer Price Index (PPI), which showed 6.5% inflation on an annualized basis in October. It was the largest year-over-year increase since November 2022. That came only days after the Consumer Price Index showed monthly inflation of 0.4%.

“Unfortunately, the CPI number that we got earlier this week has set off bond yields, and bond yields were probably up almost 25 basis points from where they were at the end of the previous week,” Cohn said Friday in a statement. “It’s not just because of the CPI number, but because of expectations about the Fed, where members are saying, ‘Well, we’re definitely going to have to hike rates.’ We know that the market’s expecting it.

“All of the benefit that we got in mortgage rates over the course of the past three weeks was basically just thrown out the window again, because mortgage rates are really tied to the rate of inflation. We’re back on the inflation wagon.”

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh offered some forward-looking remarks on Monday during a jobs and productivity conference in San Francisco, saying that the central bank continues to look closely at the development of “super intelligence” and its impacts on the global and national economies.

“At the Fed, our role in all this is neither advocacy nor opposition. Our responsibility is to recognize that the widespread adoption of this technology will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road,” Warsh said.

#5391. Scribd releases first transparency report on trust and safety

Report provides new visibility into content enforcement across platform spanning more than 400 million documents

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Scribd published its first transparency report, providing new data on content moderation, copyright enforcement, and user safety. Covering the first half of 2026, the report details more than 47M content moderation actions, including 42M uploads blocked before publication and 5M published items removed afterward.

The first in its nearly 20-year history, the report marks a new step in sharing how Scribd, Inc. enforces its policies across knowledge platform Scribd and sister presentation platform Slideshare. Between those two, the scale now spans more than 400M pieces of content, 250M monthly users, and 50 languages. 84M new pieces of content uploaded by users were published in the first half of 2026 alone.

Key findings from Scribd's first transparency reportContent moderation: During the first half of 2026, automated tools blocked 42M pieces of content during upload time, preventing them from appearing on the platform. Over 5M pieces of published content were removed â including content published before 2026. The vast majority of these, nearly 4.8M of the 5M removals (~94%), were caught via automated detection tools.

Copyright enforcement: Roughly 2.9M of the 5M removals stemmed from alleged copyright infringement. Scribd's proprietary copyright protection system, BookIDâ¢, caught 2.76M of them (~95%) automatically. Scribd also received 48,569 DMCA notices in this period and removed 145,248 pieces of content in response. How to report copyright infringement on Scribd.

Content appeals: Scribd received and reviewed 3,539 appeals of content removal decisions, upholding 3,296 (~93%) of original decisions.

Community reporting: Community acts as another arm helping keep Scribd safe. More than 48,000 users submitted 108,638 reports covering 52,359 pieces of content.

Account removals: Scribd terminated 15,355 accounts as part of its repeat infringer policy or for other copyright infringement reasons.

"Scribd only works if people can trust what they find and feel safe sharing what they know. This report puts our enforcement numbers on the record, and it gives everyone a baseline to measure us against in 2027 and beyond." â Mike Lewis, head of Scribd.com

How content moderation works on ScribdPeople upload content without pre-approval by Scribd. This allows openness and has helped build a vast and diverse collection. Our Community Rules define what people can upload and publish. Scribd combines human and automated methods to review content against those rules.

"Unlike many other forms of user-generated content, documents can include a mixture of text, images, different formats, and languages. The average document length on Scribd runs 24 pages. That means we need a layered content moderation strategy, combining technology, human review, and our community." â Nicole Pauls, head of trust and safety

What's next for trust and safety at ScribdThis first transparency report establishes a baseline for how to measure and share this work, and compare future reports against. The next report is expected in 2027.

Scribd will continue to invest in trust and safety, including expanding its team, refining content policies, implementing new technology, and improving content classification.

Read the full Scribd Transparency Report here for more information on Scribd's content moderation work and additional metrics.

Note to editors: This report covers Scribd.com, with some information about presentation-sharing platform, Slideshare. It does not cover the other Scribd, Inc. products, Everand and Fable.

MethodologyThis is Scribd's first transparency report. It covers the first half of 2026 (January 1 to June 30, 2026). The data includes all content uploaded to or moderated on Scribd and Slideshare worldwide during that period, and every action taken by our automated moderation systems and human review teams.

About Scribd, Inc.Scribd, Inc. is a knowledge company on a mission to advance human understanding. Scribd, Inc. is the parent company to four distinct products: ScribdÂ®, Slideshareâ¢, Everandâ¢ and Fable. Scribd is an applied knowledge platform containing documents on every topic imaginable. Slideshare provides millions of presentations and other professional content. Everand is a digital content subscription home to millions of audiobooks and ebooks. Fable is the leading social reading platform, where readers discover, discuss, and share books through curated book clubs and personalized reading experiences. You can use these products on any web browser, and Everand, Fable, and Scribd are also available as iOS and Android apps.
