#5390. Hammerspace enters the hardware market with new storage and intelligence capabilities

Hammerspace Inc., which provides high-speed access to distributed data, is expanding beyond its traditional role as a software provider to offer complete, integrated data systems for artificial intelligence workloads, adding its own high-performance flash storage hardware and new data intelligence capabilities to its existing data orchestration platform.

The company said the Hammerspace Data System combines data discovery, management, orchestration and storage into a single offering designed to simplify the infrastructure needed to support AI training and inference. Customers can purchase fully configured systems with hardware, software and support or continue deploying Hammerspace software on existing infrastructure.

The announcement marks a significant expansion of Hammerspace’s business model as enterprises increasingly seek turnkey infrastructure for AI applications rather than assembling systems from multiple vendors.

“We also see plenty of opportunities, particularly in the AI space, where they just want one [stock-keeping unit],” said Floyd Christofferson, vice president of product marketing at Hammerspace. “They want a system, end-to-end, hardware, software, fully integrated and supported.”

While software companies have historically had limited success expanding into hardware, Hammerspace’s approach is more than just a bundled, said Mark Nossokoff, research directory at Hyperior Research Holdings LLC.

“Hammerspace is working with distribution partners to develop and fulfill a branded system optimized for their software stack, maintaining their software business model,” he said in e-mailed comments. “This can be advantageous when the hardware is based on an emerging standards-based platform, such as the Open Flash Platform, until the hardware platform becomes a standard offering from multiple suppliers.”

Hammerspace has traditionally specialized in providing unified access to data distributed across different storage systems, data centers and clouds. Its software creates a global namespace that allows applications to locate and access files regardless of their physical location, eliminating the need for large-scale data migrations.

In March, the company introduced an AI-focused data platform that automates the discovery and delivery of enterprise data directly to graphics processing units. The technology builds on Hammerspace’s parallel Network File System, which uses enhancements to Linux to accelerate data access without requiring proprietary client software.

The new offering extends those capabilities with integrated hardware and data intelligence.

A major addition is the Hammerspace Open Flash Platform, a high-density storage system built around data processing units rather than conventional storage servers. The architecture integrates processing, networking and solid-state drives into compact hardware designed to reduce power consumption, cooling requirements and rack space.

Hammerspace said the platform achieves throughput of 350 gigabytes per second per rack unit. Broader performance testing is still underway.

The storage complements the company’s existing Tier 0 technology, which aggregates local Non-Volatile Memory Express storage across GPU servers into a shared resource. That capacity can be used to store key-value caches for AI inference, allowing applications to reuse previously computed context rather than repeatedly processing the same information.

“The flash subsystem employs a unique design and touts some impressive performance and storage density metrics,” said Hyperion’s Nossokoff. “More compelling will be results based on end user workloads, including relative improvements and comparisons with respect to performance, performance/power, and cost/performance metrics, among others.”

The company said customers can combine tier 0 storage, the new flash platform and lower-cost disk or object storage within a single namespace. The new hardware is optional. Customers can continue using third-party storage systems, with Hammerspace handling data access and orchestration across the infrastructure.

Another addition is a data intelligence module that extends Hammerspace’s existing metadata management capabilities.

The software can catalog distributed files, index detailed metadata and scan content to identify sensitive information, including personally identifiable information and regulated data. Users can search the catalog using natural language and translate requests into automated data management policies.

For example, an administrator could identify files containing personal information and establish policies preventing that material from entering an AI training pipeline.

Christofferson said the new capabilities extend beyond the file attributes traditionally used to manage storage.

The module also supports integration with existing enterprise catalogs and governance tools through application programming interfaces, avoiding the need to replace established systems.

For current Hammerspace customers, the intelligence capabilities will be added through a software upgrade. The company said existing deployments won’t need to change their underlying architecture.

Hammerspace will assemble, install and support systems using configurable server hardware, metadata nodes and storage components based on customer requirements. The company will continue basing software pricing on the capacity of data under management. Hardware configurations will be priced individually, with no standardized public price list.

Senior Product Marketing Director Eric Bassier said the company doesn’t intend to collect hardware revenue or impose a hardware markup. Instead, components will flow through suppliers and distribution partners, while Hammerspace provides integrated deployment and support.

The strategy addresses the struggles customers often encounter with the logistics of acquiring servers, storage and other components, said Molly Presley, senior vice president of global marketing.

“They’re looking to their vendors to simplify getting things deployed to start with,” he said. “As long as Hammerspace doesn’t dilute their resources and continues to prioritize their investments on addressing the needs of the growing scientific and engineering communities adopting AI into their advanced technical workflows, they appear well poised for continued momentum.”

Nossokoff said Hammerspace’s distributed data architecture using a global namespace is well suited to emerging AI workload requirements. “Hammerspace has been building out their Data Intelligence software stack to address the requirements of the AI pipeline,” he said. The expansion follows a $100 million funding round in April 2025 that supported Hammerspace’s international expansion. The company says its customers include Meta Platforms Inc. and the U.S. Department of Defense.

#5389. Make it 8: Connecticut joins first responder homebuying push

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”

Seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan said in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

“I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel said. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

“A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really important component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”

#5388. Renting as a financial strategy, what real estate agents should know

Entrata’s Virginia Love says renters are making intentional tradeoffs, prioritizing savings, debt reduction, and flexibility. Agents can better serve renters by discussing full ownership costs, budget comfort, and timelines without assuming buying is the next step.  AI Summary

Renting isn’t always a stepping stone to homeownership. Multifamily expert Virginia Love of Entrata explains how financial priorities, flexibility and the true cost of ownership are reshaping renters’ decisions.

The story we’re telling ourselves about renters is outdated, Virginia Love, industry principal at Entrata, told me recently.

Entrata is a property management operating system built to improve operational efficiency at multifamily communities. In its recent “Resident Pulse” survey, conducted in partnership with YouGov, the company asked renters about their financial priorities, attitudes toward homeownership, definitions of success and other lifestyle factors.

That gives Love a bird’s-eye view of the state of renting and, by extension, homeownership.

“I feel like people think that renters are less-than,” she said. “I think the real story is, people are trying to do what’s right for them and what’s right for their family.”

With homeownership increasingly out of reach for people of all ages, it’s time that real estate agents rethink the role of renters in the housing market. Entrata’s insights can help.

Love said that renters are prioritizing healthy financial hygiene and making decisions based on a more complex economic environment, reducing their existing financial obligations before pursuing longer-term financial goals.

“They are eating out less, they’re shopping less, they’re spending less, they’re switching to cheaper brands,” she said, with the goal of prioritizing emergency savings, debt reduction and other budgetary line items.

For previous generations, the initial barrier to homeownership was a down payment, Love said. Now, it’s the rising costs of everything that comes after the initial upfront purchase price: the mortgage payment at today’s higher rates, insurance, maintenance, repairs and other expenses. Managing the unexpected requires greater levels of financial stability.

“It’s then I have insurance, then I gotta take care of the yard. Then what if the tree falls on the driveway?” Love said.

Beyond the cost of rent vs. buy, maintenance, amenities and the ability to relocate can have real value for renters, especially when they’re working to pay down debt, pursuing educational goals, navigating career shifts or deciding where and when they’re ready to settle down. What they’re paying for, Love said, is freedom.

Love describes Gen Z in particular as pragmatic about money and more willing to take a gradual path toward major financial milestones.

For those who plan to buy, “they’re absolutely fine with starter homes,” Love said. “And I don’t think that that is something that we’ve seen for a while. Everybody kind of wanted to go from zero to 60, and this is a generation that’s willing to take those steps.”

She explains that some renters are working toward a purchase while others prefer to invest, maintain flexibility or avoid being tied to one address.

Real estate agents often approach renters with an ingrained belief in the superiority of homeownership, but it’s not right for everyone. Spend time upfront with renters to find out what matters to them, and don’t just push them toward homeownership automatically, Love said.

Stop assuming buying is the client’s next step: Renters aren’t necessarily buyers who simply haven’t saved up a down payment yet. They may have other financial priorities, like paying down student loans, building an emergency fund, investing for retirement or prioritizing flexibility. Ask what a client’s financial priorities are before assuming homeownership is the goal.

Talk about the full cost of homeownership: Down payments aren’t the whole story here. Monthly payments, rising insurance and repair costs, home maintenance and other expenses can affect whether, and when, buying makes sense. Make sure you’re sharing updated costs of ownership along with the upfront costs, and be realistic about affordability.

Ask what payment feels comfortable, not just what a lender will approve: A client’s maximum purchasing power isn’t necessarily the same as their target budget. Understand the buying budget that matches their comfort level, other financial considerations and personal priorities before locking in on a price range.

Understand that delay isn’t the same as giving up: Some renters may aspire to own a home, but they’re not necessarily in a rush. Maintain relationships over the long haul without turning every conversation into a homebuying pitch.

Recognize that renting has value beyond the monthly payment: The benefits of renting — maintenance support, amenities, flexibility and freedom — may outweigh those of homeownership, even though they don’t build equity for the renter. Understand what the renter values before presenting ownership as an obvious upgrade or superior choice.

“I think the real story is, people are trying to do what’s right for them and what’s right for their family,” Love said. By understanding timing, goals and price sensitivities, agents can help potential clients evaluate their options without prescribing the outcome ahead of time.

Troy Palmquist is the founder of HomeCode Advisors.

#5387. Wonder Unveils Wonder Create, Empowering Anyone with an Idea to Launch Their Own Restaurant

Founding Creators and brands set to launch their own concepts using Wonder Create include Ally Love, Andy Cohen, Chopt Creative Salad Co.,Girl Scouts of the USA, Livvy Dunne and more.

NEW YORK, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Wonder, the vertically integrated platform built to make great food more accessible, today announced the launch of Wonder Create, a groundbreaking new platform that allows anyone with an idea to design and launch their own restaurant.

Wonder Create unleashes a brand new path to restaurant ownership, where traditional barriers to entry are removed, and where creativity and technology will allow for a new era of culinary innovation. The Wonder Create platform allows creators and brands to bring their vision to life by helping craft their menu, build their brand and connect with their audience. Wonder's team handles the full process including sourcing, cooking, delivery and pick-up, with dishes instantly available across Wonder, Grubhub and Seamless.

Moving far beyond standard sponsorships and limited-time offers, Wonder Create's inaugural Founding Creators are among the first to launch their own concepts through the platform with fully tailored menus and distinct branding. Founding Creators are using Wonder Create in a wide variety of ways, including:

"No company can imagine all the food the world wants to eat. Wonder Create gives the world the tools to create it," said Marc Lore, founder and CEO of Wonder. "We're putting our culinary expertise, robotics and AI in the hands of anyone with a great idea, so they can build and own a food brand and reach millions of customers without building or operating a single kitchen. As our network grows and our robotics expand what each kitchen can make, the possibilities for creators grow with us. That means more variety for customers and more ways to make great food accessible. I believe the next great food brands will come from people who never thought they could start one."

Wonder Create will give creators and brands the flexibility to build restaurants their way from menu composition and pricing to logos and branding. Wonder's AI-powered tools help shape original ideas into full concepts, allowing users to utilize as much or as little of the platform's design and culinary capabilities as they want and make changes along the way. Users can lean on the platform for custom development, or upload their original photography, recipes and logos to personalize their restaurant's taste, look and feel. Wonder Create orders are prepared using Infinite Makeline, Wonder's automated food assembly system, which is designed for accuracy, speed and consistency.

Creators will own their concept and brand, set their own prices (subject to a minimum price) and earn a revenue share on every order, while paying as little as $10 a month per location for each restaurant.

Every Wonder Create concept will get a content screening and review before it goes live. Now, creators and brands can build salad, bowl, wrap and burrito-focused restaurant concepts across cuisines from Mexican to Mediterranean to Hawaiian pokÃ©, drawing on a library of more than 130 ingredients, with plans to expand into more categories and cuisines over the coming year.

Concepts will have access to the same ingredients and culinary standards as Wonder's own restaurant brands, which have been developed with the support of chef partners like Bobby Flay, Jonathan Waxman and Marc Murphy. Every order features the concept's custom branding for instant recognizability.

"I'm a dad, a host, a producer and now a 'restaurant owner,'" said Andy Cohen. "Wonder Create makes it possible to bring a new idea to life without slowing anything else down, and I can't wait to see where it takes me."

"Some of the most exciting moments in Girl Scouts happen when a girl discovers something new about herself, a passion she didn't know she had, an idea she wants to bring to life or a creative spark she wants to follow," said Meridith Maskara, Chief Development Officer of Girl Scouts of the USA. "Our partnership with Wonder brings together two organizations that believe in the power of ideas and possibility. With Wonder Create, we are excited to introduce our food to communities where we don't have a Chopt restaurant yet."

"We congratulate Wonder Create on bringing this innovative platform to life and are grateful for their commitment to making a difference in our communities," said Leslie Gordon, President & CEO of Food Bank For New York City. "Through this collaboration, New Yorkers have an opportunity to help nourish their neighbors with something as simple as ordering food from our restaurant concept on the platform. #5386. Jensen Huang says he’s willing to return to Nvidia, in first statement since resignation

Former Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang today said he’s open to returning to his old post.

Huang expressed his willingness to be reinstated in a post on X. It marks his first public statement since his ouster from Nvidia last week. He resigned following revelations that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former cloud executive suspected to be a Chinese spy.

Huang apologized for his conduct in today’s X post. He went on to cite recent calls for him to return as a factor behind his willingness to resume his work at Nvidia.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang wrote. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

Huang’s statement isn’t a complete surprise. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that he had discussed a comeback with confidants. The paper said that a member of Huang’s circle was working to assemble a group of tech executives to support the effort.

Last Thursday, an anonymous user launched an online petition to reinstate Huang. It drew the support of several prominent tech executives including Elon Musk, Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games Inc. CEO Tim Sweeney. The petition also garnered 180,000 other signatures, although it appears that not all of them are genuine. One entry spotted by Business Insider read “Tim Cruise, Hollywood actor.”

It’s unclear whether the efforts to reinstate Huang are realistic. On Monday, CNBC reported that Nvidia’s board is not considering bringing him back. And today, on Nvidia’s earnings call, Chair Harvey Jones repeated that the board doesn’t intend to reinstate him. Earlier, sources had told Reuters that he had misled the chipmaker’s general counsel and chief marketing officer about his relationship with Alice Huang.

While some U.S. officials believe Alice Huang was part of an espionage operation, others see the evidence as inconclusive. On Thursday, sources told CNN that the intelligence collected on her doesn’t prove she’s a spy. The same day, the Justice Department stated it had not yet concluded Alice Huang is a Chinese asset.

Huang is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud provider that has ordered billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips. The Justice Department is investigating the company over alleged export control violations. As early as 2024, officials identified “suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential ​sensitive semiconductor diversion.”

The Wall Street Journal today reported that Nvidia has hired a prominent executive search firm to find a new CEO. According to the paper, it plans to evaluate both internal and external candidates. Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress currently leads the company as interim CEO.

Kress also supervises a new national security and export control oversight committee that Nvidia formed today. It will be responsible for the company’s national security policies, adherence to export control rules and global trade risk management.

The committee comprises three Nvidia directors on launch. It will carry out its work in collaboration with the chipmaker’s executives and external experts in fields such as law, national security and global trade compliance. Nvidia says that the committee will meet at least once per quarter.

#5384. Prophetic unveils SiteAI Drafter for homebuilder land teams

Prophetic has launched SiteAI Drafter, a new feature for its SiteAI platform that lets land acquisition teams draw high-precision, compliant subdivision site plans and see lot yields update in real time. With added CAD export, both automated and drafted plans can move directly into detailed civil engineering, therefore cutting feasibility time and early design costs.  AI Summary

Prophetic has launched SiteAI Drafter, a tool that lets land teams draw high-precision, compliant subdivision site plans in minutes and export them directly to CAD.

The company, which describes itself as the operating system for land acquisition, introduced SiteAI Drafter on Tuesday as a new feature designed to help residential land teams move from site concept to engineering faster and at lower upfront cost, according to its announcement.

SiteAI Drafter is now available to all SiteAI users and adds manual, CAD-ready drafting to a platform that has focused primarily on automated layouts and early-stage feasibility analysis.

SiteAI generates subdivision site plans with lot and unit yield that account for setbacks, wetlands, flood zones, open spaces and stormwater ponds. Builders and developers use the system to run feasibility studies in seconds instead of weeks, replacing initial engineering reports that can cost from $3,000 to more than $10,000.

The platform’s automated layouts estimate maximum theoretical yield and quickly screen large numbers of parcels. Because SiteAI incorporates site constraints at the outset, it can flag issues that might not surface until much later in a traditional workflow, when engineering work is further along and sunk costs are higher.

For acquisition and development teams working in a competitive land market, this kind of early, standardized analysis is used to compare sites on a level playing field and decide which deals to advance before ordering surveys or full design work.

While automated layouts help screen many parcels at once, land teams often have a preferred concept for a specific site based on local jurisdiction standards, topography and planned product types. Under traditional processes, testing that concept typically requires drafting in CAD or waiting for an engineer, which can slow decisions and tie up billable time.

SiteAI Drafter allows users to draw their own road network and configure lots while the system enforces basic subdivision rules in the background. The tool understands roads and rights of way, lot dimensions and product mix so users can experiment with different layouts while staying within buildable constraints.

According to Prophetic, SiteAI Drafter enables land teams to:

The result is a customizable subdivision plan that can reflect the specific community a builder wants to take to a seller, investment committee or municipal review, while still providing a defensible yield number.

Beyond drafting, Prophetic is adding CAD export so that plans created either by SiteAI’s automated engine or by SiteAI Drafter can be used as a starting point for detailed civil engineering design.

This is intended to shift engineers and planners away from redrawing concepts from scratch and toward refining the land team’s preferred layout. Prophetic said the export capability also opens the platform to civil engineers, planners and land developers who want to generate quick concepts before full design or to show builders what a site can hold before a first meeting.

“Every land team plans a site a little differently,” said Oliver Alexander, founder and CEO of Prophetic. “Sometimes you want an answer in seconds across dozens of parcels. Sometimes you already know exactly where the entry and the main road go, and you want to see what your plan yields. SiteAI now works however you do. And with CAD export, the plan doesn’t stop with the land team. It goes to the engineer as a starting point, not a sketch to redraw. That’s what an operating system for land acquisition should do: carry the work forward and help our users win more deals.”

As higher rates and tighter capital make land bets more costly, builders, developers and their capital partners are under pressure to vet more sites with fewer people and less time. Early engineering work is expensive, and using consultants for preliminary concepts can slow down offers in competitive bid situations.

Tools that combine automated yield analysis with guided drafting give acquisition leaders a way to pressure-test their preferred community design before committing to full engineering fees. For homebuilders and land developers, the ability to walk into a seller or investment committee meeting with a concept plan, yield range and CAD-ready file can help shorten decision cycles and reduce the risk of surprises later in entitlement or design.

#5383. My Home Delivery Unveils an AI-Enabled Technology Platform to Power the "Uberization of All Things Big & Bulky"

Revolutionizing local commerce through an upgraded mobile app connecting consumers, retailers, and professional delivery networks for big & bulky delivery, white-glove services, and haul-away solutions.

ENGLEWOOD, N.J., Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- My Home Delivery (MHD), an AI-enabled local commerce and direct-to-consumer home delivery technology platform, today announced a major technology upgrade designed to accelerate the "uberization" of all things Big & Bulky, transforming how consumers and retailers access professional delivery and haul-away services for furniture, appliances, consumer electronics, and any oversized merchandise. This new capability features AI-powered routing to get customer orders where they need to go, faster and more efficiently by analyzing traffic, distance, and delivery windows in real-time so consumers can count on their delivery showing up when they want it.

MHD brings same-day, on-demand, and scheduled delivery, room-of-choice placement, white-glove services, assembly, installation, and haul-away into one convenient platform. Available on the Apple and Google Play stores, the My Home Delivery app empowers consumers to independently arrange pickup and delivery from any retailer with a few taps and without the hassle and expense of renting a truck and lifting heavy items.

Whether purchasing a television at Costco, furniture at IKEA, appliances at Sam's Club, building materials from Lowes or merchandise from a local store, consumers can schedule delivery directly and seamlessly through the MHD app. And My Home Delivery goes beyond retail. Consumers can also easily arrange home-to-home deliveries, whether sending an old sofa to their kid's college dorm or first apartment, delivering furniture from an estate sale, or transporting large items, like patio furniture, purchased through local marketplaces.

"Our vision is simple: consumers should be able to shop wherever they want and to move whatever they need without worrying about how they're going to get it from point A to point B," said Arelis Bonilla, Founder and CEO. "We're bringing the 'uberization' of all things Big & Bulky to local commerce by putting white-glove professional delivery services directly in consumers' hands."

Retail Partnerships and Seamless POS Integration

MHD's existing retail partnerships, including Bob's Discount Furniture outlets and Mattress Warehouse, demonstrate how the platform complements traditional retail delivery operations.

For national and regional retail partners, MHD's technology offers optional API integrations to major retailer Point-of-Sale (POS) systems, allowing delivery services to be incorporated into existing checkout and fulfillment experiences. Retailers can also promote the MHD app through approved in-store marketing and QR codes without integrating their POS systems.

Consumers can also use the My Home Delivery app regardless of whether a retailer has partnered with MHD. Retail partnerships simply expand consumer awareness and convenience but are not required for consumers to directly access MHD services from any retailer.

#5382. What music sells a house? Agents say it’s not about genre

Taylor Swift, classical or silence? Agents explain how they pick open house music, the one rule most follow and why none can prove it works.

Ask real estate agents what soundtrack sells a house, and you’ll get two answers. One is a carefully curated playlist, while the other is silence.

Inman asked agents and brokers from Manhattan to Breckenridge, Colorado, and they described the music they play at showings and open houses and how they match it to the property.

None could point to hard numbers showing a playlist moved a home faster or for more money. What they did offer was a clear set of rules from the agents who use music, and an equally firm argument from those who won’t touch it.

Ben Jacobs, co-founder of the Chestler Jacobs Team at Douglas Elliman in New York City, thinks music raises more questions than it answers. He said he’s not a fan of playing music during showings.

“Buyers may wonder if the agent is trying to mask something, whether it’s street noise, construction nearby, sounds within the building or even a noisy appliance,” Jacobs told Inman. “You want buyers to experience the home as it actually is, without anything distracting from their ability to evaluate the space.”

His co-founder, Jessica Chestler, said music has its place. That place is just not a private showing.

“Music can be wonderful for setting a mood at a cocktail party, listing launch or special event, but during a showing, I think there’s something to be said for letting the property speak for itself,” Chestler said.

Megan Sullivan works at the same brokerage, and she uses music for the very reason Jacobs avoids it. Sullivan sells large estate homes across Fairfield and Westchester counties out of Douglas Elliman’s Greenwich, Connecticut, office. Some of those homes sit within earshot of things a seller can’t fix.

“I actually do like incorporating music into certain showings, particularly when a property is impacted by outside noise from planes, trains or automobiles,” Sullivan said. “Thoughtfully selected background music can help create a more welcoming atmosphere and soften those distractions, allowing buyers to focus on the overall experience of the home. I think it’s very property-specific.”

Jeffrey Hensel is a broker associate with North Coast Financial, a California hard money lender that funds fix-and-flip and probate deals. He looks at it from the investor side.

“Dead silence can amplify every creak, clank, and drip in an otherwise quiet home,” he said. “Background music masks these sounds and provides some white noise to help set a calm mood.”

Agents in the pro-music camp mostly aren’t trying to cover anything up. They simply want buyers to stay longer.

Sandra Daniels of Harry Norman, Realtors | Forbes Global Properties serves the East Cobb and Marietta area outside Atlanta. She’s currently listing a $3.9 million estate in The River Club in Suwanee, Georgia.

For those showings, she rotates light classical piano, The Macarons Project and a Spotify playlist called “Nora Ephron + Nancy Meyers Dinner Party.”

“Put a buyer in a home with a glass of Champagne or a cup of coffee and the right music playing, and that cozy, inviting atmosphere encourages people to stay, relax and feel at home,” Daniels told Inman.

Daniels also has a low-tech trick for vacant listings she expects to sell in the first week. She bought an old-school CD player and a few classical CDs. She leaves it on repeat through the first weekend of showings and stops by each evening to turn off the lights and music and lock up.

Natalia Bassova, founder and CEO of Resort Real Estate in Breckenridge, Colorado, saw the same effect at a luxury mountain listing. The home looked great, she said, but it showed cold.

“By adding some background instrumental music, it gave the buyers more time to spend in the home. They spent more time in the kitchen and great room areas,” Bassova said. “The property didn’t change, but the atmosphere did.”

For mountain and luxury homes, Bassova plays acoustic and piano music, including Ludovico Einaudi and The Piano Guys. For condos and new construction, she switches to soft contemporary instrumentals.

Agents who play music disagree on genre, but almost all agree on one thing: avoid lyrics.

“If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact,” Bassova said. Her never-play list covers anything with strong lyrics, politics, swearing or heavy bass.

Andrea Seeney is a global real estate advisor with Atlanta Fine Homes Sotheby’s International Realty and a trained opera singer and classical pianist. She compared lyrics to a seller’s personal effects.

“Acoustic performances are best because they set a tone and allow the buyer to fill in the blanks with their own thoughts,” Seeney said.

She leans toward jazz and usually plays Spotify’s Coffee House radio or its Ella Fitzgerald playlist. She says music works on buyers through memory: a song can take someone back to a time and place they enjoyed, “and that memory then reflects positively on the home.”

Hensel takes the lyrics rule a step further, to genre itself. If an agent plays hip-hop or country for a buyer who doesn’t listen to it, he says, that signals an assumption about who the buyer is. That can create friction neither side notices. His pick is quiet cocktail-lounge jazz like Miles Davis or Bill Evans, at a steady tempo and volume.

He also cited retail research by psychological scientists Adrian North and Lorraine Sheridan of Curtin University and Charles Areni of Macquarie University. It found that shoppers who heard classical music rated merchandise as higher quality and were willing to spend more.

Some agents ignore the rulebook completely.

Rachel Kilmer, an agent with ReeceNichols Real Estate in Kansas City, Missouri, plays Taylor Swift at nearly every open house. She swaps in country for more rural listings.

“In Kansas City, she’s a conversation starter,” Kilmer said. “People come in, and it’s, ‘Are you a Swiftie?’ ‘No, but I love the Chiefs!’ It really helps loosen up the conversation.”

She added, “I’m the one sitting there listening to it for two hours!”

Monica Shea, a broker with KW Aspire in Colorado Springs, Colorado, builds whole open houses around a theme, and the music follows.

She played the Eras Tour set list at a Taylor Swift–themed open house and the Frozen soundtrack at a hot cocoa bar event. A Halloween open house got not-too-spooky Halloween music. For regular showings, she has sellers put on a YouTube channel with seasonal background music and scenery.

Shea’s never-play list puts her directly at odds with a few other agents: smooth jazz. Shea says she never plays “anything that sounds like the Weather Channel.”

Marcel Finkelstein of Team BlackStar at eXp Realty hosts open houses every Sunday across Monmouth County, New Jersey. He sees music as more of an icebreaker than a staging tool.

His Apple Music rotation includes lounge instrumentals, vocal-free dance-pop and Bon Entendeur. It also has Afro house from DJ Alex Niyazov and the warm trumpet and sax of Fausto Papetti and Paul Mauriat.

He uses the same approach whether the listing is a $600,000 two-bedroom condo in Manalapan or a $2 million six-bedroom in Colts Neck.

“I want the atmosphere to feel calm, comfortable and welcoming, rather than like a sales presentation,” Finkelstein said.

Finkelstein added that his Instagram followers also know how much he loves music.

“Every week, I share new songs and incorporate music into my stories and posts about homes,” he said. “It’s a personal interest that carries through into how I present properties.”

On setup, agents who play music give similar advice. Keep the volume low enough that buyers can ask questions and the agent can hear their feedback. Use one good speaker rather than several.

Bassova puts hers in the middle of the home, and Seeney puts a small Bluetooth speaker in the kitchen. When sellers have a Sonos system, Daniels connects to it from her MacBook or iPad. Otherwise, she brings her own Bose speaker.

Kilmer runs her music from an iPad instead of her phone. “That way, incoming calls and texts don’t interrupt the music,” she said.

As for proof, none of the agents Inman spoke with track music as a performance metric. Bassova said she gets buyer feedback that certain homes feel relaxing, but nothing tied to days on market or offers.

So the evidence is anecdotal, and the playlists don’t agree. Agents can’t even settle on jazz. Both camps share one goal: the buyer should notice the home, not the soundtrack.

As Bassova said, “If the buyer begins to think about the music, then it is having a negative impact.”

#5381. How reverse mortgage LOs can help borrowers to self-service

Reverse mortgage servicers are investing in borrower portals, mobile apps and smarter phone systems to reduce call volumes. Celink is launching ReverseLink soon, while Onity is expanding digital draw requests and emphasizing closing checklist steps for loan officers.  AI Summary

Reverse mortgage servicers are investing in portals, mobile applications and smarter phone systems so borrowers can manage their loans without contacting a human customer service representative. Servicing executives say that loan officers can play a key role in whether these tools actually work.

Gail Balettie, senior vice president of client satisfaction at Celink, and Ryan McIntire, director of reverse mortgage servicing controls at Onity Mortgage, outlined their companies’ self-service offerings during a panel discussion moderated by Chris Downey of CrossCountry Mortgage at last week’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Meeting & Expo.

“In today’s world, where we are conditioned to some extent to be able to go online, get immediate satisfaction, to do things without talking to somebody, the more we can do that, the better we can reach our customers,” McIntire said.

Balettie announced at NRMLA Annual that her company’s mobile app, ReverseLink, will be launching “in the next few weeks.” Its design is similar to Celink’s website and borrowers will receive an invitation to download it. The company is the largest independent subservicer of reverse mortgages and has an estimated market share of about 75% across federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) and proprietary loans.

McIntire told the audience that Onity‘s servicing app is already available on iPhone and Android devices and mirrors its borrower portal. He stressed the importance of providing familiar technology to senior homeowners so “they don’t feel like they’re having to learn something all over again.”

Celink’s soon-to-be-released app will allow clients to accomplish multiple tasks, Balettie said. They’ll be able to request payoff quotes, make voluntary payments, upload forms and download up to two years of statements. The app automatically generates confirmation that an uploaded form has been received, cutting down the number of calls needed for this purpose.

“They can request a line-of-credit draw, and if they do so, they’re going to get their funds a day or two faster than the typical five-day turn time, because it comes in an automated fashion,” she added.

ReverseLink also has a number of FAQs and educational videos, covering subjects like how to manage the account online, what happens to the reverse mortgage when the borrower dies, how to shop for insurance coverage and how to file a claim, and how to find help with small home repairs.

Onity’s portal ties into the company’s system of record, McIntire said. It shows three months of transactions and includes an introduction package that’s tailored to the structure of the loan — for example, any funds set aside for required repairs. Onity is also in the process of building fully digital draw request forms. Today, borrowers have to download and complete these forms before returning it via email or fax, but the goal is to process e-signed draw requests within a few business days, McIntire said.

“Obviously, information that’s available to the borrower via this site is very sensitive. We obviously, as servicers, have to be very cognizant and mindful of fraud. So it does have multifactor authentication that just helps provide that additional sense of security,” he added.

Borrowers commonly contact their loan officer, rather than their servicer, when they have questions about their loan. Balettie said that LOs can take an “ABCD” role to approach to providing assistance in this area.

Making sure a servicer has the correct contact information for a borrower may seem obvious, but it doesn’t happen with perfect uniformity. “We get about 70% of our loans that board with an email address. I want to see that be 100%,” Balettie said. “I don’t know very many people who don’t have an email address in this day and age.”

Balettie sought to distinguish between the alternate contact on the loan application and an authorized third party. The latter may discuss the account but cannot change contact information or request a draw or payoff. Conversely, servicers use the alternate contact only when they cannot reach the borrower, she said.

A power of attorney can act for a living borrower, but legal authority ends at death, the panelists noted. Downey urged originators to execute the authorized party form at closing and warned that without it, payoffs for a borrower “can be a nightmare.” Having this information on file removes the need to hire an attorney to search for heirs after the borrower dies.

Balettie said originators should collect a canceled check and the direct deposit form at closing. Borrowers without a check can provide a redacted bank statement or bank letter with their account and routing numbers. Due to security concerns, servicers don’t allow bank details to be added online, but they’ll accept faxed or emailed documents, and closing is the best time to gather them.

#5380. ELEGOO Showcases New Solutions Across Resin Printing, FDM Printing and 3D Scanning at Formnext 2026

FRANKFURT, Germany, Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ELEGOO, a rapidly developing brand in the global smart manufacturing industry, kicked off its participation at Formnext 2026 today, showcasing its latest product developments and offering visitors an exclusive first look at upcoming innovations. At booth 12.0-C02, ELEGOO brought together live product demonstrations, new innovation previews, and creator-led sessions, highlighting its continued exploration of resin printing, multi-material FDM printing, and connected creative workflows.

Kevin Wang, Co-founder and Vice President of ELEGOO, said, "We're continuously exploring new possibilities across different technologies to bring more versatile tools and solutions to creators. At Formnext this year, we're excited to share a preview of our upcoming developments in resin and FDM printing, alongside our latest 3D scanning solutions. The show also gives us a great opportunity to connect with creators and industry partners, exchange ideas, and be part of the conversations shaping the industry."

A First Look at What's Next in Resin and FDM Printing

Among the highlights, ELEGOO presented the Saturn 5 Ultra, its upcoming resin 3D printer. Designed as an all-round desktop resin printer, it combines high-precision performance and improved durability with enhanced productivity and ease of use. Its intelligent resin management system automates resin monitoring and replenishment, while design improvements simplify setup, maintenance, and operation. The Saturn 5 Ultra is currently planned for an early Q1 2027 launch.

ELEGOO also gave visitors an exclusive first look at the Centauri X Ultra, marking a significant milestone in the evolution of the Centauri series with its move into multi-printhead technology. Featuring four independent printheads, this upcoming FDM 3D printer explores new possibilities in multi-color and multi-material printing. Quick printhead switching helps minimize material waste during color changes, while compatibility with rigid and flexible materials enables a wider range of functional and creative applications. Its unexpected debut at Formnext drew visitors to the ELEGOO booth, sparking curiosity about the new addition to the Centauri series.

Experiencing the 3D Scanning Workflow with M1 Ultra

Another key highlight at the booth is the M1 Ultra, ELEGOO's first all-in-one smart 3D scanner. Through live demonstrations, visitors can experience its scanning capabilities and explore a complete workflow, from capturing physical objects to processing digital models with ELEGOOSCAN software. With metrology-grade accuracy of up to 0.02 mm and multiple scanning modes for different object sizes, surfaces, and levels of detail, the M1 Ultra supports applications ranging from reverse engineering and product development to digital archiving and 3D printing.

Connecting with Creators and the Global 3D Printing Community

Beyond product demonstrations, ELEGOO is hosting daily creator workshops at around 4:00 p.m., featuring experienced 3D printing creators who share practical insights, creative applications, and firsthand experiences with ELEGOO products. The sessions have attracted groups of visitors gathering around the booth to watch live demonstrations and interact with the creators, adding an engaging, community-driven dimension to the exhibition. ELEGOO is also holding daily prize draws, offering visitors the chance to win 3D printers and ELEGOO-branded gifts and accessories.

ELEGOO will continue showcasing its products and innovations at Formnext 2026 through November 20 at booth 12.0-C02, Messe Frankfurt, Germany. Visitors are welcome to stop by to experience live demonstrations and explore ELEGOO's latest developments firsthand.

Founded in 2015, ELEGOO is a rapidly developing brand in the global smart manufacturing industry, specializing in R&D, manufacturing, and sales of consumer-grade 3D printers, laser engravers, STEM kits, and other smart technology products. Located in Shenzhen, the Silicon Valley of China, the company has sold millions of products across more than 150 countries and regions. In 2025, the company's total sales revenue surpassed 300 million USD, with more than 1000 employees and over 430,000 square meters of office and manufacturing area. With a focus on programming and 3D printing technology, ELEGOO provides unique and smart creation spaces for diverse consumers to enhance personalized experiences.

#5379. Dell bets liquid-cooled, software-defined storage can keep AI factories fed

AI factories are growing so dense that storage, not just compute, now decides how quickly they turn data into tokens. For Dell Technologies Inc., the answer starts with turning its PowerEdge servers into flexible, software-defined storage nodes that can change roles as workloads shift.

The move from training toward inference and agents has put new pressure on time to value. Dell has spent the year extending its AI Data Platform with a semantic layer for agentic workloads, and its AI factory pitch now reaches well beyond compute and graphics processing units, according to George Papadopoulos (pictured), senior vice president of product and engineering at Dell.

“We look at our AI factory not just as a set of CPUs and GPUs, but networking becoming more and more important, particularly around speed, reliability of storage, and the ability to take your raw data and generate context and knowledge from it,” Papadopoulos said.

Papadopoulos spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. (* Disclosure below.)

Customers want storage they can buy for today’s needs and repurpose later. A customer might start with file, for instance, and move to object or parallel file as workloads evolve. Agentic workloads lean on small input/output operations rather than streaming, so the right storage type can shift quickly, Papadopoulos explained. Dell’s answer is Dell Exascale Storage, which runs as licensed software on Dell servers.

“It’s our really purpose-built software-defined solution for allowing us to take a PowerEdge-based node and … with flexible licensing, allow you to deploy a file persona, a block persona, an object persona, or a parallel file persona, and allow that flexibility to change over time as your needs change,” Papadopoulos said.

Density is also forcing a rethink of cooling. The power envelope of today’s AI systems is so large that customers are planning for 100% liquid-cooled data centers, according to Papadopoulos. That requirement now extends to storage.

“So the conversations have really gotten down to how can we most effectively provide a direct liquid cooled solution and the storage that means even liquid cooling the drives, which is something that hasn’t been done as of yet,” Papadopoulos said.

Dell used SC26 to unveil a 2U, 32-drive node with 100% liquid cooling, which it bills as the first direct liquid-cooled storage for rack-scale AI. The node deploys as an Exascale system with any persona. Separating the software from an appliance also lets Dell bring new PowerEdge generations to market faster. That flexibility matters for neocloud operators, who need an off-ramp for every purchase, Papadopoulos noted.

“That allows them to make an upfront purchase and know that they won’t be locked into one particular storage type,” Papadopoulos said, “or have a set of data silos that they can’t leverage as they go forward.”

#5378. NAR’s latest data, must-have AI tools, Compass’ 15 new lawsuits

Congratulations, you’ve made it to Friday again this week. But before you head out for the weekend, we’re bringing you a quick catch-up on the biggest headlines and the most helpful how-tos for your business. So, Take 5 and peruse our top editor picks for this week and why they matter to your business.

P.S. Don’t miss The Download, our weekly column that breaks down one of the week’s top stories and equips you with what you’ll need to meet next Monday head-on.

Homeownership is slipping further out of reach for young Americans, according to the National Association of Realtors’ 2026 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers. The report, released on Thursday, revealed that the share of first-time homebuyers rose 1 percent year over year to 22 percent. Despite the small gain, first-time buyer activity remains near historic lows (21 percent) and 18 percentage points below pre-2008 trends (40 percent). Same as last year, the median age of a first-time homebuyer was 40 — roughly a decade older than the typical median age in the 1980s.

Why it matters: This annual report gives you a pulse on national real estate trends and how you might want to pivot your strategies. For example, as noted above, the median age of the first-time homebuyer is 40, and the share of single women homeowners has risen to 20 percent. A longer nurture campaign might be in order (ahem, see below), and if you’re not already marketing toward single women, perhaps you should. Read the full report for more.

EXTRA: The buyer who can’t close for a year is your best asset in 2026

AI has been the topic of conversation for the past couple of years. And there’s a lot of talk. So how do you suss through the noise and find what works for your business? Jimmy Burgess has created a no-nonsense list of seven AI tools that are actually worth your time.

Why it matters: Burgess shares not only his top tools but also how to use them. These tools will help you turn prompts into better questions, find the questions your future clients are asking, remember the details that matter, evaluate your AI search visibility, turn one video into multiple pieces of content, make video editing easier and use AI as a strategist rather than a writing assistant. Don’t feel overwhelmed. You don’t have to use all of them at once.

Krystopher Benyamein recently sold a property in San Pedro where his team hosted nine open houses, mailed 500 postcards, ran digital advertising and created a video that generated more than 1.5 million organic views. They found a buyer and opened escrow, but shortly before closing, that buyer backed out, and they had to start again.

They eventually found another buyer and successfully closed, but when they shared the case study on Instagram, they didn’t lead with the sale price or how much marketing they’d done. They opened with, “Imagine finally selling your house. Then the buyer backs out right before closing.”

That opening puts the reader in the seller’s position. Most homeowners can imagine how frustrating that experience would be, and it naturally creates curiosity about what happened next. From there, they explained how they responded, got the property back in front of buyers and ultimately closed.

Why it matters: In today’s market, there are many stories of buyers backing out of deals. This approach allows you to create content that keeps you top of mind, show sellers exactly how you work and reach a wider audience. Benyamein shows you how to do it and shares a FREE Canva template to help get the job done.

VA loans often get passed over for conventional loans. Inman’s Nick Pipitone spoke with Fathom Realty’s Lindsey Schmidt, an Army veteran who served in Iraq, about why VA financing still carries a stigma among sellers and listing agents, how she gets around it and why VA assumptions remain one of the most misunderstood tools in the market.

Why it matters: Military members often have to move. Understanding and busting myths about VA loans can help you get ahead of objections before making an offer, which will help you get more deals across the finish line and get more service members into homes.

Compass has been busy, creating and formalizing policy around employees in association leadership positions and how Compass brokerage agents cooperate on private listings.

The company announced Thursday that it is filing 15 federal antitrust lawsuits against MLSs across eight states, accusing the organizations of illegally restricting how agents can publicly market homes outside their systems. Compass alleges that the MLSs unlawfully fine agents for publicly marketing listings outside the MLS, with penalties it says can reach $15,000.

Why it matters: Compass International Holdings is currently in litigation with 16 total MLSs across 18 federal lawsuits. Not only is this big news that’s making waves throughout the industry, but its ripple effects could impact your MLS’s rules, if they haven’t already.

#5377. Dark Matter, ServiceLink add automated closing to Empower

Dark Matter Technologies integrated ServiceLink Accelerated Close into its Empower LOS, automating title, valuation and closing orders through Exchange. ServiceLink data shows 82% of borrowers expect refis to close in under one month and 87% value self-scheduling.   AI Summary

Dark Matter Technologies and ServiceLink have partnered to bring automated title, valuation and closing services to lenders using Dark Matter’s Empower loan origination system.

The partnership integrates ServiceLink’s Accelerated Close platform, powered by its NowIntelligence technology, into Empower. The service automates title and valuation orders, as well as closing orders, and allows lenders or borrowers to schedule appraisals and closings.

Using loan data, Accelerated Close automatically determines whether a loan qualifies for an expedited workflow. NowIntelligence evaluates eligibility using real-time market intelligence, including public and proprietary data, vendor information and market analytics.

For eligible loans, Empower automatically places title and valuation orders with ServiceLink through Exchange, Dark Matter’s partner marketplace. Once a loan reaches clear-to-close status, closing orders are also placed automatically through Empower.

The companies said the integration reduces manual work for lender operations teams and can shorten the time between underwriting approval and a scheduled closing.

Borrower expectations are also driving demand for faster and more flexible closing processes. According to ServiceLink’s 2026 State of Homebuying Report, 82% of borrowers believe a refinance should take less than a month to close, while 87% said the ability to schedule their own appraisal or closing would influence their choice of lender.

“Borrowers judge their lender by how fast and frictionless the process feels, and knowing when their appraisal and closing will happen matters a great deal,” said Vikas Rao, CEO of Dark Matter Technologies. “Accelerated Close takes routine ordering off lenders’ plates and, if desired, puts scheduling in borrowers’ hands, so loans close faster and borrowers feel in control of one of the biggest financial decisions of their lives.”

ServiceLink CEO Chris Azur said the integration is intended to help lenders shorten cycle times, improve pull-through rates and provide borrowers with a more streamlined experience.

For lenders, shorter cycle times could also reduce costs associated with extended rate locks. Orders placed through ServiceLink will continue to use the existing Exchange workflow for order status updates, documents and messaging.

Lenders can enable Accelerated Close through their Dark Matter or ServiceLink account managers, through self-service configuration or as part of a new Empower implementation, the companies’ release stated.

#5376. City of Benicia Wins Statewide Award for Cutting Red Tape and Modernizing Permitting

BENICIA, Calif., Nov. 17, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What once required paper applications, multiple trips to City Hall and time-consuming steps can now be completed online in Benicia. This transformation has streamlined permitting for residents, contractors and businesses, earning the City a 2026 Helen Putnam Award for Excellence from the League of California Cities.

Selected from 161 submissions statewide, Benicia was one of 12 cities recognized for innovation in local government. The City received the award in the Internal Administration category for its Permit Services Approach, a five-year initiative that transformed its paper-based permitting process into an electronic system.

Today, 74% of Benicia's permits are processed through automated Express Permits or SolarAPP+. Permits that required hours of in-person processing can now be approved automatically.

Making Permitting Easier for Residents, Contractors and Businesses

Previously, obtaining a permit required in-person visits during limited hours, paper applications and physical plan sets. Development Services staff managed permit counter traffic, data entry and an average of 30 to 40 phone calls daily.

To address these challenges, the City invested in technology, expanded 24/7 online resources and prioritized personalized customer support. The improvements include:

These changes have shifted Benicia's permitting services from a process limited by counter hours and paperwork to a more accessible, efficient and customer-focused system.

By combining technology, community feedback and dedicated staff support, Benicia has created a permitting experience that serves as a model for local governments across California.

#5375. NAR saved for his $541K exit; now it won’t pay, ex-CFO says

License under the Creative Commons Attribution 2.0 Generic license.

Former National Association of Realtors Chief Financial Officer John Pierpoint has sued the organization for unpaid retirement compensation totaling more than $541,000, according to a complaint filed on Tuesday.

Pierpoint alleged NAR has paid senior vice presidents one year of their base salary at retirement since 2005. To avoid booking the full expense when a senior vice president retired, NAR created a Compensation Reserve that let it steadily set aside funds throughout the executive’s tenure, which it would release at retirement. Pierpoint helped establish the reserve in 2005 at the direction of former NAR CEO Dale Stinton, court documents said.

Pierpoint retired from NAR on March 31, 2025 — a date he chose with the 2023 Sitzer | Burnett buyer-broker commission lawsuit in mind. The former CFO said he was key in executing the buyer-broker commission settlement payout, which totaled $418 million. The first settlement payment, totaling roughly $200 million, was issued in February 2025, with subsequent payments of $72 million per year until the full $418 million is paid.

Pierpoint said he notified NAR of his impending retirement in late 2024 and requested his retirement payout. However, six days before his last day with NAR, Pierpoint alleged that a Grant Thornton auditor named White — there is no first name listed in the court documents — emailed him and said that “NAR had been ‘unable to locate any policy or verify any consistent practice’ concerning the Compensation Reserve or ‘the payout to executives of a full year of salary upon retirement.'”

White also allegedly said that the Compensation Reserve “was not used to fund” the exit packages of eight other senior vice presidents who retired before Pierpoint, which are listed in the court documents as L.J., F.S., B.M., D.H., J.G.,  J.B., D.G. and B.G. Real Estate News said L.J., D.G. and B.G. are likely former general counsel Laurie Janik, former SVP of talent development and resources Donna Gland, and former senior vice president and CEO Bob Goldberg.

As a result, Grant Thornton said it was “unable to approve the payout of a full year’s compensation without any concrete proof that such act is mandated by an employment agreement, policy or plan.”

Pierpoint claimed NAR had the funds to pay his retirement benefit and provided a ledger outlining what the Association allegedly reserved from December 2014 to December 2024. He also said the trial balances NAR provided to outside auditors, including Grant Thornton, included evidence of the Compensation Reserve’s existence and purpose.

“NAR carried its obligation to Pierpoint at approximately 97.6 cents on the dollar three months before it refused to pay him anything,” the complaint read. “The practice NAR now claims it cannot verify is documented in NAR’s own ledger, its own year-end schedules, its own payroll records and its own audit files, and was paid to every one of Pierpoint’s predecessors who retired. NAR did not stop believing in its obligation; it stopped wanting to pay it.”

Pierpoint’s counsel accused NAR of shirking its obligation to pay the former CFO due to its financial woes after the settlement. In December 2025, former NAR president Kevin Sears said the buyer-broker commission settlement saved the Association’s finances — the other option was to file an appeal and declare bankruptcy.

“John Pierpoint helped guide NAR through an extraordinarily challenging period in its history, including the financial consequences of the antitrust litigation,” said David Fish, an attorney with Workplace Law Partners, P.C., who represents Pierpoint. “After nearly four decades of service, he expected the organization to honor the same retirement compensation practice it had followed for other senior executives.”

“We believe the evidence will establish that the financial pressures following the antitrust verdict did not relieve NAR of its obligation to pay compensation earned by its employees,” he added.

Pierpoint’s counsel is requesting that NAR pay the $541,059 retirement payout, statutory damages of 5 percent of the unpaid amount for each month it remains unpaid, attorneys’ fees and costs, and prejudgment and post-judgment interest. They also seek a jury trial.

NAR denied Pierpoint’s claims, saying that the former CFO has “[mischaracterized] a varied set of individual arrangements with departing executives as a uniform and guaranteed retirement benefit.”

“Mr. Pierpoint was not entitled to the payment he now seeks, and NAR’s decision was unrelated to its antitrust settlement or its financial condition,” an NAR spokesperson told Inman in an emailed statement. “NAR is committed to appropriate financial controls and responsible stewardship of its members’ dues dollars. NAR pays compensation and benefits that are actually owed, not just because a former executive requests payment. No such obligation exists here, and we intend to vigorously defend against these claims through the appropriate legal process.”

#5374. Homebuilder confidence sinks to a 14-year low as buyers hibernate

NAHB’s HMI fell 4 points to 25 in November, the lowest since 2012. Builders reported heavier concessions, with 46% cutting prices and 68% offering incentives as rates above 7% weighed on demand.  AI Summary

Homebuilder confidence fell in November to its lowest point since the latter days of the Global Financial Crisis, as elevated mortgage rates, persistent inflation and buyer hesitancy continue to weigh on demand.

The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) fell four points to 25 in November, representing the weakest homebuilder confidence reading since April 2012.

Builders have relied ever more heavily on discounts and mortgage buydown tactics to move inventory, with NAHB reporting that 46% of builders cut prices during the month, the highest share since the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic. Typical discounts ran flat at 6% for the eighth straight month, and 68% of builders used sales incentives, another post-Covid high. It was the 20th consecutive month that at least 60% of builders had featured margin-eroding price-cut promotions.

Further, in November, all three of the key HMI components sank. The index of current sales conditions declined six points to 28, while the measure of sales expectations over the next six months slipped two points to 30, signaling a prolonged pessimistic outlook. Meanwhile, the gauge of prospective buyer traffic dropped two points to 16, the lowest level in 15 years outside of the early months of the pandemic in 2020.

“Builders are confronting multiple challenges in today’s economy,” NAHB Chairman Bill Owens, a home builder and remodeler from Worthington, Ohio, said in a statement. “Stepped-up immigration enforcement is keeping legal workers off job sites, deepening labor shortages and driving up costs. Higher fuel prices are prompting subcontractors to raise their rates sharply, and with fewer buyers in the market, more builders are scaling back construction.”

NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz said in a statement that a combination of policy and macroeconomic pressures is straining both supply and demand.

“The housing market faces a range of supply-side challenges, including building material costs pushed higher by tariffs, an ongoing shortage of construction workers and excessive regulations that undermine housing affordability,” Dietz said. “Mortgage rates above 7%, softer consumer confidence and an uncertain economic outlook are holding buyers back.”

Public homebuilders echoed that picture on recent earnings calls, citing hesitant buyers, heavier discounting and thinner margins.

Century Communities Executive Chairman Dale Francescon, during an earnings call on October 28, noted that high mortgage rates, continued inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty weighed heavily on consumer confidence, particularly among first-time buyers.

“As we moved through the quarter, our buyers became more cautious, did not feel an urgency to transact and felt more comfortable moving to the sidelines,” Francescon said during the call.

It’s not that buyers have abandoned the market. Rather, they are waiting out volatility and elongating decision-making timelines. At the same time, the number of households that can qualify for a mortgage at today’s borrowing costs and sales prices continues to shrink.

LGI Homes chairman and CEO Eric Lipar noted the increasingly challenging market conditions during an earnings call on November 3.

“As expected, the market became more challenging as the quarter progressed,” Lipar said. “Affordability remained the defining story of the quarter.”

The homebuilder, which primarily serves rate- and payment-sensitive entry-level buyers, reported a cancellation rate of 53.8%, compared with 33.6% a year earlier and 26.2% two years ago. While this trend was an outlier among most of its public homebuilding peers, it underscores how strained entry-level buyers are right now.

During PulteGroup’s earnings call on October 22, the builder’s president and CEO Ryan Marshall agreed that market conditions have become more challenging in recent months, leading many buyers to put their homebuying process on the back burner.

“What changed in the quarter…is that the big move higher in interest rates, along with inflation, global tensions, and waning confidence, reached the point where more consumers simply put their search on pause,” he said during the call.

Traffic to PulteGroup communities fell 14% year over year and 11% sequentially in the third quarter, with first-time buyers making up most of the missing traffic.

Marshall also noted that, with 30-year mortgage rates still sitting at around 7.5%, move-up buyers are increasingly having a difficult time selling their current home, further dragging on homebuying demand.

“One of the biggest impediments that we’re seeing right now is that our move-up and active-adult buyers need to sell their existing home, and that is tough,” Marshall noted.

With homeownership increasingly out of reach for the average working American, renting has become the more affordable option. Zillow research found that renting a home costs more than $1,000 less per month than buying one, a gap that draws many would-be buyers away from for-sale homebuilders and toward the rental market.

For many homebuilders, winning over cautious buyers now means resorting to more and more incentives, in effect paying for sales. Concessions are climbing, and total sales prices are coming down with them. The median new-home sales price in September was about $400,000, down nearly 4.0% from a year ago.

Builders continue to use mortgage rate buydowns as a sales tool, and the numbers show it. A recent Realtor.com report found that the average new-home buyer had a starting mortgage rate of 5.01% during the third quarter, compared with 6.15% for existing-home buyers.

Century Communities is among the builders leaning hard on incentives to facilitate sales. The company reported that, during Q3, incentives averaged about 13.0% of the total sales price, up from 12% in Q2 and 11.0%. The builder’s CFO Scott Dixon noted on an October earnings call that incentives will likely rise in the fourth quarter as Century pushes to meet its year-end goals.

“We expect incentives on closed homes in the fourth quarter of 2026 to be 200-250 basis points higher than third quarter levels as we navigate a higher rate environment, muted consumer confidence and compete with other builders for year-end closings,” he said during the call.

Meritage Homes Executive Vice President and CFO Hilla Sferruzza concurred that the incentive environment is likely to stay elevated for some time, as she addressed analysts on an October 29 earnings call. The builder continues to use incentives and price discounts, with its average closing price down 4% year over year to $365,000.

“Absent a sustained market-driven catalyst that provides meaningful mortgage rate relief, we expect incentives to remain at this elevated level for the near term,” Sferruzza said.

On the other hand, during a session at the HousingWire Homebuilder Summit last month, Taylor Morrison CEO Sheryl Palmer warned that homebuilders have trained today’s buyers to expect more and more concessions.

“We, as builders, created this environment,” Palmer said during the session. “We created this place where the longer the house has been sitting there, the more we’re going to give you.”

For builders, the question is how much profit they are willing to trade for sales. Those who protect margins risk losing volume, while those who chase volume are watching margins thin.

Most public homebuilders reported lower gross profit margins in the third quarter than a year earlier, including:

Beyond the immediate sales and margin challenges, many homebuilders are struggling to determine how much inventory to carry and what their 2027 production plans should look like.

Meritage Homes, for example, declined to give formal Q3 guidance, arguing that volatile market conditions limit their visibility.

PulteGroup’s President and CEO Ryan Marshall agreed that “the current environment has made it a more difficult planning time.”

And D.R. Horton Executive Vice President Jessica Hansen echoed this sentiment during an October 29 earnings call.

“Given the uncertainty in these conditions and the broader economy, our initial fiscal 2027 guidance reflects wider ranges than usual,” Hansen explained.

Builders have navigated this challenging market by cutting cycle times, extracting costs, improving floor plans and leveraging AI to improve operational efficiency. What’s out of their control is whether buyers feel ready to commit, or when that will change.
