#5353. What AI changes in cyberattacks, and the old weaknesses and defenses that remain

Free daily briefing on global business news.

AI cyberattacks vs traditional hacking, compared across 10 points, from AI-written phishing and voice cloning to prompt injection, plus the old weaknesses and defenses that still matter

Generative AI has not given attackers a new way into most organizations. It has made the old ways cheaper, faster and harder to spot. A phishing email that once betrayed itself through clumsy grammar can now arrive fluent and personalized, in the recipient's own language. A phone call from a familiar voice may come from software rather than a person. A video call full of recognizable colleagues may not include a single real one.

Comparing AI cyberattacks vs. traditional hacking shows a shift in scale and cost more than a clean break. Traditional hacking rewarded scarce skills. A con artist needed a convincing voice and a good script. A phishing crew needed fluent writers. An intruder needed someone who could read code and find a flaw. Language models and AI agents now handle parts of that work. That lets a small group attempt operations that once required a larger, more specialized team.

AI has also created attack surfaces that did not exist before. Chatbots, coding assistants and AI agents read text from emails, web pages and documents. That text can carry hidden instructions the system then follows. Attacks aimed at AI systems themselves have no direct equivalent in older forms of hacking.

Less has changed in how most intrusions finish. An attacker still typically needs a working password, an unpatched system, a misconfigured server or an employee willing to approve a payment. That continuity shapes the defensive picture. Many of the controls that blunted older attacks, from multi-factor authentication to call-back checks on payment requests, still work when the attacker is using AI.

The 10 slides that follow cover a selection of these shifts, not a complete list. They start with social engineering, from fluent phishing to cloned voices and deepfaked video calls. They then look at the underground market for criminal chatbots and at university research on AI agents exploiting known software flaws. Other slides examine a reported espionage campaign run largely through an AI tool, automated bug hunting and prompt injection. The final two turn to the weaknesses attackers still rely on and the defenses that hold up. Together they show how hackers use AI today and where the old rules still apply.

Large language models let attackers write phishing emails that are fluent, personalized and available in many languages. Spelling mistakes and awkward grammar, long treated as the easiest way to spot a scam, are no longer a reliable warning sign.

For years, much phishing was written by people working outside their native language. Misspelled brand names, odd capitalization and stiff phrasing were common. The advance-fee "Nigerian prince" emails became shorthand for how clumsy fraud messages could look. They are known as 419 scams, after a section of Nigeria's criminal code. Security awareness training often taught employees to treat sloppy writing as a red flag.

A language model removes that tell. An attacker can ask for a polite invoice reminder, a password-reset notice or a note from a colleague, and get clean copy in seconds. The same tools can shift the tone of a message or translate it into another language. That widens the pool of potential targets to readers of languages the attacker does not speak.

Personalization is the other shift. Spear phishing — messages tailored to one person or a small group — has been around for years, but it took effort. An attacker had to research the target and learn the names of their manager and vendors. Then the note had to be written by hand. A model can turn public details from a company website, a press release or a professional profile into a tailored message quickly. That lowers the cost of producing many customized lures at once.

The mechanics have not changed. A phishing email still has to reach an inbox, which means getting past spam filters and email security tools. It still has to persuade someone to click a link, open an attachment, enter credentials or approve a payment. The attacker still needs infrastructure behind the message, such as a lookalike domain or a fake login page.

Other signals remain visible no matter how polished the writing is. The sender's actual address, the real destination of a link, an unexpected sense of urgency and a request that breaks normal procedure can all be checked. Business email compromise is a fraud in which criminals pose as executives or suppliers to redirect payments. Those schemes relied on context and timing long before AI writing tools existed.

Voice cloning software can produce a convincing imitation of a person's voice from a short audio sample. Scammers use it to place calls that sound like a company executive or a family member, then ask for money or access.

Phone fraud is not new. Traditional vishing, short for voice phishing, depended on the caller. A scammer worked from a script and used acting skill to pass as a bank officer, an IT technician or a panicked relative. The scammer's real voice set a limit. It could not match the voice of someone the target knew well.

Cloning removes that limit. Text-to-speech systems can read any script aloud in a copied voice. Voice conversion tools turn the scammer's own speech into the target voice during the call. That approach allows a live back-and-forth rather than a playback of prerecorded lines.

The raw material is often public. Executives speak on earnings calls, conference panels and recorded interviews. Ordinary people post videos on social media and record voicemail greetings. Any of these recordings can supply the sample a cloning tool needs.

Two patterns recur. In the executive version, a caller who sounds like a CEO or finance chief tells an employee to move money quickly. The call often cites a confidential deal or a deadline. It is a spoken form of business email compromise, the long-running fraud in which attackers pose as company leaders over email.

In the family version, a caller who sounds like a child or grandchild claims to be in trouble. The story might involve an arrest, an accident or a stranded trip, and the money has to be sent at once. This builds on the older grandparent scam. That scheme used a generic young voice and counted on a bad line or the victim's assumptions to fill the gaps. A cloned voice supplies the recognition the scam once had to fake. Caller ID spoofing can put a familiar number on the screen as well.

For most people, a familiar voice works as an identity check. Hearing it lowers suspicion before the request even arrives. Urgency and distress then discourage the pause that might expose the fraud.

A cloned voice does not give the scammer the real person's memories. Personal questions and references to shared events can expose the impostor. The standard safeguards build on that gap: hang up and call back on a number already known, or agree on a family code word in advance.

Deepfake video lets an attacker impersonate several trusted people at once on a live call. Hong Kong police reported in February 2024 that an employee of the engineering firm Arup was deceived on a video call in which the colleagues on screen were deepfakes.

Press reports put the loss at about $25 million. The case showed synthetic video being used to take money directly from a company, not only to spread false content online.

For years, a video call worked as an informal identity check. An email address can be spoofed. A voice on the phone can be imitated. Seeing a familiar face respond in real time felt like stronger proof, and many employees treated an on-camera conversation as a safe way to confirm an unusual request.

Deepfake video fraud targets that assumption. Business email compromise, a long-running form of payment fraud, relies on a fake or hijacked email account asking for money. The victim sees only text. Finance staff learned to check for altered sender addresses, lookalike domains and pressure to act quickly.

A convincing video call removes many of those clues. The request arrives through a channel the employee already trusts. The faces and voices match people the employee expects to see.

A call with several participants adds social pressure. When multiple apparent colleagues treat a request as routine, one employee has fewer reasons to question it. Raising doubts in front of a group can also feel awkward. Staging an entire meeting of fake people would have been impractical for a human con artist working alone.

The technical barrier has fallen. Convincing synthetic video once demanded time, computing power and specialist skill. Face-swapping and voice-synthesis software is now far easier to obtain. Some tools can run during a live conversation.

The method still depends on old-fashioned groundwork. Attackers need to know who works with whom, what a plausible request looks like and where to send the money. Public video and audio of executives, such as conference talks and earnings calls, can supply raw material for the fakes. The deepfake makes the request believable. It does not replace the research behind it.

For finance teams, the change is that appearing on camera no longer settles who someone is. Confirming a large transfer through a separately known phone number or an in-person check forces an attacker to defeat a second, independent channel.

WormGPT and FraudGPT were chatbots advertised on underground forums in 2023 as tools for writing phishing messages and malware. Their real capabilities were limited, but their appearance showed that a market for AI-for-crime services had formed.

Both products were pitched to buyers who wanted a language model without the refusals built into mainstream chatbots. The sales pitch was simple. Ask for a fake invoice email or a piece of malicious code, and the tool would write it without pushing back.

What buyers received fell short of that marketing. The tools largely wrapped existing language models rather than offering new technology of their own. Their output did not exceed what a skilled attacker could already produce by hand.

The packaging was the larger shift. Criminal forums have long sold ready-made attack tools to people who could not build them. Examples include phishing kits that copy bank login pages and ransomware-as-a-service, in which developers rent malware to affiliates for a cut of the ransom payments. WormGPT and FraudGPT applied the same business model to generative AI.

The contrast with traditional hacking comes down to who can take part. Writing a convincing lure or a working script once required either skill or money paid to someone who had it. A subscription chatbot, even a weak one, offers a novice attacker a shortcut around both.

The branding was part of the offer. Names that echo ChatGPT told buyers the service promised the same convenience, minus the safeguards. That framing gave the products an easy hook in forum advertisements.

Neither tool changed what an attack needs to succeed. A phishing email still needs a delivery route and a recipient who clicks. Malicious code still needs a way onto a target system. What changed is that AI assistance became something criminals could shop for as a product, alongside the hosting, tools and access they already buy from one another.

A 2024 study from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign found that an AI agent built on GPT-4 could exploit most of a test set of known, recently disclosed software flaws. The experiment ran in a lab. The other models the researchers tested did far worse.

The paper was written by Richard Fang, Daniel Kang and colleagues. It focused on one-day vulnerabilities. These are security flaws that have already been publicly disclosed, often with an official advisory and a patch, but that many systems have not yet fixed. A zero-day, by contrast, is a flaw the vendor does not yet know about or has not yet addressed.

The researchers gave the agent the public description of each vulnerability. This is the kind of entry published in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures system. They also gave it tools it could use to act on a target. The agent then had to work out how to turn that written description into a working attack.

When the researchers withheld the description, the agent's performance fell sharply. That gap indicates the agent was much better at acting on known information than at discovering flaws on its own.

In traditional hacking, turning an advisory into a working exploit is skilled, manual work. An attacker reads the disclosure and studies the patch or the affected code. Then the attacker writes and tests an exploit by hand. Public frameworks such as Metasploit package many exploits for reuse, but someone still has to write each module first. The UIUC result points to a way part of that step could be automated.

The timing matters because of the window between disclosure and patching. Once a flaw is public, defenders work to apply fixes. Attackers, meanwhile, try to use the flaw against systems that remain unpatched. Anything that shortens the attacker's side of that race leaves organizations less time to update.

The study has clear limits. It was a controlled experiment on a small, fixed set of vulnerabilities selected by the researchers. It did not show AI agents carrying out attacks against real organizations. It is not evidence of criminals using this technique in the wild. The results also apply only to the specific models and versions tested at the time.

For security teams, the lesson is narrow. Skilled humans were exploiting disclosed vulnerabilities long before language models existed. The research suggests the effort needed to weaponize those flaws could fall. That puts more weight on how quickly patches get applied after a flaw becomes public.

Anthropic reported in November 2025 that a group it described as Chinese state-sponsored used its Claude Code tool to run most of an espionage campaign. The company tracks the group as GTG-1002 and said roughly 30 targets were involved, with humans making the key decisions.

The account comes from Anthropic's own report. It is a company disclosure about misuse of the company's own product, not an independent forensic investigation. The details reflect what Anthropic chose to publish about the case.

The case differs from earlier misuse because of the role the AI played. In earlier misuse cases, language models mostly helped attackers draft messages or fix code. In this campaign, Anthropic described the tool acting more like an operator than an assistant. It worked through reconnaissance, vulnerability research and data handling across several targets. People stepped in at a limited number of decision points rather than directing every step.

Anthropic said the targets included large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturers and government agencies. The company reported that only a small number of the intrusions succeeded.

Getting the tool to cooperate took deception. Anthropic said the attackers split the operation into small tasks that each looked harmless on its own. They also told the model it was working for a legitimate cybersecurity firm carrying out defensive testing. Both tactics resemble social engineering, aimed at software instead of a person.

The report also described limits. Anthropic said Claude sometimes overstated its results. It claimed to have obtained credentials that did not work and presented publicly available information as a discovery. Anthropic described those errors as an obstacle to fully autonomous attacks.

The contrast with traditional state-backed hacking is about labor and pace. Espionage campaigns have long relied on skilled operators working through each stage by hand. Anthropic reported that at the campaign's peak, the tool made thousands of requests, often several per second. The company said that pace would be impossible for human hackers to match.

Anthropic said it banned the accounts involved, notified affected organizations and coordinated with authorities during its investigation.

DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge tested whether automated systems could find and fix vulnerabilities in open-source code without a person steering each step. Team Atlanta won the competition's finals, held at DEF CON in Las Vegas in August 2025.

DARPA is the U.S. Defense Department's research agency. It launched the competition in 2023 with ARPA-H, the federal agency that funds health research. The target was open-source software, the shared code inside everything from web servers to hospital equipment. A semifinal round took place at DEF CON in 2024 before the field narrowed for the finals.

Each team built what the competition called a cyber reasoning system. These systems pair large language models with conventional program analysis. They scan code for flaws and confirm that a flaw can be triggered. Then they write a patch that closes the hole without breaking the program.

For decades, bug hunting relied on two main methods. One was manual auditing, in which a skilled researcher reads source code line by line in search of mistakes. The other was fuzzing, which feeds a program huge volumes of malformed or random input until something crashes. Google $GOOGL's OSS-Fuzz service has run fuzzing against open-source projects since 2016. Fuzzing scales well, but each crash typically still has to be diagnosed and fixed by a person.

The systems at the AI Cyber Challenge were built to close that gap. Discovery, diagnosis and repair run in a single automated pipeline. The aim is to shorten the time a flaw sits in code that anyone can download and inspect.

The technology is dual-use. A tool that finds a vulnerability so it can be patched also finds a vulnerability that could be exploited. In traditional hacking, uncovering a new flaw in widely used software took specialist knowledge and sustained effort. Automated systems lower that cost for whoever runs them, defender or attacker.

That puts the weight on who finds a flaw first. A flaw found and patched by a maintainer is closed for everyone who updates. A flaw found first by an attacker stays open until someone else notices it.

Prompt injection is an attack that hides instructions inside text an AI system reads, so the model follows the attacker's commands instead of its operator's. OWASP lists it first, as LLM01, in its Top 10 for large language model applications.

The weakness comes from how language models handle input. A model receives its developer's instructions and outside content as one stream of text. It has no reliable built-in way to tell trusted commands apart from untrusted data. A line such as "ignore your previous instructions" can carry the same weight as the system's real rules.

Programmer Simon Willison coined the term "prompt injection" in September 2022. The name echoes SQL injection, an older attack in which malicious database commands are slipped into ordinary input fields. The parallel is only partial. SQL injection can be blocked with parameterized queries that keep code and data separate. Language models have no equivalent separation. That gap is why the problem remains open.

OWASP distinguishes two forms. Direct prompt injection happens when a user types manipulative instructions straight into a chatbot. The usual goal is to bypass its safety rules or pull out its hidden system prompt. Indirect prompt injection works differently. The malicious instructions sit inside content the AI processes later, such as a calendar invite, a shared file, a product review or a code comment.

The indirect form matters more as AI tools gain access to real systems. An assistant that can read an inbox, browse the web or call software tools can be steered by text its user never sees. A hidden line on a web page might tell a summarizing assistant to send private data to an outside address. White text on a white background, or instructions buried in metadata, can be invisible to a person yet readable to a model.

The target here is the model's interpretation of language, not a memory error, a weak password or a person's trust. The attacker does not need access to the victim's network to plant the instructions. Any content an AI agent might read becomes a possible entry point.

Mitigations exist, but none is complete. OWASP's guidance includes limiting the actions and permissions a model has, requiring human approval for high-risk steps and keeping external content separate from trusted instructions. It also calls for filtering inputs and outputs and for regular adversarial testing. These measures reduce the damage a successful injection can cause rather than eliminating the underlying flaw.

Stolen credentials, unpatched software, misconfigured systems and social engineering are still the usual ways attackers get in. Even when AI helps with an earlier stage, AI-assisted attacks usually end in familiar steps. Those steps include logging in with a stolen password or running malware on a machine.

A language model can draft a lure or summarize a target's public profile. The break-in itself still depends on a weakness that existed long before generative AI.

Credentials are the clearest case. A valid username and password let an attacker walk through the front door instead of breaking a window. Passwords leak through data breaches at other services. They also leak through malware that harvests saved logins from web browsers. A person who uses the same password on a shopping site and a work account exposes both when either one leaks. Credential stuffing is the practice of trying leaked username and password pairs across many sites. It is an automated technique that predates the current wave of AI tools.

Unpatched software is the second constant. Vendors publish fixes for known flaws, but organizations do not always install them quickly. During that gap, the flaw is public and the fix has not been applied. Internet-facing systems such as VPN gateways, email servers and file-transfer tools have been repeated targets for this reason.

Misconfiguration is quieter and often needs no exploit at all. A cloud storage bucket left open to the public can expose data to anyone who finds it. An administrator account still using a default password, or a remote desktop service exposed to the internet, can hand an attacker direct access.

Social engineering completes the group. It works by persuading a person to do something on the attacker's behalf. That might mean approving a login request, resetting a password or reading out a one-time code to someone posing as the help desk.

AI can make each of these openings faster to find or easier to exploit at scale. It does not remove the need for one of them.

Multi-factor authentication, phishing-resistant passkeys, prompt software patching and call-back verification of payment requests all hold up against AI-enhanced attacks. None of them depends on a person spotting whether a message, voice or face is fake.

Multi-factor authentication, or MFA, asks for a second proof of identity beyond the password. A stolen or guessed password alone does not open the account. A fluent phishing email can still trick someone into typing a password. The attacker then needs the second factor as well.

Not every form of MFA is equally strong. One-time codes, whether sent by text message or generated in an app, can be phished. Push approvals can be relayed too. A fake login page can pass these to the real site in real time. The attacker signs in while the victim believes nothing went wrong.

Passkeys close that gap. They are built on the FIDO2 standards developed by the FIDO Alliance and the W3C. A passkey is a cryptographic key pair. The private key stays on the user's device or in their password manager, and the user never types it or reads it aloud.

Each passkey is tied to the web domain of the site that created it. A look-alike site on a different domain cannot obtain a valid sign-in. That holds however convincing the page, or the AI-written email that led there, happens to be.

Call-back verification applies a similar principle to payment and account-change requests: confirm through a channel the attacker does not control. The employee ends the conversation and calls the requester on a number already on file, not one supplied in the message. A cloned voice or deepfaked face cannot answer a call placed to the real person's known number. Some companies also require a second approver for transfers above a set amount.

Patching software promptly covers the technical side. If AI tools shorten the time between a flaw's disclosure and a working exploit, the deciding factor becomes how quickly an organization installs the fix. Automatic updates and an accurate inventory of internet-facing systems shrink that window.

Defenders also use machine learning, and that practice predates the current wave of generative AI. Paul Graham's 2002 essay "A Plan for Spam" helped popularize statistical filtering of junk email. Fraud and threat detection tools apply similar methods to flag sign-ins from unfamiliar devices or transactions that break an account's usual pattern.

#5352. Nvidia’s interim CEO spent 13 years behind the scenes at Microsoft

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 10:45 amNovember 14, 2026 at 11:15 am

Colette Kress, named Nvidia’s interim CEO on Thursday after Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation, spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, including four as chief financial officer of the Redmond company’s Server and Tools business.

But to say she was under the radar would be an understatement: a search of Seattle-area news archives turns up a single mention of her name from her Microsoft years, in a 2007 press release listing her as a presenter at a Hotel 1000 seminar on Microsoft’s budgeting software.

Of course, that’s to be expected. Divisional finance execs aren’t typically public faces at Microsoft or anywhere else. But now she finds herself in the global spotlight, running the chipmaker at the center of the AI boom — at least for the time being.

Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang resigned as president, CEO and a member of the board, effective immediately, following reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials reportedly concluded was a Chinese spy, and a second affair with a direct report.

Kress will remain CFO while the board searches for a permanent CEO, considering internal and external candidates. Director Harvey Jones, the former Synopsys CEO, becomes Nvidia’s first board chair. Nvidia shares fell more than 13% in early trading.

Wall Street analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co. wrote in a note Thursday morning that Kress has built “enormous credibility” inside and outside Nvidia. “We always believed she would eventually be CEO of a major public tech company, but she would have to leave Nvidia after many years there,” he wrote.

Kress joined Microsoft in 1997 after finance roles at Texas Instruments, and held senior positions in corporate planning and finance before becoming chief financial officer of the Server and Tools business, which sold Windows Server, SQL Server and Visual Studio. Her LinkedIn profile lists her as a Microsoft corporate vice president from April 2006 to November 2010.

Server and Tools was also a training ground for Microsoft’s current leadership. Satya Nadella took over the business in 2011, after Kress left, and used it as a springboard to the CEO job three years later. Amy Hood, now Microsoft’s CFO, served as its chief of staff earlier in her career.

From Microsoft, Kress went to Cisco as senior vice president and CFO of its Business Technology and Operations Finance organization. Nvidia hired her as CFO in September 2013, ending a search of more than two years.

Now as Nvidia’s interim CEO, her first major test comes quickly. Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results Tuesday, Nov. 17, with an earnings call scheduled for 2 p.m. Pacific.

#5351. Why floods kill more people than tornadoes or lightning in the U.S.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Why floods kill more people than tornadoes or lightning in the U.S. on long-term average, from flash flood speed and driving into water to storm surge and dam failures

Water, not wind or electricity, is the more consistent weather killer in the U.S., on long-term average. National Weather Service (NWS) fatality records show floods claiming more lives than tornadoes or lightning over that span. The pattern is easy to miss. Tornadoes and lightning arrive with visible violence, while floodwater can look calm, shallow or distant until people are already in it.

The comparison needs a clear scope. It holds for the U.S. when long-term NWS averages are set side by side. It does not hold in every year. In 2011, tornadoes killed more than 500 people in the U.S., more than flooding killed that year. That season included the tornado that struck Joplin, Missouri. A violent tornado season can upend an annual tally. Over decades, though, the average tilts toward water.

Understanding why floods kill more people starts with how water behaves. Flash floods can build within minutes to hours of heavy rain. They often reach places where no rain is falling. Moving water also carries more force than its depth suggests. A road can be washed out beneath a surface that looks passable. Many flood deaths happen inside vehicles.

Human choices and the built environment shape that risk. Pavement sends rainwater toward low points, including underpasses and underground transit. Dams and levees can fail. Hurricanes, often remembered for their winds, can kill through storm surge on the coast and freshwater flooding far inland. Once the water recedes, cleanup brings its own hazards.

The exposure is global. Large populations live on floodplains and along coasts worldwide. When rivers overflow in densely settled regions, a single flood season can take lives across an entire country.

The 10 slides that follow are a selection of reasons and examples, not a ranked or complete account. They cover the speed of flash floods, the physics of moving water and the decisions drivers make at the water's edge. They also explain why lightning and tornadoes tend to kill fewer people on average. Hurricane rainfall, storm surge, dam failures and urban flooding each get their own slide. Each slide addresses a separate part of the same question: why water so often turns out to be the deadlier hazard.

A flash flood can build within minutes to a few hours of heavy rain. Its water often reaches places where no rain is falling at all. People downstream may get almost no time to react.

That short lead time separates a flash flood from a river flood. A river swollen by days of steady rain or snowmelt rises slowly enough to track. A flash flood arrives as a sudden surge. It can turn a dry creek bed or a quiet street into a fast channel before anyone nearby sees the danger.

Intense rainfall over a small area is the usual trigger. Slow-moving or repeating thunderstorms can drop rain faster than the ground can absorb it. Soil already saturated from earlier storms takes in very little more. Rock, clay and pavement take in almost none. The excess runs downhill and collects in the lowest available path.

Terrain decides how fast that runoff moves. Steep slopes, narrow canyons and small streams funnel water together and speed it up. In the arid U.S. Southwest, dry washes known as arroyos can fill with water from a storm miles upstream. Hillsides burned by wildfire add another risk. Scorched ground sheds water easily and has lost the plants that would otherwise slow it down.

The result is a flood that can arrive under clear skies. Hikers in a slot canyon or families camped beside a creek may hear no thunder and feel no rain. Meanwhile, a surge from a distant storm can be moving toward them. A flash flood that strikes at night is harder still to see and to escape.

The National Weather Service uses tiered alerts to match that speed. A flash flood watch means conditions favor flash flooding. A flash flood warning means flash flooding is happening or about to happen. The highest tier is a flash flood emergency. The NWS reserves it for rare cases where a flash flood poses a severe threat to human life and catastrophic damage is occurring or expected.

The more serious flash flood warnings can also reach mobile phones through the Wireless Emergency Alerts system. The NWS tells people under a warning to move to higher ground right away instead of waiting to see the water rise.

The National Weather Service says six inches of moving water is enough to knock an adult off their feet. The agency's thresholds climb quickly from there. It says 12 inches can carry away a small car, and two feet can carry away most vehicles, including SUVs and trucks.

Those depths run against instinct. Six inches of water sits well below the knee of any adult. Standing water at that level is a nuisance. Moving water at that level is a hazard. The current pushes against the legs, while the ground underneath offers little grip.

Water is heavy. A cubic foot of fresh water weighs about 62 pounds. When that mass moves, it presses steadily against anything in its path. The push grows sharply with speed. In basic fluid physics, the drag force on an object rises with the square of the current's velocity. Water moving twice as fast pushes roughly four times as hard.

A person wading through a current has only the friction under their feet to resist that force. Mud, gravel, slick pavement and submerged debris all make that friction unreliable. Once a person falls, getting back up in moving water is difficult. The current can then carry them downstream.

Vehicles face a second problem: buoyancy. A car body traps a large volume of air. As water rises around it, the car displaces that water, and the water pushes upward on the vehicle. The lift reduces how firmly the tires press against the road. Less pressure on the tires means less traction. A modest current can then shove the vehicle sideways or float it off the road.

Buoyancy is one reason a small car can be carried away by about a foot of moving water. Larger SUVs and trucks sit higher and weigh more, which gives them some margin. NWS guidance still says two feet of moving water can carry away most of them. That depth reaches around or just above the knee of a standing adult.

Depth is also hard to judge from above. Floodwater is usually brown with sediment, which hides whatever lies beneath the surface. A stretch that looks uniform can conceal a dip or a ditch. Speed is just as deceptive. A smooth surface can mask a fast current. Floodwater also often carries branches and other debris that can strike a person or a vehicle.

The National Weather Service and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report that more than half of flood drownings happen when someone drives a vehicle into hazardous water. That puts one decision at the center of many flood deaths: whether to drive forward.

The choice often comes quickly. A driver reaches a flooded dip, underpass or creek crossing. The water looks like a thin layer over the pavement, and the driver decides to keep going. The surface shows little of what lies underneath.

Floodwater can scour a roadbed from below while the water on top looks calm. The asphalt may be undercut or gone entirely, leaving a drop-off where the lane used to be. A car that enters at what seems like a safe spot can end up in a channel far deeper than the driver expected.

Muddy water hides the edge of the road, the centerline and any debris moving in the current. Darkness adds to the problem. Headlights glare off the surface and flatten any sense of depth. A familiar route offers no guarantee. A single storm can change the ground beneath it.

Low-water crossings raise the danger in parts of the U.S. where roads dip straight through creek beds. In central Texas and much of the Southwest, many of those creeks sit dry for long stretches and then fill after heavy rain. Drivers who cross them dry most of the year can misread how much conditions have changed.

The NWS built its Turn Around Don't Drown campaign around this moment at the water's edge. The message asks drivers to treat water covering a road as a reason to stop and choose another route. The slogan is four words long and easy to recall when there is little time to weigh options.

Road closure barricades carry the same message. Driving around one puts the driver into the water and can pull rescue crews in as well. Swift-water rescues expose firefighters and emergency teams to the same currents that trapped the motorist.

If a vehicle stalls in rising water, NWS safety guidance is to get out and move to higher ground if it is safe to do so.

Lightning kills fewer people than flooding in the U.S., on long-term average, because each strike hits a single point, endangering one person or a small group at a time. U.S. lightning deaths have also fallen over the decades. Flood danger, by contrast, can spread across whole valleys and neighborhoods at once.

The difference comes down to geography. A flood can cover miles of road, homes and farmland in a single event. Anyone inside that footprint is exposed, whether they are at home, at work or trying to leave. A lightning bolt discharges at one spot. Its harm reaches the person struck and anyone close by, through current that travels along the ground or jumps from a nearby object.

The danger also has a clear end. A thunderstorm moves through, and the electrical threat passes with it. The National Weather Service tells people to wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back outside. Floodwater does not follow that kind of timetable. It can stay high, or keep rising, for hours or days after the rain stops.

The NWS sums up its guidance in five words: "When thunder roars, go indoors." If thunder is audible, the storm is close enough to strike. The agency treats no outdoor spot as safe during a thunderstorm. A substantial building with wiring and plumbing offers protection. So does a hard-topped metal vehicle with the windows closed. Open-sided shelters, tents, picnic pavilions and lone trees do not.

Lightning can strike well away from the heaviest rain, sometimes from what looks like clear sky overhead. That is why the NWS ties its advice to the sound of thunder rather than to rainfall or dark clouds.

Most people struck by lightning survive, though many live with lasting injuries such as nerve damage, memory problems and chronic pain. A person who has been struck carries no electrical charge. Bystanders can safely start CPR and call for emergency help right away. Fast CPR can save a victim whose heart has stopped.

Tornadoes kill fewer people than floods in the U.S., on long-term average, because each one damages only a narrow path. Warnings and sturdy shelter also reduce the risk for people inside that path. The rare violent tornado that strikes a populated area is the main exception.

A tornado concentrates its destruction. Even a large tornado with a long track leaves the ground on either side of its path largely untouched. One neighborhood can be flattened while streets a short distance away keep their roofs. Floodwater spreads differently. It can fill whole valleys, road networks and low-lying districts at the same time.

The warning system gives people in a tornado's path a chance to act. The National Weather Service issues a tornado watch when conditions over a region favor tornadoes. It issues a tornado warning when a tornado has been spotted or detected by radar. A warning is the signal to take shelter right away.

The NWS advises moving to a basement, a storm cellar or a small interior room on the lowest floor of a sturdy building, away from windows. Mobile homes offer little protection. The agency advises leaving them for a stronger structure before a tornado arrives. It also advises covering the head and neck to guard against flying debris.

None of this rules out mass casualties. The Tri-State Tornado of March 18, 1925, tracked across Missouri, Illinois and Indiana and killed 695 people. It remains the deadliest tornado in U.S. history. It struck decades before public tornado warnings of the kind used today existed.

Modern forecasting has not removed the danger. On May 22, 2011, a tornado rated EF5, the highest category on the Enhanced Fujita scale, tore through Joplin, Missouri. It killed 158 people. Sirens sounded in Joplin before the tornado arrived. The death toll still placed it among the deadliest U.S. tornadoes on record.

The Tri-State and Joplin tornadoes show how tornado deaths tend to arrive. Most tornadoes cause no deaths, and many touch down over open country. The toll comes mainly from the few violent tornadoes that cross towns. That pattern makes tornado deaths uneven from one year to the next.

Rain from a hurricane can kill more people than its winds, often far from the coast where the storm made landfall. Hurricane Harvey in 2017 and Hurricane Helene in 2024 both became deadly freshwater flood disasters.

Harvey came ashore on the middle Texas coast in late August 2017 as a Category 4 hurricane. It then weakened and stalled over southeast Texas for days. That slow movement let rain bands pass over the same areas again and again, including the Houston metro area.

One Texas location recorded more than 60 inches of rain from Harvey. That total is a record for any tropical cyclone in the U.S. Most of the storm's deaths came from freshwater flooding, not from wind.

Helene followed a different path to a similar result. It made landfall in Florida's Big Bend region in late September 2024 as a Category 4 hurricane. It then moved north into the mountains of the southern Appalachians.

Western North Carolina, hundreds of miles from the landfall point, took the worst of the flooding. Rivers and streams in steep mountain valleys rose fast. Communities around Asheville saw roads, homes and businesses swept away. Helene killed more than 200 people across several states.

A hurricane's category does not capture this risk. The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale rates storms by sustained wind speed alone. It says nothing about how much rain a storm will drop or where that rain will land. A weaker or slower storm can still produce extreme flooding.

Forward speed also shapes the flood risk. A storm that crawls, as Harvey did, keeps dropping rain on one region. Terrain plays a role too. When moist tropical air is pushed up mountain slopes, as happened during Helene, it cools and releases more rain onto the ground below.

Distance from the coast does not remove the danger. Harvey and Helene showed that a storm's deadliest water can reach cities and mountain towns well away from any beach.

Storm surge, not wind, is the hurricane hazard most likely to kill people along the coast. The National Hurricane Center has long described the surge as the greatest threat to life when a hurricane reaches a shoreline.

Storm surge is an abnormal rise in seawater pushed ashore by a storm's winds. It comes on top of the normal astronomical tide. When the surge arrives near high tide, the combined water level is known as the storm tide, and it climbs even higher.

The height of a surge depends on more than a storm's strength. Its size, forward speed and angle of approach all play a part. So do the shape of the coastline and the slope of the seafloor offshore. A broad, shallow continental shelf, like much of the northern Gulf of Mexico, lets water pile up higher than a steep drop-off would.

The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale does not account for any of this. It rates hurricanes on sustained wind speed alone. A large storm with a lower category can still push a destructive surge far inland.

Surge water does not behave like a slowly rising river. It arrives with breaking waves riding on top. The force of that moving seawater can knock buildings off their foundations. It also floods escape routes and cuts off people who did not leave in time.

Hurricane Katrina showed how surge and failing defenses can combine. In 2005, the storm drove water against the levees and floodwalls protecting New Orleans. Those barriers failed. Much of the city, which sits partly below sea level, flooded. Katrina killed more than 1,800 people.

The National Weather Service sums up its coastal advice in a short phrase: "Run from the water, hide from the wind." Coastal evacuation zones in the U.S. are based largely on surge risk rather than wind. The National Hurricane Center also issues storm surge watches and warnings separately from hurricane watches and warnings.

A storm surge warning can cover stretches of coast where hurricane-force winds are not expected. That separation lets forecasters flag life-threatening inundation on its own terms.

A dam failure releases stored water all at once, and a steep canyon can turn one thunderstorm into a wall of water. The Johnstown Flood of 1889 and the Big Thompson Canyon flash flood of 1976 are one deadly U.S. example of each.

Johnstown, Pennsylvania, sat in a narrow valley where the Little Conemaugh River and Stonycreek River join. Upstream stood the South Fork Dam, an earthen embankment holding back a reservoir called Lake Conemaugh. The lake served as a private retreat for the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club. Its members included Pittsburgh industrialists Andrew Carnegie and Henry Clay Frick.

On May 31, 1889, after heavy rain, the dam gave way. The reservoir emptied into the valley below and surged toward Johnstown. It collected trees, rail cars and the wreckage of homes along the way. More than 2,200 people died. The disaster ranks among the deadliest in U.S. history.

The aftermath drew a national relief effort. Clara Barton brought the American Red Cross to Johnstown, in one of the young organization's first large relief operations. The flood also raised public questions about who was responsible for maintaining a private dam above a populated town.

Big Thompson Canyon in Colorado involved no dam at all. On July 31, 1976, a slow-moving thunderstorm stalled over the canyon. The canyon carries the Big Thompson River between Estes Park and Loveland. Its steep rock walls shed the rain straight into the river channel. The river rose into a torrent that tore through campgrounds, cabins and the road along the canyon floor.

The flood killed 144 people. The canyon was crowded that evening with visitors marking the weekend of Colorado's centennial. Many of the dead were visitors who had little warning before the water reached them.

The two disasters share a basic physical problem. In each case, a large volume of water was concentrated and sent through a narrow space with people in its path. In a canyon flash flood, climbing the walls on foot to higher ground offers more protection than staying on the canyon floor. That floor is where roads and campsites sit. It is also where the water runs deepest and fastest.

Cities can turn heavy rain into deadly floods quickly because pavement and rooftops shed water instead of absorbing it. On July 20, 2021, floodwater poured into a subway line in Zhengzhou, China, and trapped passengers underground. Fourteen of them died.

In a field or forest, much of the rain that falls soaks into the soil. In a city, roads, parking lots, sidewalks and roofs block that path. Rain runs off these hard surfaces almost as soon as it lands. It then moves toward the lowest places it can reach.

Storm drains and sewers are built to carry that runoff away, but every system has a limit. When rain falls faster than the pipes can take it, the excess stays on the surface. Streets begin to behave like channels. Underpasses and dips in the road fill like basins.

Underground spaces sit at the bottom of this system. Subway stations, rail tunnels, underground garages and basement rooms all lie below street level. Water that enters them often has nowhere to drain. The people inside may have only one or two ways out. Those exits lead up through the same openings the water is coming down.

Zhengzhou is the capital of Henan province in central China. During extreme rainfall in July 2021, water flooded Line 5 of the city's metro. Passengers on a stopped train were left standing in rising water inside the tunnel. Many were rescued.

The same pattern has appeared far from China. In September 2021, the remnants of Hurricane Ida brought intense rain to New York City. Water filled basement apartments, and residents drowned inside their homes.

Urban flash flooding does not need a river or creek nearby. It can develop blocks away from any stream, wherever runoff gathers faster than drains can remove it. That makes the danger harder to read from a window or a sidewalk.

The Zhengzhou disaster shows how a city's layout shapes flood risk. During intense rain, the spaces built below ground are among the first to fill and among the hardest to leave.

Flooding kills on a global scale partly because so many people live where water naturally spreads. In 2022, floods in Pakistan killed more than 1,700 people.

Floodplains have drawn settlement for thousands of years. The land is flat and easy to build on. Floods leave behind silt that keeps soil fertile for farming. Rivers supply drinking water, irrigation and routes for trade. The same features that make these places productive put homes, farms and roads in the path of high water.

Coastlines follow a similar pattern. Many of the world's largest cities sit on the sea, at river mouths or on deltas. Low elevation and dense development leave little room for water to go when rivers rise or the sea pushes inland.

Pakistan's 2022 disaster showed that exposure at national scale. The floods followed an exceptionally heavy monsoon season. Water spread across farmland, villages and towns in the Indus River basin. Much of the country's population and agriculture is concentrated there. Many people lost homes, crops and livestock at once.

A flood's danger also continues after the water stops rising. Floodwater mixes with sewage, fuel and chemicals. It can contaminate wells and public water supplies. Drinking or washing in that water can spread illness. The risk is highest where clean water and sanitation were already limited.

Damaged power lines create a separate hazard. Downed or submerged lines can energize standing water. People wading through flooded streets or basements can be electrocuted without seeing any sign of the danger. Any downed line can still carry current, even when it looks dead.

Carbon monoxide poisoning is another cleanup risk. When grid power fails, households turn to portable generators, gasoline pressure washers and fuel-burning heaters. Running that equipment inside homes, garages or basements lets the odorless, colorless gas build to deadly levels. People can be overcome before they notice symptoms.

Each of these hazards can claim lives well after the floodwater has drained away.

#5350. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5349. XML pioneer Jean Paoli’s startup Docugami acquired by Inveniam after open-source partnership

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 12:15 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 12:16 pm

Docugami, the Seattle-area startup led by XML co-creator Jean Paoli, has been acquired by Inveniam, a Detroit-area company that uses blockchain to help investors verify the data behind assets such as commercial real estate and private loans.

The deal follows a partnership this summer in which the companies released DGML, Docugami’s open-source format for turning business documents into data that AI agents can use and check.

Financial terms of the acquisition weren’t disclosed. All of Docugami’s employees are joining Inveniam, a Docugami spokesperson said. The team numbers about 50 including contractors. Paoli becomes Inveniam’s chief product and technology officer, and Docugami will keep operating from Kirkland, according to the announcement.

Paoli co-founded Docugami in 2018 after more than 20 years at Microsoft, where he helped create XML and the Office file formats.

The startup, based in Kirkland, Wash., raised a $10 million seed round in 2020 led by SignalFire, with backing from Bob Muglia, the former Microsoft executive and Snowflake CEO. Grammarly, the writing-assistant company now known as Superhuman, later disclosed that it had taken part in the round, its first investment in another company.

Prior to the acquisition, Docugami ranked No. 155 on the GeekWire 200, our list of the Pacific Northwest’s top independent, privately held startups.

DGML labels each piece of a document by what it is — a base rent, a loan payment, a liability cap — so a single figure can be traced back to the page it came from. Inveniam records a digital fingerprint of each of those data points on its blockchain, called NVNM Chain, so any later change shows up.

Inveniam executives said Thursday morning on a livestream with Paoli that DGML solves a problem they’ve had in bringing on new clients: every client’s documents are different, which required templates and standard formats before the data could be used.

“One promise I want to make personally: DGML stays open and its openness is strategic to Inveniam,” Paoli wrote in a LinkedIn post.

Inveniam, led by CEO Patrick O’Meara, also acquired Mantra, a crypto company that provided the original technology for NVNM Chain, earlier this year. Mantra co-founder John Patrick Mullin said on the livestream that NVNM Chain will move to its own independent blockchain, with the main network expected to launch in the next few weeks.

Fees on that network will help fund buybacks of an NVNM cryptocurrency token, Mullin said. O’Meara proposed a separate session on when that token will launch.
