#5268. Crunchbase Data: Nvidia’s Startup Funding Deals Hit A Record. What’s Next After Huang?

Before it was thrust into crisis this week, Nvidia was steadily continuing its pace as one of the busiest startup investors around, including backing many of the biggest venture deals of 2026.

The chipmaker and its NVentures arm have participated in more than 120 startup funding deals so far this year, according to Crunchbase data, already topping last year’s record-setting pace and marking its most prolific year yet as a private-company investor.

With co-founder Jensen Huang’s sudden departure this week amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs including with employees and a woman U.S. intelligence experts suspect of spying for China, we took a fresh look at where Nvidia and NVentures have been investing and what the future could hold.

Nvidia is the most active corporate investor so far in 2026, an analysis of Crunchbase data shows. It and NVentures together are also among the top 20 most active investors in startups this year overall.

Nvidia’s startup investments this year total 121 and span AI model developers, data center operators, robotics startups and healthcare companies. That continues the broad approach we examined last year, when the company and its venture arm participated in 91 known startup financings, up from 54 the year prior.

The largest Nvidia-backed deals in 2026 include OpenAI’s Series G, which closed at $122 billion in March, and Anthropic’s $30 billion Series G in February. (Those figures represent the entire rounds, including other investors’ contributions, rather than Nvidia’s individual checks.)

The company also participated in a $3.9 billion September Series F for AI infrastructure provider Crusoe and a roughly $3.5 billion September Series D for model developer Mistral AI.

Of course, large as those deals are, Nvidia’s startup bets represent a small fraction of the company’s incredible market capitalization. Even as its share price tumbled this week with Huang’s departure and the surrounding news, Nvidia’s valuation remains close to $4 trillion.

NVentures’ activity shows how far that investment footprint extends beyond the best-known model developers.

The venture arm’s larger bets this year include robot intelligence developer Skild AI’s $1.4 billion January Series C, and autonomous driving startup Waabi’s $750 million Series C in the same month. It also backed two rounds for Bedrock Robotics, which develops technology to automate construction equipment: a $270 million Series B in February and a $600 million Series C in October. Its healthcare investments included a $150 million April Series E for medical imaging AI company Aidoc.

As in years past, Nvidia and NVentures usually participate alongside other investors. The company or its venture arm are listed as lead or co-lead investors in about 1 in 5 of its deals this year, per Crunchbase data.

For startups, Nvidia’s value as an investor also extends beyond its deep pockets. NVentures describes its offering as access to technical teams, technology integrations and help reaching customers.

Nvidia’s new leadership could bring a different approach to risk. Before this week’s news, CFO and now interim CEO Collette Kress had pushed back on Huang’s increasingly large AI investments, Reuters reported this week, citing two people familiar with the matter.

Nvidia’s board has said it expects operations, customer commitments and its product roadmap to continue without interruption. That assurance leaves the pace of future investments an open question. With earnings scheduled for Nov. 17, founders and investors will be watching for signs of how much of Huang’s investment playbook continues under new leadership.

#5267. October 29, 2019

Chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in New Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

More specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he says that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a new sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”

Park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own company. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a new home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

The now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the company has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as quickly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

#5266. XRP Risks Losing $1 Amid Aggressive $2.5 Billion Shift

As XRP continues to struggle amid the broad crypto market volatility while failing in multiple attempts to recover, key on-chain metrics are pointing to increased selling pressure among traders.

While momentum remains extremely weak, latest data from crypto analytics platform, Cryptoquant, shows that sellers have dominated both XRP’s spot and futures markets, putting it at risk of losing the long-held $1 mark.

Per the data, XRP’s cumulative volume delta (CVD) across major cryptocurrency exchanges shows that aggressive selling has dominated both its spot and futures market since September 23.

As of November 12, XRP’s Perpetual CVD on Binance has fallen from -$109 million to about -$1.1 billion. It is important to note that the CVD of an asset is a key metric that measures the difference between the volume of aggressive buy orders and aggressive sell orders over time.

While the metric turns negative when more traders are aggressively selling than buying, the -991 million negative balance in the Binance perpetual CVD signals stronger selling pressure.

With the negative balance on Binance exceeding its previous level by more than 10 times, this shows that traders have placed significantly more market sell orders than buy orders, either by opening short positions or closing existing long positions.

Apart from its futures market, further data shows that sellers have also dominated XRP’s spot activity across all major crypto exchanges, including Binance.

Notably, XRP’s All CEX Estimated Spot CVD moved from -$400 million to -$2.9 billion over the same period.

While this marks a $2.5 billion increase in the imbalance favoring sellers, it indicates that XRP spot traders have also been selling XRP more aggressively rather than buying, propelling the asset for further price declines.

#5265. Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

According to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

Those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

Denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

The sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

Timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

This removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

App developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

This is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams plan to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec says it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

The coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

#5264. VC Firm Plural Closes On $1.1B To Invest In European Startups With Potential For ‘GDP-Level Impact’

Early-stage startup investor Plural says it has closed on its largest fund to date — just over $1.1 billion, or 1 billion euros — to lead early-stage investments across Europe.

With the announcement, Plural joins a select group of European venture firms that have raised funds of a billion dollars or more in recent years. Others include Balderton Capital, Atomico and Index Ventures, which is co-headquartered in London and San Francisco. It also follows a Q3 that marked Europe’s strongest venture funding quarter in years.

“Our common theme is ambition. We go after the founders that are building the most ambitious things we can humanly find,” Sten Tamkivi, a co-founder of the firm, said in an interview with Crunchbase News. “Our stated objective remains to have a GDP-level impact on Europe with the companies that we back.”

Plural’s portfolio is a mix of energy, compute, defense, robotics, health and software. The firm first backed fusion energy company Proxima Fusion in its 2023 pre-seed round and has also invested in energy storage company Ore Energy. In defense and aerospace, its investments include European defense tech company Helsing and hypersonic flight and missile company Hypersonica, whose Series A it led in 2026. Plural also led the 2024 Series B for The Exploration Co., which develops space transportation.

In robotics and manufacturing, Plural has backed Monumental, which develops bricklaying robots; Sunrise Robotics, which builds robots for manufacturing; CircuitHub, which manufactures circuit board assemblies; and Upside Robotics, which develops agricultural robots. In compute, its investments include optical AI accelerator company Olix and photonic networking company Oriole Networks. More recently, Plural led the pre-seed round for Callosum, which is building a routing layer for heterogeneous compute.

Its investments have shifted year to year and fund to fund based on where the most ambitious founders are pulling the firm, said Tamkivi.

“Europe has agonized maybe a little bit too much about, ‘Hey, we missed this wave in the models, and the big labs are in the U.S. and China,’  and so forth. But if you look at the rest of the pyramid, we’re doing well,” he said.

The latest fund is the firm’s third and is double the size of its fund 2, raised in 2024, and 4x its first fund, closed in 2022.

Plural’s portfolio companies have had a breakout year, raising more than $3 billion in follow-on capital so far in 2026.

The team has six equal partners, all prior founders and operators based in London, Tallinn and Paris. Plural was founded by Taavet Hinrikus, co-founder of Wise, and Tamkivi co-founder of Teleport, both early employees at Skype, as well as Ian Hogarth, co-founder of Songkick, and Khaled Helioui, former CEO of Bigpoint.

The team has two other partners: Carina Namih, co-founder of HelixNano, and Pierre-Dimitri Gore-Coty, a former Uber executive.

Each partner aims to make one to three new investments per year, leaving  bandwidth to work hands-on with founders.

The firm’s entry point is seed and Series A, where it likes to lead. “We’re still early-stage investors, so two-thirds of this money that we raise goes into early stage. What we’ve tagged on top is that now we have more capital to follow through in our winners, and  double down and triple down,” Tamkivi said, adding: “there’s more reserves to do that.”

#5263. October 31, 2019

Album VC, a Lehi, Utah-based early-stage venture firm that’s been known until now as Peak Ventures, just gathered up $75 million in capital commitments for its third early-stage fund.

The development shows investor confidence in Album’s young team, which came together in 2014 after the founder of Zinch — a site connecting colleges and students that sold to the ed-tech company Chegg in 2011 — decided to try his hand at investing in other startups.

As that founder, Sid Krommenhoek — who stayed on with Chegg for several years, running its international efforts — explains it, “I thought I’d do another startup. But I also knew from our own experience in struggling to raise money the need for more capital in Utah, and I thought having that operator-entrepreneur perspective could be useful.”

A first fund, like many in the industry, was more of an experiment, though it was a decent $23 million, thanks largely to the support of Chegg CEO Dan Rosensweig, who was early to commit capital to the fund. A second ($56 million) fund followed when Krommenhoek and John Mayfield — a friend who joined him from a marketing role at Qualtrics — began investing more seriously in their backyard and beyond.

They were soon joined by a third investor, Diogo Myrrha, who began as a principal with the firm and is now a general partner. Explains Krommenhoek of one of the many things that binds the three Brigham Young University grads, “We all came into Utah’s orbit when it wasn’t necessarily a place where you could live out your career, but that’s changed.”

#5262. Bitcoin Mining Legend Chun Wang Rebuys ETH at 14% Discount After $18.5 Million Sale

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

F2Pool co-founder Chun Wang, known on X as Satofishi, bought 5,246 ETH worth $10.78 million over the past two days at an average price of $2,054, according to Lookonchain and Arkham data.

On Nov. 5, with ether trading near $2,400, Wang sold 6,200 wrapped staked ETH (wstETH) for $18.5 million in USDC. Wrapped staked ETH is a version of Lido's staked ether (stETH) that can be used in DeFi protocols.

This week, ether traded about 14% lower than on the day of the sale, and Wang started buying it back.

He withdrew 5,246 ETH from Binance hot wallets in two transfers of 3,996 ETH and 1,250 ETH. The purchase cost him $10.78 million, so about $7.7 million from the Nov. 5 sale is still left in USDC, according to Lookonchain.

Wang then sent 3,996 ETH ($8.23 million) to Lido. Lido is the largest liquid staking protocol on Ethereum. He deposited the wstETH he received into Spark, a lending protocol in the Sky ecosystem, which was previously known as MakerDAO. In Spark, wstETH can be used as collateral, while it continues to earn staking rewards.

He started out arbitraging Bitcoin between overseas exchanges and China's Taobao and later co-founded F2Pool. He launched the pool in 2013 together with Mao Shixing. At that time, F2Pool was one of the first Bitcoin mining pools in China.

In 2015, he bought a condo in Pattaya for 2,900 BTC. He later sold it for 7 BTC, as the price of Bitcoin had risen many times over.

In 2025, Wang also funded and commanded Fram2, the first crewed spaceflight over Earth's polar regions, on a SpaceX Crew Dragon.

F2Pool also mined ether until Ethereum moved to proof-of-stake in September 2022. Before that, Wang launched the non-custodial staking service stakefish. According to Wang, he decided to do it after a conversation with Vitalik Buterin in 2017. Stakefish was also one of the first node operators of Lido.

Ether is down more than 15% since the start of the month amid outflows from spot ETFs, according to SoSoValue. At press time, ETH is trading at $2,020.

In a recent announcement, Binance Wallet stated it will discontinue support for the Blast chain effective November 30, 2026, at 10:00 (UTC). After this date, the crypto exchange said that users will no longer be able to view, send, or receive Blast assets within the Binance Wallet.

Ethereum layer-2 network Blast announced in October 2026 that it was shutting down, a little over two years after its launch, as fading activity left it unable to cover operating costs.

Binance noted that this change only affects the display and management of Blast assets within Binance Wallet, as users can still claim their assets on the official Blast site. In light of this, users are strongly advised to manage or transfer their Blast assets before November 30, 2026, at 10:00 (UTC).

This update only affects the Blast network and does not impact other blockchains supported by Binance Wallet.

Binance has resumed its cryptocurrency listing activity after a brief pause, introducing new perpetual contracts for Hyperliquid (HYPE) and TRON (TRX).

The late-October hack had interrupted the exchange's listings; its last addition was on October 29, when it announced it was listing the Predict token.

In the last 24 hours, Binance has made two listing announcements: one for HYPE and TRX perpetual contracts, and one for TradFi perpetual contracts on Nu Holdings Ltd. Class A Ordinary Shares and Freedom Holding Corp. Common Stock.

Binance Futures will launch HYPEUSDC and TRXUSDC Perpetual Contracts with up to 75x leverage on November 16, 2026, at 08:30 (UTC) and 08:35 (UTC), respectively. The move is intended to expand the list of trading choices offered on Binance Futures and enhance users’ trading experience.

To expand the list of trading choices offered on Binance Futures and enhance users’ trading experience, the NUUSDT USDT-Priced Perpetual Contract and the FRHCUSDT USDT-Priced Perpetual Contract have been admitted to trading on Binance RIE and to clearing and settlement by Binance RCH today, November 12, 2026.

#5259. In The AI Era, Keep Hiring New College Grads — And Make Them Managers From Day One

A few months ago, I was sitting lakeside with a neighbor. He is the head of AI for a pharmaceutical company, and he mentioned the truly incredible productivity his senior team is receiving from AI.

Then he paused and turned to me and said: “You know, I may never hire another junior engineer again. Which is great for the business right now, but who’s the next generation that is going to run this when we retire?”

The concern over what will happen to young people just entering the workforce is one many of us are grappling with right now, and it has a human dimension. Not just what happens to employment rates, but what happens to my students or my children?

College graduates typically do the individual contributor knowledge work that AI is evermore capable of delivering. To cite one statistic, a recent Stanford study found employment of 22 to 25 year olds in occupations most exposed to AI is running 19% below rates for their peers in less AI-impacted sectors, and that gap has been widening.

What role will new graduates play in the age of AI? And how will we develop the generation of managers who will supervise AI? Fortunately, we have thriving examples with 200 years of history on how to teach 22 year olds to do exactly that.

Our claim is that the reason senior folks get more out of AI today is not primarily because they have greater subject knowledge, but rather because they are good managers. They have to trust folks who work for them without completely trusting them, they have to divide tasks, delegate clearly, check results and patiently correct, coach, and sometimes shift personnel on their teams.

The future for new graduates is to become great managers now, at the very beginning of their career, and not after a long period of individual contribution.

The nature of the innovation of AI is that it delivers knowledge work. We know a lot about human knowledge workers and the analogy to AI knowledge workers is strong.

Knowledge workers know much more about their individual sphere of expertise than their managers do. Good managers routinely organize and lead knowledge workers who are just flat-out much smarter than they are. They do this through the craft of management.

These same qualities, as AI behaves more like AI executives, naturally give good managers the skills to manage AI agents, who become the individual contributor knowledge workers.

It is no secret that the investment industry culture values most highly the brilliance of the individual contributor who delivers the incisive observation, makes the correct investment call, and closes the one-on-one negotiation with a win.

I have lived this culture for a long time. Calling an investor a “great people manager” is a backhanded compliment at best. In the investment industry, the jump from individual contributor to manager usually arrives midcareer or later, and typically with little to no formal training in the craft of management.

The analyst, associate and vice president are primarily acting as individual contributors (though of course they may mentor a few junior folks), and are not shifting to acting primarily as managers of other knowledge workers until principal or perhaps partner.

When I was an analyst at Morgan Stanley many years ago, the hierarchy ran from analyst to managing director. Analysts were the ultimate individual contributors, and whenever an analyst would attempt to delegate some work to others, we had a name for that: “managing analyst.” This clever put-down reflected the cultural belief that real credit goes to those who do, not those who deliver through the work of those they manage.

This blind spot on the importance of management is not limited to the investment industry. As another salient recent example, let’s look at the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Much has been written about this event, where OpenAI agents hacked into Hugging Face.

In OpenAI’s own report on the incident, its proposed long list of fixes, including stronger security, alerts on breaches and post-incident remediation, does not address directly training its employees to be better managers of these agents. That’s even as the company acknowledges that members of an internal team at OpenAI knew of many of the concerning behaviors (including message board and unauthorized internet access) in late May, and did not act until July.

This may be an unfair analogy, but imagine if we hired 1,200 workers to operate a warehouse complex, gave each of them detailed written instructions, and then had all the line managers and senior managers leave for a week. If we came back to find that someone had stolen a delivery van, the problem wouldn’t be that these weren’t the right workers or that the instructions weren’t clear enough. The problem is lack of management.

As I was wrestling with this problem, I talked with my business school classmate Michael Quoia, who attended the U.S. Naval Academy and served as an officer, and then built a career in executive leadership development. He recalled:

“When I met my division of 25 sailors in Yokosuka, Japan at the young age of 22 years old, I was greeted by my senior chief petty officer, who already served for nearly 20 years. Behind him, we had several organizational levels including the first line sailors who conducted maintenance on the fire control systems. This was actually a harder problem than we are facing with AI. This was about supervising at least three levels without experience. I was expected to provide character, judgment, problem solving and leadership, despite not having come up through the ranks. How did the Navy develop these qualities in me so that I could bypass time in the seat as a frontline worker?”

Like companies facing the AI dilemma we have been exploring, the military needs to develop capable leaders who lack entry-level experience. And while the military is a very relevant example, it is not the only one. The Home Depot’s store management program and General Electric’s Crotonville are two examples of corporations who recruit high-potential talent and put them through an accelerated leadership development program to prepare them to lead people in jobs they have not done.

Let’s look, though, at how the Naval Academy provided Michael’s training, and what that may mean whether you are 22 years old or hiring 22-year-olds.

First, the foundation of developing future officers is the development of moral leadership. The mission of the United States Naval Academy begins with the phrase “To develop midshipmen morally, mentally, and physically … .” In an age of AI, first-line managers of AI agents will need integrity and a moral compass, because AI does not come with that reliably pre-installed. It is no overstatement to suggest that moral leadership of AI could have societal implications and needs to be developed.

Second, the service academies are intentionally designed as leadership laboratories. From plebe summer to commissioning, midshipmen progress from learning how to be a good subordinate to true manager. What is most relevant to the age of AI is that simulated leadership learning is possible and proven if designed with care.

Third, the service academies build high-pressure situations into their leadership laboratory. While most companies are not placing their first-line managers in life or death situations, the ability to lead in high stakes situations, for instance to take personal responsibility for an AI agent swarm you launched which is now “going rogue,” requires composure and decisiveness under stress and pressure.

If a 22-year-old ensign can manage 25 sailors on a Yokosuka destroyer, albeit with support from senior officers and enlisted, our 22-year-old college graduate can certainly be trained to manage 25 super-intelligent agents. The moment for practicing the craft of management will shift from 32 years old to 22 years old, across the businesses of knowledge work.

In short: We need to bring back the “managing analyst.” We need to recognize that AI agents behave like knowledge workers and therefore need to be managed. We should reset the culture in knowledge work industries that management is a valued skill, beginning at the start of one’s career and not midcareer.

These entry-level workers are smart, motivated, learn quickly and work hard. There is a huge unmet need for the craft of management in corralling this new generation of AI agents. We have the proof points across nearly 200 years from our service academies that these skills can be taught to the young, and the young can deliver them with distinction. The future for college graduates is a redefinition of their jobs away from being individual-contributor knowledge workers and toward being effective managers and leaders from the very beginning of their careers.

Bob Morse co-founded Strattam Capital in 2014 and is managing partner. He has served on numerous private and public technology company boards, and currently is a director of CloudHesive, Contegix, Daxtra Technologies, Green Security, Resource Navigation and Trax Group. Previously, he was a partner and member of the investment committee at Oak Hill Capital Partners. He also worked at GCC Investments and Morgan Stanley. Morse serves on the board of directors of Austin PBS and as member of the advisory board for the HMTF Center for Private Equity Finance at The University of Texas at Austin McCombs School of Business. He attended Princeton University, graduating summa cum laude with a BSE, and Stanford Graduate School of Business, where he earned his MBA and was an Arjay Miller Scholar. Morse lives in Austin.

Michael Quoia is co-founder and partner at KSE Leadership, which assesses and develops leaders and teams. A 25-year leadership advisory veteran with partner-level roles at Heidrick & Struggles and Russell Reynolds Associates, he began his career as a U.S. Navy  surface warfare officer. He is a graduate of the U.S. Naval Academy and holds an MBA from the Stanford Graduate School of Business.

The Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) will connect its tokenization service to Solana (SOL) in the second half of 2027, the company said on Nov. 12.

The integration will allow "digital twins" of Russell 1000 stocks, major ETFs and U.S. Treasuries to be issued on the Solana blockchain. In December 2025, the SEC issued a no-action letter that allowed DTC to tokenize these assets.

In 2025, DTCC processed $4.7 quadrillion in securities transactions. Its depository, DTC, holds and services $114 trillion in assets from more than 150 countries.

The DTCC Tokenization Service (DTS) will let large market participants convert conventional securities into tokens, move them across the Solana network and redeem them.

"DTC-tokenized assets made available on Solana – and all blockchain networks integrated with the service – will retain the same investor protections, ownership rights and regulatory safeguards that apply to traditionally held securities," said Brian Steele, president of DTCC Clearing & Securities Services.

According to DTCC CEO Frank La Salla, the integration will also free up securities for use as collateral.

DTS went live on Oct. 28, 2026. At launch, it worked with Canton Network and a private ledger. DTCC said that it adds new networks at clients' request.

"DTCC is committed to providing an open and connected platform that provides our users with access to mature distributed ledger technology networks like Solana that have established performance, security and governance features," said Nadine Chakar, global head of DTCC Digital Assets.

Nick Ducoff, general manager for institutional at the Solana Foundation, also commented on the news. "Institutions choose Solana because it already runs real financial activity at scale," he said.

According to Ducoff, the integration "connects one of the most trusted names in post-trade infrastructure with a network built for always-on markets."

As of Nov. 12, distributed real-world assets (RWA) in the Solana ecosystem reached $5.13 billion across more than 1.02 million holders, according to RWA.xyz. Transfers over the past 30 days totaled $16.48 billion.

The stablecoin market cap on Solana stands at $13.85 billion, with monthly turnover of $387.41 billion.

#5257. PwC’s IPO Lead On A Selective Market, AI Valuations And The Outlook For 2027

The U.S. IPO market has rebounded, but the recovery remains uneven. Companies seeking to go public face investors focused on durable revenue, profitability and valuation, while uncertainty has prompted some issuers to postpone their offerings.

Mike Bellin, a partner and U.S. IPO services leader at PricewaterhouseCoopers, sees a market that remains open to companies with the right scale, financial metrics and preparation.

In a recent conversation with Crunchbase News, Bellin discussed the slowdown in IPO momentum, how public investors are evaluating AI companies, biotech’s resurgence and why SPACs are attracting renewed interest. He also outlined what could set the stage for a stronger start to 2027.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Crunchbase News: How healthy is the IPO market right now?

Bellin: A good IPO year in the U.S. is anywhere from 125 to 175 traditional IPOs, and year to date we’ve seen just south of 90 or so.

The breadth of the market shows me that it’s been a healthy market. We’ve seen industrial products come back to market. We’ve seen tech, consumer markets, energy, utilities and some financial services come back to market.

For the majority of the first three quarters of the year, it was a pretty strong and broad IPO market. But the momentum has halted significantly since September and October.

Is the market in trouble? I would say no. It’s very selective. It’s not shut. Quality issuers with readiness, the right story, the right metrics can still get their deals done.

Bellin: The macro environment in general was the big mover: rates, inflation, geopolitical concerns. Just that uncertainty was a big factor.

One of the big factors that I’ve seen is valuation. Some fairly aggressive valuations were being asked for in certain transactions, certain offerings, and I think the market — with all those uncertainties that I mentioned — was looking at those valuations and thinking it was maybe a bit rich.

I believe many issuers decided to hit pause and wait for another window to open.

What are public market investors looking for?

Bellin: What investors are really looking for is durable revenue — revenue that’s backed up by strong customers, diverse customers and a growing revenue base. I think it’s that revenue reliability where there is a significant backlog of demand for the product, the services of the IPO issuer. That’s always a strong sign.

The other item is leverage. For companies with significant leverage in a rising-rate environment, the questions are: Can they take on new leverage that creates profitable value opportunities going forward? Can they refinance existing leverage given rates are higher?

Making sure that you’re going into the capital markets with a reasonable leverage ratio, or explaining through your equity story how you’re getting a return on the capital that you have invested from a debt perspective, makes a significant difference.

Is the market open to a broad range of venture-backed startups, or primarily larger companies?

Bellin: Scale matters. Companies that have that scale, whether it’s from a revenue perspective or an asset-based perspective, depending on the sector, make a big difference. Those are the types of companies that can almost dictate the window that they’re going to go out in and do well.

Some of the smaller companies, the midmarket companies, smaller-cap companies — again, outside of life science and biotechs — they’ve been a little bit challenged.

If you’re growing at the right rate, you’re showing the right metrics, the IPO market is fully available to those types of companies. But if you’re still on the lower-scale side of the house, your opportunities may be limited to hit the market.

Will enthusiasm for AI companies carry into public markets, or will investors be more skeptical?

Bellin: I think investors aren’t skeptical of AI; they’re skeptical of spend without visibility — visibility to future earnings, visibility to that revenue durability that I mentioned.

The market is separating AI companies with visible demand from the ones with only a narrative out there, and I think that demand, that growth, the backlog is key.

The other factor we’re seeing in today’s market again comes down to cash generation and profitability. If you’re not profitable, when will that profitable period come? Profitability comes in many different measures. Could be GAAP income, could be EBITDA income, but also cash flows and free cash flows and levered free cash flows that are available to the company.

We haven’t seen a period like this of development, of growth, ever before. It’s exciting, but I do think the market will discern between those companies that are public-company worthy and those that are not.

What does the uneven performance of newly public companies signal?

Bellin: It signals selectivity. There have been some really big winners in the IPO market, and others that, post-issuance, haven’t traded as well as many expected.

Many of the companies that are coming to market have to be very thoughtful on the valuation and what you’re going to go price at. If you’re trying to be too aggressive on pricing, you may trade down post-IPO, which is going to impact those metrics.

Overall, we’re seeing strong candidates come to market. I do think companies are coming to market better prepared now than ever, given this volatility.

Bellin: The M&A market for many of these companies is very strong today. As some of the larger health company names lose the patents to some of the profitable drugs, they’re looking at that next generation of development and where there could be value.

Many of these biotechs were purchased by large pharma companies even before coming to the public markets. That competition for these assets and companies is creating a nice horse trade between an IPO opportunity with a lot of upside and an M&A exit with more certainty day one.

I think M&A is the engine behind the IPO market’s resurgence for these companies.

In the IPO markets, many of these assets have traded very well, and that’s where the momentum and that flywheel effect in the IPO market is very important. We’ve seen that flywheel and that momentum in biotech. We haven’t seen it in the rest of the market in the last couple of months.

Why are SPACs attracting renewed interest?

Bellin: With market volatility, we’re seeing more conversations around SPACs. Because SPACs set valuation certainty on day one, a company looking to exit via SPAC understands the potential cash that may come their way. It’s not certain, of course, given redemptions, etc.

Another factor driving a healthy SPAC market may be these serial SPAC issuers. They understand the SPAC product. They understand what makes a good de-SPAC candidate, and they know whether the target company can be ready, show growth and hit the milestones that may be discussed in the offering document.

The market is healthier and more mature today than in the past. That said, we’re still seeing many SPACs continue to look for a target, given the massive SPAC inventory available to target companies.

Bellin: Hundreds of companies are in the pipeline, and they’re ready to go when the market is. Much of the remainder of ’26, and the start of 2027, depends on market momentum.

I’m an eternal optimist. There’s a lot of demand on the buy side; there’s still significant capital available to the right companies. So if we can create that momentum here in the remaining months of 2026, I think we’re going to see a strong start to 2027.

The AI ecosystem that we’ve been talking about is healthy. Demand for energy is always significant, and the right energy companies are coming to market. Consumer and industrial products — those are coming back.

Private equity has been very active in ’26, and I’d expect them to continue that activity in 2027.

I think we’re in for a strong year, but it will remain selective.

#5256. Hyperliquid Burns $1.53 Million in HYPE Tokens in 24 Hours Amid Price Dip

The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. Decentralized exchange Hyperliquid has bought back and burned 21,200 HYPE over the past 24 hours, spending $1.53 million on the purchase at an average price of $72.31, according to Onchain Lens.

The on-chain analytics platform also reported that Hyperliquid has permanently removed a total of 50.47 million HYPE from circulation since the launch of the token. That is 5.05% of the max supply of 1 billion HYPE, and at the current price, the burned tokens are worth around $3.51 billion.

The latest buyback comes amid the decline in the price of the cryptocurrency. On Nov. 12, the price of HYPE went down by 3.45%, and at press time, the token stands at $69.52, according to TradingView. Earlier this autumn, the price of HYPE was above $90.

Hyperliquid pays for the buybacks in dollars, so the decentralized exchange is able to buy more HYPE with the same amount of money when the price of the token goes down.

DeFiLlama data shows that Hyperliquid has earned $1.41 billion for HYPE holders since December 2024. Over the past 30 days, the decentralized exchange earned $68.82 million, and its earnings for the past week stand at $15.04 million.

Over the last day, the platform collected about $1.46 million in fees, slightly less than the amount it spent on the buyback. Besides, DeFiLlama data shows that Hyperliquid currently earns more in fees than Ethereum, Tron and Base.

The largest part of the burned tokens, 48.85 million HYPE, was bought back by the Assistance Fund. The fund automatically receives between 97% and 99% of the fees from perpetual and spot trading on Hyperliquid, and the rest of the fees go to the HLP liquidity pool and to the builders of individual markets.

The Assistance Fund buys HYPE on the open market and sends the tokens to the "0xfefe...fefe" address. It is a system address that does not have a private key. In December 2025, Hyperliquid validators formally recognized the tokens held at this address as burned.

In August 2026, Hyperliquid also introduced the AQAv2 upgrade. Under the upgrade, around 90% of the yield generated by the USDC reserves on the platform now goes to the Assistance Fund. Each of these transfers brings between $14 million and $16 million to the fund.

Besides the Assistance Fund, HYPE is also burned through network fees. Around 1.24 million HYPE has been burned through fees and slashing on HyperCore, the base layer of Hyperliquid. Another 376,060 HYPE has been burned as gas fees on HyperEVM, the smart contract layer of the network.

#5255. MSCI Drops Saylor's Strategy From Its Index Amid BTC Sell-Off

MSCI has published the results of its November 2026 Index Review, with Strategy among the companies set to leave the MSCI USA Index.

Metaplanet, the Tokyo-listed Bitcoin treasury company, is also scheduled for removal from the MSCI Japan Small Cap Index.

The changes will take effect after the market close on November 30, 2026.

Across the MSCI ACWI Index, 13 securities will be added and 100 deleted. The two additions to the MSCI World Index, measured by full company market capitalization, are Moderna (USA) and Aritzia (Canada).

The latest review follows the new rules proposed by MSCI in October, among which are new measures regarding crypto treasury holding companies.

MSCI evaluates whether a company maintains substantial operating assets and applies five financial ratio tests.

A company that fails at least four criteria across consecutive annual reporting periods may face removal from the MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes.

MSCI indexes track public companies based on market cap and investment risks. Global mutual funds and ETFs use these benchmarks to build their portfolios.

Dropping out of such index could influence investment flows as well as stock prices.

Strategy continues to accumulate BTC despite the crypto market staying in red zone.

Between November 2 and November 8, 2026, the company acquired another 1,036 BTC at an average price of $79,012.

As of November 12, Strategy holds 850,364 BTC. The company also reported about $5.5 billion in USD reserves.

However, Bitcoin's recent decline below $75,000 pushes Strategy's holdings into an unrealized loss of $500 million.

Strategy's stock (MSTR) fell 7% on Thursday, while Bitcoin is down 3.5% at the time of writing.

#5254. Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path shows how far the probing went.

One token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

Loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, says user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

The loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction shows a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

An independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

The numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

That arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

The harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

That detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

Loopscale's November 6 update named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale says its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

So the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team says it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

Loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

The two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

The loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

The takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

Vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

This looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem shows pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

#5253. The Money Cleared The Bank. Now The Founder Is The Risk.

The round closes. The announcement goes out. For about a week, everyone is happy. Then the pressure doubles.

The number that used to be a hope is now a promise. The board that used to be patient now has a timeline. And the founder who just finished the hardest sales job of their life is expected to make the best decisions of their life, immediately, on less sleep than they’ve had in months.

I’ve spent 17 years coaching about 1,500 leaders, including venture-backed founders. The pattern repeats often enough that I treat the first 90 days after a raise as a danger window.

Founders don’t get complacent in that window. They get flooded, and most of them won’t say so out loud.

Neuroscientist Amy Arnsten’s review in Nature Reviews Neuroscience puts it plainly: “even quite mild acute uncontrollable stress can cause a rapid and dramatic loss of prefrontal cognitive abilities.” The prefrontal cortex weighs options and holds a plan steady.

Notice the word uncontrollable. After a raise, a founder controls less than the cap table suggests: the hiring market, customer timelines, the board’s expectations. The founder hasn’t become less intelligent. The judgment that built the company is just harder to reach.

Porcelli and Delgado, writing in Psychological Science, stressed volunteers with a hand in ice water then offered them financial gambles. They grew more cautious about potential gains and more willing to gamble on potential losses. It was a lab study, but I see the same shape in a founder six weeks after a Series B: hesitant about the bets that justified the round, and suddenly willing to roll the dice on anything that feels like a threat.

The decisions that go wrong in this window rarely feel reckless. They feel rational, because the nervous system is treating uncertainty like an emergency.

Senior hiring. An investor who advises 20 fast-growing technology startups told me one of the biggest sources of leadership friction he sees is a CEO hiring a head of sales because they know the person. The relationship feels safe, so the offer is generous. Then the results don’t come. Under pressure, familiarity feels like certainty. But knowing someone isn’t the same as knowing they can lead sales at the company’s next stage.

Expansion. Pressure condenses time. The new market planned for month 12 moves to month three. The data didn’t change. Waiting became unbearable. One founder I coached pulled a 12-month expansion into three, bragged about how little sleep he was getting, and did everything himself. The second-market launch was a sloppy, drama-filled disaster. The board brought me in to put him back together and triage the launch. Ask whether the evidence changed or your tolerance for uncertainty did.

Co-founder relationships. Harvard Business School professor Noam Wasserman, who studied 10,000 founders for “The Founder’s Dilemmas,” has put the share of high-potential startups that fail because of co-founder conflict at 65%. One founder withdraws because they’re overwhelmed. The other interprets the silence as distrust. A trauma-informed lens doesn’t treat every disagreement as trauma. It builds enough trust that a disagreement doesn’t become one more emergency.

If you sit on the board, the week the wire clears is when you start paying attention. Composure can mean steadiness. It can also hide exhaustion.

The founders who come through this window well tend to have one person outside the cap table, the org chart and the family they can think out loud with before a decision hardens. Investor Matt Cohen has written here that founders often have no one inside their company to confide in. Founders, who is that person for you right now? If you can’t name one, that’s useful information too.

The capital is in the account. The open question is whether the person deciding how to spend it can still reach the judgment that raised it. Find that out before the first big decision, not after.

Executive coach Kelly Meerbott is principal of YOU – Loud & Clear. Her performance coaching is trauma-informed, neuroscience-backed and somatic. For more than 17 years she has coached roughly 1,500 leaders, including venture-backed founders, Fortune 500 executives, and more than 500 senior military leaders. She was named Top Coach in America in 2025, is a TEDx speaker, and has written for Fast Company, Training Magazine and Hotel Executive. She is based in Narberth, Pennsylvania, and holds Professional Certified Coach and Certified Clinical Trauma Specialist certifications.

Democrats’ historic victories in this week’s U.S. midterm elections could also transform the tech industry.

The public voted on 41 data center-related ballot measures on Tuesday — in all but one, the majority voted to impose more restrictions on data center development. And even when data centers weren’t on the ballot directly, they were a major talking point, with newly-elected Democratic governors and congressmembers likely to support additional regulation.

#5251. XRP, SHIB, BTC and Other Tokens Hit Hard by Abrupt Resignation of Nvidia CEO

Top digital assets like Bitcoin (BTC), XRP, Ethereum (ETH) and Shiba Inu (SHIB) are facing heavy selling pressure following a severe setback in the crypto market after the sudden exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

The unexpected exit of the Nvidia co-founder has created pandemonium in the financial world as shares of the artificial intelligence company have been hit by a heavy sell-off, further straining an already weak crypto market.

According to reports by Reuters, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Nov. 12. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has taken over as interim chief executive.

There are controversies surrounding Huang's personal life and doubts about his future at the company he co-founded over three decades ago.

The news of Huang's exit has triggered a heavy sell-off in Nvidia stock, with shares dropping over 12% in early trading, wiping out an estimated $500 billion in market value.

The sell-off has also affected crypto-related trading markets.

As recently revealed by blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain, a trader known as 0x7368 had his leveraged long position in Nvidia stock fully liquidated.

According to Lookonchain, the trader had 9,959 units of Nvidia (NVDA), worth about $1.54 million, liquidated after news of Jensen Huang's resignation hit the market.

Meanwhile, the crypto market itself is reeling from heavy losses as some top altcoins are faring worse than Bitcoin.

The recent crypto market data shows that Bitcoin (BTC) is currently trading around $71,323, shedding about 3% in the last 24 hours.

Over the last seven days, the largest cryptocurrency by market cap has lost even more, shedding about 10.2%.

#5250. Hackers Hijack 178 Major Websites, Including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, and Ledger

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Hackers have turned some of the world’s most recognizable websites into potential crypto theft traps after compromising a third-party platform used by 178 major organizations. The attack injected malicious JavaScript through Optimizely, a website experimentation platform trusted by companies including BBC, Zoom, CNN, HSBC, Salesforce, IKEA, and crypto hardware wallet maker Ledger.

Visitors could unknowingly load malware simply by opening an affected webpage, and the consequences go far beyond stolen browsing data. The malicious code can replace crypto wallet addresses copied to the clipboard, redirecting payments straight into attackers’ wallets. Security researchers have already identified $7,040 in crypto received by wallets linked to the campaign.

🚨 BREAKING: Ledger and 177 other major organizations, including Zoom, CNN, and Salesforce, were affected by a massive JavaScript attack.The malware stole cryptocurrency, payment card details, and user data, while also targeting iPhones with exploit kits.

The investigation by cybersecurity firm Report URI identified 188 infected JavaScript snippets belonging to 178 organizations after examining 1,611 Optimizely scripts. The malware operated through trusted website infrastructure, making the attack particularly dangerous. Rather than breaking into every company’s servers individually, attackers injected malicious code into Optimizely customer projects.

Affected websites continued loading JavaScript through Optimizely’s legitimate content delivery network. Visitors had little reason to suspect that a familiar website was serving malicious instructions. This is a dangerous clipboard hijacking mechanism.

The malware searched webpages for crypto wallet addresses and replaced legitimate destinations with addresses controlled by attackers. It could also intercept copied addresses, meaning someone browsing an affected website could potentially paste a fraudulent wallet address elsewhere.

The attack targeted several major crypto networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, TRON, and Litecoin.

A victim could believe they were sending funds to an exchange, another wallet, or a friend. Instead, the transaction could land directly in an attacker’s wallet.

Report URI identified $7,040 in receipts across attacker-controlled wallets by November 16. The funds included Bitcoin, Litecoin, Ethereum, TRON, and stablecoins.

The scale of the incident raises questions about how much trust businesses place in third-party website services. The affected organizations span several industries, including banking, technology, media, retail, and crypto.

HSBC was among the financial institutions affected, alongside Equifax and other major organizations. BBC, CNN, Fox News, Zoom, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, and Air France-KLM also appeared in Report URI’s investigation.

Ledger’s inclusion makes the incident particularly concerning for crypto users. The company is known for its hardware wallets, which help customers store private keys away from internet-connected devices. However, the incident demonstrates how threats can reach users through ordinary browsing activity, outside the hardware wallet itself.

The malicious campaign also contained capabilities targeting Apple devices. Researchers identified exploit infrastructure associated with Coruna and DarkSword, two iOS exploit kits designed to target vulnerabilities in iPhones and iPads.

This means the operation was not limited to stealing crypto or payment information. It also carried tools capable of targeting mobile devices through malicious webpage content.

Optimizely confirmed that attackers exploited a vulnerability in its Experimentation account signup flow to inject malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The company said it blocked access to the vulnerable pathway, deployed a fix, removed injected code, revoked active tokens, and reset access for affected accounts.

Earlier today, Optimizely identified and contained a security incident affecting some Optimizely Web Experimentation customers. The vulnerable path is blocked, the injected code was removed, and customers have been contacted directly. Updates: https://t.co/ptZHZviIeC

However, the incident raises serious questions about third-party website security. Report URI’s investigation found that even Optimizely’s own websites carried the malicious code. Researchers also observed the attacker rebuilding the malware 26 times during the campaign, adding capabilities and additional cryptocurrency wallets.

Most infected snippets were subsequently cleaned up, with Report URI finding only one remaining infected snippet in its final November 16 sweep.

But the financial damage and potential exposure remain difficult to measure. Researchers have identified crypto receipts, but the number of affected visitors, compromised payment cards, and exposed browser sessions remains unknown.

The bigger problem is that website visitors rarely know which third-party scripts are running behind the pages they trust. A familiar banking website, news outlet, or crypto platform can become an unexpected entry point for malicious code without its visitors noticing anything unusual.

Yoshitaka Kitao, head of Japanese financial group SBI Holdings, answered "YES" when asked point-blank whether he still trusts XRP.

Kitao answered in English. Most of his recent posts on X are in Japanese, and the rest of them are reposts of other accounts.

Kitao previously worked as an executive at Nomura Securities and later served as CFO of SoftBank. In 1999, he founded SoftBank Investment, which later became SBI Holdings. Today, SBI includes banks, brokerage, and insurance businesses, as well as crypto services.

The partnership began in 2016. SBI joined Ripple's Series B round and launched a joint venture with Ripple, SBI Ripple Asia. SBI owns about 60% of the venture, and Ripple owns the remaining 40%.

The same year, SBI Ripple Asia set up a consortium of Japanese banks to test Ripple's technology for payments, and the consortium later grew to more than 60 banks.

In 2018, SBI launched the interbank app MoneyTap. The same year, SBI's crypto exchange, now called SBI VC Trade, started operations with XRP trading. In 2019, Kitao joined Ripple's board of directors.

From 2020, SBI began handing the token out to shareholders as bonuses, and the payment service SBI Remit launched remittances using it with on-demand liquidity (ODL), including in the major Japan-Philippines corridor.

SBI kept working with Ripple during the SEC lawsuit against the company, which lasted from December 2020 until 2025.

Back on February 15, 2026, in rare long-form tweets in English, Kitao denied rumors that SBI holds $10 billion worth of XRP: "Not $10 billion in XRP, but around 9% of Ripple Labs. So our hidden asset could be much bigger." By his account, the combined valuation of Ripple Labs and its ecosystem is "enormous," and SBI owns more than 9% of all of it.

Kitao also talked about XRP at SBI's quarterly briefing on November 2, 2026. He said that investors buy Bitcoin mostly to hold it, and that the value of XRP depends on its use in payments and business ecosystems.

In August 2025, SBI VC Trade and Ripple agreed to bring the RLUSD stablecoin to Japan. In October 2025, SBI also invested $200 million in Evernorth, a company that holds XRP in its treasury. By now, SBI VC Trade has more than two million accounts.

#5247. Genesis AI Raises $500M At $3.5B Valuation To Bring Its Robots To Factories And Warehouses

Genesis AI, a startup teaching robots to perform physical tasks by learning from human movements, announced Tuesday it has raised $500 million in Series A funding at a $3.5 billion valuation.

Premji Invest, Khosla Ventures and Eclipse co-led the round, which brings the company’s disclosed funding to $605 million since its 2024 inception. Genesis previously raised $105 million in a round announced in July 2025.

The company is developing both robots and the AI software that controls them. Its approach combines recordings of human hand movements with training in simulated environments, where robots can practice skills before attempting them in the physical world.

Genesis is initially targeting manufacturing, logistics and laboratories with its robot, Eno.

“We just want to bring something more elegant, more timeless,” co-founder and CEO Zhou Xian told Crunchbase News in an interview. “In the end, this is a very full-stack company. … We have to build all different pieces across the entire stack to make sure we can tightly integrate our technology stack together, and hopefully build the most well-polished and reliable product.

Other participants in the new financing include T. Rowe Price Associates, Durable Capital Partners, Bpifrance, HSG, Nvidia, AMD Ventures, Zoom, Samsung Next and Ericsson. Individual backers include Eric Schmidt, Eric Yuan, Jerry Yang, Xavier Niel and Zach Kirkhorn.

The company plans to use the capital to expand its computing infrastructure, increase robot production and hire more employees, Xian told Crunchbase News. Presently, Genesis has close to 100 employees. It is headquartered in Paris, with offices in San Carlos, California.

Venture funding to robotics startups has soared in 2026, with most of the investment going to companies based in China and the U.S., Crunchbase data shows. All told, global venture funding to robotics startups totaled $9.9 billion in Q3, more than double the $4.3 billion invested in Q3 2025, per Crunchbase data.

The closely related field of physical AI has also seen a surge in venture investment this year.

Genesis’s approach grew out of a challenge Xian encountered during his robotics research: The difficulty of finding enough examples for robots to learn from.

Language models have vast amounts of text to draw on. But robots need a different kind of data to learn how to move and for example, pick up and handle objects. They also need that data to better understand what they’re touching and what happens when they act.

Genesis works by using cameras and gloves to capture people’s hand and finger movements as they work, along with touch information. The company says its robotic hand closely matches the human hand and recording glove, making it easier for robots to learn those movements. Historically, collecting this kind of training data involves hiring people to remotely control robots, Xian said. Genesis aims to collect it from people doing their regular jobs instead.

Those recordings help train the company’s AI model, GENE. Genesis also uses its simulation software, Genesis World, to train and test robot skills in virtual environments. The company claims this speeds up a process that would take longer with physical machines alone.

Genesis traces its origins to a research collaboration Xian started in 2022, also named Genesis, while he was pursuing a robotics Ph.D. at Carnegie Mellon University. The project brought together researchers from more than a dozen universities to develop robotics simulation tools.

After graduating at the end of 2024, Xian teamed up with Theophile Gervet and decided to start a company. Genesis formally launched in March 2025 and expanded beyond simulation into AI software and robot hardware.

Xian said developing those components together would help Genesis make them work reliably as a finished product.

“That requires the intelligence, hardware and everything that goes into training and testing the robots to work as one system,” he said.

Genesis is exploring a rental model in which customers would pay for the robot and its software as a combined service. It has announced a partnership with LG CNS and has other Fortune 500 companies in its prospective customer pipeline, according to Xian. He declined to disclose revenue and did not provide a paying customer count.

Premji Invest partner Vedant Agrawal said in a release that the firm was drawn to demonstrations of robots completing extended tasks independently.

“Completing full tasks in real time, not just short clips, is what turns a robot into something a business can rely on,” he said.

Genesis says it is ramping up Eno production for industrial customers. Looking ahead, it plans to expand into hospitality and healthcare, then consumer and outdoor uses.

#5246. After challenging Google’s Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era

Almost a decade after Cyanogen shut down its Android operating-system business following a years-long, unsuccessful effort to loosen Google’s dominance, its co-founder, Kirt McMaster, is now targeting Microsoft’s Windows with a new operating system designed for people who rely heavily on artificial intelligence in their everyday work.

McMaster’s company, Kora Systems, on Tuesday unveiled a Linux-based desktop operating system that integrates AI models and autonomous agents directly into the computing experience, allowing them to work across applications, access files, and retain context between tasks. The software is expected to launch in 2027 as a free-to-use desktop operating system, with support for existing Intel- and AMD-powered PCs as well as machines running Qualcomm’s Snapdragon chips.

Kora is developing the eponymous operating system with a team of about 50 engineers, relying on AI coding tools, including OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude. McMaster told TechCrunch that these tools have accelerated development by at least fivefold, with most of the gains coming over the past six months.

Microsoft has long dominated the PC operating-system market, making it hard for newer players to establish a foothold. Windows held about 77% of the worldwide desktop operating-system market in October, compared with nearly 10% for Apple’s OS X, according to Statcounter’s web traffic data.

However, McMaster believes Kora does not need to compete for Windows’ entire user base. Rather, he is targeting people who use AI extensively and are willing to pay for access to powerful models and services.

“Microsoft can keep its billion users,” McMaster said, estimating that 45 million to 50 million people currently account for much of AI usage and revenue. He expects that market to exceed 200 million users by 2033.

McMaster told TechCrunch that his experience at Cyanogen, where he spent over five years, taught him the dangers of relying on the very company he was trying to challenge. Cyanogen remained heavily dependent on Google Mobile Services despite offering features beyond Google’s version of Android. That ultimately restricted its ability to build an independent ecosystem.

“If you are trying to compete with an incumbent but are still reliant on them, you have no chance,” he said.

Kora, McMaster said, builds on an idea he pursued toward the end of his time at Cyanogen, when he began exploring ways to integrate third-party services directly into the operating system. With Kora, he wants AI models and agents to work across applications and access files without being confined to individual apps.

Previously known as Playtron, a gaming operating-system company led by McMaster, the Palo Alto-based company rebranded as Kora in July 2025 as it shifted its focus to AI. The decision came as early companies, including Perplexity and OpenAI, were moving into AI-powered web browsers, McMaster said. He believed browsers would not give AI agents enough access to a computer to carry out more complex tasks, making an operating system a better starting point.

The shift also allowed Kora to build on nearly three years of work developing Playtron’s Linux-based gaming operating system, called GameOS, instead of starting from scratch.

Kora is designed to let users work with different AI models and agents across applications, while keeping track of conversations, documents, and other information. It also allows AI agents to operate in separate workspaces with restricted access to files and other resources.

While McMaster has drawn on his experience at Cyanogen, none of Kora’s engineers worked there. Instead, the company recruited heavily from the Linux gaming community, he told TechCrunch.

Kora’s software is built on Linux and uses Nix. It replaces the Fedora Silverblue foundation of Playtron’s earlier GameOS.

While Linux and Nix are open source, McMaster said Kora’s own technology, including its Cortex AI engine and desktop interface, remains proprietary. The company, he said, intends to support AI models and services from different providers, although it has not committed to making its own software open source.

Gaming also remains part of Kora’s plans. McMaster said the company intends to introduce AI-powered tools that would allow developers to create, publish, and play games directly within the operating system. He added that support for Android apps is also on its roadmap.

McMaster told TechCrunch that Kora’s team has worked closely with Qualcomm’s engineers for nearly a year to optimize the operating system specifically for Snapdragon-powered PCs. The collaboration includes support for Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite chips.

Alongside Qualcomm, Kora is working with Saudi Arabia’s AI company Humain on an enterprise version of the operating system, called Humain OS, which is expected to run on Snapdragon-powered laptops in 2027. Kora also plans to announce partnerships with PC manufacturers at a later date, though McMaster did not identify any companies or provide a specific timeline.

Kora plans to generate revenue through subscriptions that bundle access to AI models and agentic services. Moreover, its Cortex engine is designed to run AI tasks locally when possible and use cloud-based models for work requiring more computing power.

Kora’s investors include Samsung Next, Square Enix, Alumni Ventures, Polychain, VanEck, and Circle, all of which previously backed Playtron. The company, McMaster said, has raised additional funding since shifting its focus to AI. However, he declined to disclose the total amount raised or its valuation. Kora has enough funding to operate for several years, he said.
